#3153. iPhone Duo vs. Galaxy Z Fold 8 Camera Comparison: Frolicking With Apple’s and Samsung’s Foldables

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

I snapped some photos in a dreamy garden with these passport-size phones to see how their rear cameras stack up.

There are a handful of things Apple’s iPhone Duo and Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 have in common. They both feature a passport-size design, two rear cameras and roughly the same battery capacity. They’re also two of my favorite phones I’ve reviewed this year.

The compact, book-style configuration feels like the future of foldables, and Apple and Samsung have each nailed their offerings. Both phones are incredibly versatile, giving you the option to quickly swipe through apps on the palm-sized cover display or open up to a more sprawling 7.6-inch inner screen that’s great for watching videos and multitasking. That innovation comes at a cost, though, with the Duo starting at $1,999 for 256GB and the Z Fold 8 starting at $1,900 for the same storage level.

There are some drawbacks to having a more compact design, namely when it comes to the rear cameras. There’s no telephoto camera on either phone, which can make the high price tags a little harder to swallow. Plus, the wide and ultra-wide cameras aren’t quite as capable as what you’ll get on premium non-folding phones such as the iPhone 18 Pro and Galaxy S26 Ultra, which have more advanced optical zoom capabilities and larger main-camera sensors.

Still, the iPhone Duo’s and Z Fold 8’s cameras are nothing to scoff at. The Duo has a 48-megapixel wide and 48-megapixel ultrawide camera, as well as a 12-megapixel selfie camera on the cover screen and a FaceTime camera on the inner display (Apple hasn’t shared the resolution). Meanwhile, the Z Fold 8 has a 50-megapixel wide and 50-megapixel ultrawide camera, plus 10-megapixel selfie cameras on the cover and inner displays. That means you should still get photos that impress, whether you’re in the brightly lit outdoors or in a dark, moody setting.

To compare the cameras, I took the iPhone Duo and Galaxy Z Fold 8 to Filoli, a historic house and garden in the San Francisco Bay Area. These are some of my favorite shots, highlighting the strengths and unique characteristics of each phone’s cameras.

Both phones do a great job depicting the vibrancy of the lush background, but the iPhone Duo has the edge here. It better preserves the detail in the stone bench and flooring, and the greenery takes on a deeper, more satisfying hue.

These photos turned out very similarly, and both are equally dazzling. But the Z Fold 8 image is slightly sharper, as seen in the lines on the tree bark and the brighter, more pigmented greenery and flora. So I’m giving this one to the Z Fold 8.

These portrait images highlight some of the key differences in color and tone between the iPhone Duo and Galaxy Z Fold 8. I prefer the richer blacks and more vibrant colors captured by the iPhone Duo. It also does a better job of keeping the raven in focus, allowing the bird to stand out more distinctly against the background and creating a more striking overall image. By comparison, the Z Fold 8 produces a softer, gentler look, with a more subdued overall tone.

I like the brightness of the iPhone Duo image, and while the Z Fold 8 shot has slightly deeper shadows, the hydrangeas are also more vibrant. The blues and greens pop more on the Z Fold 8, as does the sky, which is a little washed out on the Duo. So this one goes to the Z Fold 8.

I keep flipping on this one, but ultimately, the richer colors and texture on the Duo image have won me over. The iPhone’s camera tends to cast a warmer glow, as you can see in the stone benches, while the Z Fold 8 takes on a more neutral tone. In the end, the differences are subtle and a matter of personal preference.

And finally, here’s me unwinding with a book. By default, the iPhone Duo applies a pleasing background blur, which I appreciate for the added dramatic effect. (This effect can be disabled when taking a photo, but I rarely choose to do so.) The Z Fold 8, by comparison, keeps the distant lawns and forested hills in sharper focus, preserving those details remarkably well. Ultimately, I prefer the Duo’s approach, which keeps the book in sharper focus and makes it stand out from the background. That said, I do appreciate the Z Fold 8’s ability to capture finer details throughout the scene, particularly the crisp individual blades of grass.

Because I’m a fan of both the iPhone Duo and the Galaxy Z Fold 8, it’s difficult to wholeheartedly recommend one camera over the other. Each has its strengths, and there are moments where one preserves detail and color better than the other.

In general, photos from the iPhone Duo tend to have warmer tones and richer, deeper colors, which can also lead to more pronounced shadows. Meanwhile, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 often produces brighter images, though this can sometimes come at the expense of finer details. But these results can vary depending on factors such as lighting and angles.

Ultimately, both foldable phones deliver impressive results, and the choice comes down to which image characteristics you value most. Thankfully, you really can’t go wrong with either.

Another competitive model developed outside of China could change the open-weight landscape.

Thinking Machines Lab, a small AI startup from ex-OpenAI CTO Mira Murati, has released its latest model, Inkling 2 Small — and according to third-party tester Artificial Analysis, it’s set to give Chinese models a run for their lead. It’s technically proprietary until now, but Thinking Machines said it will release its weights next week.

Also: Open weights vs. closed: An AI civil war’s afoot

Chinese companies have led the pack on open models over the last few years. Models from DeepSeek and Moonshot regularly top leaderboards and rival the capabilities of much more expensive, closed models from OpenAI and Anthropic.

Since DeepSeek’s R1 performed similarly to OpenAI’s o1 in January 2025, Chinese open models have given investors and high-paying enterprise customers reasons to rethink their expensive contracts with US-based labs. Western labs creating more competitive open models changes the landscape.

Thinking Machines’ latest model has 594 billion parameters and supports image inputs but outputs only text. The company noted its web and game design capabilities and that it evaluated the model’s approach to coding problems alongside the code it generated during testing.

“The result is a model that is both stronger at coding and easier to use inside real agent loops,” the company said.

Also: Nvidia takes another step forward for US open-weight AI

Inkling 2 Small scored a 31 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, a composite test “for tracking progress toward artificial general intelligence” that combines benchmark scores spanning coding, science, and general categories. A score of 31 is above average for models in its class and is tied with Gemini 3.8 Flash. For context, Gemini 4 Carbon and Claude Opus 5.5 top the index at 60 and 59, respectively.

Thinking Machines said it will release the model’s weights next week, a practice that is becoming customary. Given the heightened security concerns around AI in general, AI companies spend a few weeks testing the to-be-open model with cybersecurity teams and safety reviewers before releasing the weights, rather than leading with the weights out of the gate.

French AI lab Mistral recently released its Le Chonk model via the same staggered process — it now keeps pace with OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Terra in coding abilities, which is rare for western-made open models.

Also: Mistral’s Le Chonk is now a top open model for coding

“[Thinking Machines’] plan to release its weights would make it the highest-scoring open weights model developed outside China based on current rankings,” Artificial Analysis said.

“Inkling 2 Small is amongst the leading models in intelligence and reasonably priced when comparing to other models of similar price. It’s also notably slow per task and very verbose,” Artificial Analysis said. The organization also called Inkling 2 Small’s pricing “somewhat expensive” at $0.30 per one million input tokens, since the median cost for its class is $0.24.

Still, the model’s progress over its predecessor stands out to Artificial Analysis reviewers: Inkling 2 Small jumped 41% in automation capabilities and 20% in coding abilities. However, most models excel in certain areas or on specific benchmarks, making it hard to deem one or another the outright best coding model overall.

Also: I tried replacing Claude Code with a local AI stack that’s completely free

Inkling 2 Small also made some gains in accuracy, Artificial Analysis said.

“On AA-Omniscience v1.1, the hallucination rate falls from Inkling Small’s 61% to 27%, while accuracy rises from 32% to 34% and the attempt rate falls from 77% to 53%,” its review reported.

#3151. Traders pile into 'bubble puts' on CoreWeave as neocloud stocks plunge

A key corner of the artificial intelligence trade is taking a beating on Wednesday and traders are betting it could get even worse.

Shares of neocloud companies – businesses that offer access to the GPUs powering artificial intelligence as a service – plunged Wednesday after debt yields for Nvidia-backed CoreWeave continued to reach new heights. (An article in The Financial Times that the company is targeting insurance companies for further debt financing apparently didn't help things either.)

Meanwhile, in a post on X, Social Capital founder Chamath Palihapitiya raised questions about a private credit bubble alongside a screengrab showing CoreWeave's bonds hitting a 15% yield. Elon Musk replied "yikes." CoreWeave stock plunged 15%. Nebius Group and Iren, popular trades connected to the data centers build-out, also fell as much as 10%.

Options volume in CoreWeave surged to more than seven times the 30-day average, Nebius almost four times, and Iren twice the normal volume. More calls traded than puts in Nebius and Iren, but in both, more calls were likely initiated by sellers than buyers, according to Cboe LiveVol data.

The most bearish action was in CoreWeave, where traders bought just shy of 200,000 puts, compared to 106,000 calls.

One standout trade happened around 10 a.m. ET when someone opened a new position of 26,000 37.5-strike puts expiring Dec. 18 that traded near the ask price, suggesting the puts were purchased, according to SpotGamma data.

"These are bubble puts," said Scott Bauer, CEO of Chicago-based Prosper Trading Academy. "These are not rip-ups that you buy thinking they'll go to zero. This is the hub, the center of the AI trade, and likely some kind of margin play for someone to hedge their exposure in highly correlated stocks or maybe even the Nasdaq."

The contracts sold for 74 cents apiece for a total of $1.9 million and need CoreWeave to erase another 42% over the next two months to pay off. Prior to this trade, there were just over 1,000 open contracts, meaning the position is a new one.

CoreWeave IPO'd in March 2025 at $40 per share.

"Maybe this is someone that was in early or in on the IPO saying this is my breakeven level," Bauer added. "Maybe they couldn't get this kind of protection in other stocks, the index, or other products."

#3147. Wendy’s Just Released a Video Game Where You Can Win Fast Food

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

I won a medium fries by defeating a sinister robot that looked suspiciously similar to a McDonald’s french fry container.

Wendy’s has turned its red-headed mascot into a wisecracking warrior who battles evil french fry robots in a free mobile game called WendyQuest. The company announced the retro-style role-playing game on Nov. 4. The announcement came with a promotion where you can win codes in the game, which are redeemable for menu items like fries and burgers at Wendy’s locations.

WendyQuest is available to download on iOS and Android. Desktop users can get it through the Steam platform. Anyone can play the game, but the promotion is restricted to people who are 18 and up living in the US.

You need to sign up for a Wendy’s account to redeem a code. While the food you can win is free, it requires you to buy something when you go.

“Wendy’s has been a part of gaming culture for years, including on Twitch, Fortnite and Feast of Legends, but WendyQuest is the brand’s first fully owned video game,” a spokesperson for Wendy’s said.

In 2019, Wendy’s partnered with the online multiplayer video game Fortnite, as well as the video-streaming platform Twitch, for various promotions featuring the company’s mascot. The company even released a rule book for a traditional tabletop roleplaying game the same year, called Feast of Legends, as a free download.

I downloaded WendyQuest, and my daughter and I played it for a while. The blocky graphics are reminiscent of the home-console video games of the late 1980s and early 1990s. It plays a lot like a simplified version of the DragonQuest, Final Fantasy and Breath of Fire games from the era, only stuffed with fast-food branding.

Rather than the regular turn-based battles that come standard in the early RPGs, this game adds a timing element, where you need to press a button at the right time like you do in old golfing video games.

It’s not a bad game. The light humor is suitable for younger players, and it’s fun to play. Like many RPGs, you battle monsters to gain levels, search around the maps for hidden areas, buy items and talk to people in towns to figure out what’s going on.

It took us over an hour to complete the first region, Fryshire, and get the Fry Stone, which unlocks a promo code for medium fries, free with a purchase. But again, you have to sign up for a Wendy’s account on their website or on the company’s mobile app.

Video games have a long history of offering real-world prizes to players as promotions. Swordquest, a series of video games released in the early 1980s for the Atari 2600, famously held a contest where players tried to win actual treasure made of gold and jewels.

In 2015, a promotion for the video game Just Cause 3 offered players the chance to win a private island. Developer Square Enix clarified that it couldn’t guarantee that the island would be livable and that the winner would have to pay all the taxes involved.

The reward codes from WendyQuest expire seven days after you get them, and Wendy’s says the codes are first come, first served.

#3146. Alpine Linux and OpenSSH patch flaw that’s as bad as it can get

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

This dangerous Linux security hole must be patched as soon as possible.

The perfect nightmare scenario for a Linux server is when all an attacker needs to do is reach the server’s Secure Shell (SSH) port, waltz right in, and take it over. That’s what happened to Alpine Linux, the popular, lightweight Linux server. Adding insult to injury, this happened only days after Alpine Linux dodged a security hole-sized bullet to its GitLab implementation.

Also: Linux Mint 27 arrives next month, and I like it already: What to expect

How bad is it? As bad as it can get. Alpine Linux explained in its security advisory that if an attacker can reach a vulnerable server’s SSH port, they can get in “with one connection,” and the attack “works every time, and needs no retries.”

As security engineer Gregory Bryant explained in his LinkedIn post:

Most authentication bypasses come from complex logic chains, but yesterday’s Alpine Linux OpenSSH vulnerability (CVE-2026-123158) comes down to a single character: *.”

If you run Alpine Linux (or another musl-based distro) with the default openssh-server package (no Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM)) and PasswordAuthentication enabled, an attacker can log into password-disabled, or key-only accounts simply by sending a password between 257 and 1024 bytes long.

Alpine Linux isn’t the only operating system that uses musl, a lightweight version of the standard C library (libc). Other operating systems that use musl and are potentially vulnerable include Adélie Linux; Void Linux; Sabotage Linux; OpenWrt, an Android variant,  and the Yocto Project, which is used to build embedded Linux distributions.

Also: This clever banking scam keeps phishing by faking its own demise

Wind River, which produces the commercial embedded Linux distro, Wind River Linux, is also looking into the issue. A company representative told me, “Wind River takes security seriously. We are actively reviewing the reported vulnerability and assessing its potential impact. We will take appropriate action as needed.”

Behind the scenes, when OpenSSH is built without PAM, it verifies passwords by hashing the password attempt using the C library’s crypt() function. It then compares the result to the account’s stored password field. So far, so good.

But when a key is longer than 256 bytes, musl’s crypt() function returns the string * as an error indicator. That is also what the password field holds for any account with no password, such as a key-only account. Thus, the “hash” matches and the login succeeds, and the attacker walks in.

Also: The new Cutefish Linux distro might be the best MacOS clone around

To exploit it, an attacker only needs the name of such an account. The attacker also needs at least one other account on the machine with a 5 or 6 password hash, and then to send a password of 257 to 1,024 bytes. According to Alpine, one user with a password is enough to make every passwordless account accessible.

In Linux systems that use glibc’s crypt(), which is almost all of them, the same attempt would return NULL on error, which sshd already rejects, so Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora, etc., aren’t affected.

According to *sshole, the group that uncovered the problem, this is a side effect that has been hiding since 2016.

Alpine said every release it checked is affected: 3.21 through 3.24, edge, and the older 3.16 to 3.20 branches. Exposure requires the following:

Root is not directly exposed in most cases. It has shipped as root:* in the base image since about Alpine 3.16, but OpenSSH’s default PermitRootLogin prohibit-password blocks it. Another account that can become root, for example through doas, still gives an attacker a route to root.

Alpine singled out its official tiny-cloud images, versions 3.18.11 through 3.24.3, as especially vulnerable. These ship with an alpine user with a * password field and passwordless doas. They are safe on first boot but become exploitable once any 6 hash exists on the machine. That can happen when an administrator sets a console password or when user data adds a user with a hashed password, which means, essentially, all of them.

Alpine released 3.21.10, 3.22.8, 3.23.8 and 3.24.4 on Thursday, with the OpenSSH fix among the security changes. It also published fixed packages for each release back to 3.16. Alpine 3.21 reached end of support on Nov. 1.

The just-released OpenSSH 10.6p2 avoids the problem in sshd. Alpine’s stable branches carry a patch for the same problem. You should run apk upgrade -U -a and then restart the daemon with rc-service sshd restart. Alpine stressed that upgrading the package does not replace the running daemon. Anyone who cannot update should set PasswordAuthentication no and restart sshd, after confirming that key login works.

Also: Maze Linux is the best security-focused distro I’ve ever tested

To check for an attack, Alpine told administrators to search /var/log/messages for “Accepted password for” lines that name an account with no password. It also advised reviewing dedicated OpenBSD application subexecutor (doas) use and recently created users, files, and authorized keys. “If you cannot rule out a login, treat the machine as compromised.” Just what you wanted for your weekend, I know, but here we are.

TL;DR: Rates fell today, but not by enough to change your mortgage math.

Mortgage rates fell today, possibly helped by post-midterm election clarity and a drop in oil prices.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage ticked down to 7.01% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is six basis points lower than yesterday and 17 basis points lower than a week ago. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.)

Here are the average APRs we're seeing today, as well as movement over the past month for context:

As for what’s next: Tomorrow’s jobs report, showing October data, could potentially nudge mortgage rates in either direction. To understand the link between jobs data and mortgage rates, keep reading below the video.

» Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

Tomorrow, the Nerds will be watching the release of the October jobs report. If it shows that employment remained steady (or even improved), that will build a stronger case for the Federal Reserve to raise overnight borrowing rates again at their next meeting on Dec. 8-9.

While the Fed doesn’t directly set mortgage rates, it does set the federal funds rate, which is the fee that banks must pay to borrow from one another (which is how they fund mortgages). Lenders raise mortgage rates any time they think that the federal funds rate is about to go up.

Central bankers hiked the federal funds rate in September, so a relatively steady jobs report would suggest the labor market could withstand higher rates.

The Fed has a dual mandate to control inflation while supporting maximum employment, and raising the federal funds rate is their main tool for bringing inflation down. If they can work to lower inflation without hurting employment too badly, central bankers may feel more confident to act.

The September Personal Consumption Expenditures price index (PCE), the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, was released last Thursday. The data shows inflation was 3.6% year-over-year in September, up from 3.4% in August.

September’s federal funds rate hike came in the middle of the month, so October’s inflation data will really capture its effect on inflation. The October PCE report will come out on Nov. 25.

» Learn more: How the Fed affects mortgage rates

Refinancing might make sense if today’s rates are at least 0.5 to 0.75 of a percentage point lower than your current rate (and if you plan to stay in your home long enough to break even on closing costs).

With rates where they are right now, you may want to start considering a refi if your current rate is around 7.51% or higher — but there aren't too many people for whom that's true.

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

If you're looking for a lower rate, use NerdWallet's refinance calculator to estimate savings and understand how long it would take to break even on the costs of refinancing.

» Time to refi? Compare refinance rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates.

If the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a new home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy.

» Is now a good time to buy? See NerdWallet’s analysis

If you already have a quote you’re happy with, you should consider locking your mortgage rate, especially if your lender offers a float-down option. A float-down lets you take advantage of a better rate if the market drops during your lock period.

Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it.

🤓 Nerdy Reminder: Rates can change daily, and even hourly. If you’re happy with the deal you have, it’s okay to commit.

The chipmaker's investigation comes as Jensen Huang admits to having an affair with the suspected spy.

Nvidia on Sunday said it’s opening an investigation into whether Jensen Huang, the company’s chief executive officer and founder, was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort after Huang admitted having an affair with a business executive who was reportedly a Chinese spy.

The announcement of any investigation follows a series of reports that Huang had developed a “close relationship” with Alice Huang, no relation to Jensen Huang, who is a Chinese citizen and an executive at Megaspeed. Megaspeed is a Singapore-based data center company that buys chips from Nvidia to run data centers that sell computing power to Chinese AI labs.

The New York Times reported in late October that US intelligence agencies had Alice Huang under electronic surveillance for allegedly facilitating the sale of advanced Nvidia chips to China in violation of US law. During that surveillance, officials discovered she was also allegedly funneling information to the Chinese government in Beijing.

The announcement comes as Nvidia has solidified its position as a leader in the AI boom. The cutting-edge computer chips that Nvidia produces are what make AI and AI data centers possible, and that has made Nvidia one of the world’s most valuable companies by market cap.

“Today’s news will not slow Nvidia,” an Nvidia spokesperson said. “Jensen is committed to continuing to lead Nvidia as CEO without interruption.”

A committee of independent directors, working with outside counsel, will oversee the investigation, the board said in a statement. The company added that it “has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the Board’s inquiry will examine all available information.”

The US has tried to control China’s access to these advanced chips for years. The Biden administration banned Chinese sales of a series of advanced Nvidia chips in 2022, but President Donald Trump relaxed those rules in 2025.  But reports show that there are still illegal operations underway to smuggle banned chips from the US to China.

In his own memo to Nvidia employees, Huang said he was “deeply sorry” for the affair. “I was unfaithful to my wife,” he wrote. “My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did.” Huang, 63, added that he will cooperate fully with the board’s investigation.

The company had previously characterized Jensen Huang’s interactions with Alice Huang as “not unusual or unexpected” given that the CEO “talks with thousands of customer executives every year.”

CNET’s Katelyn Chedraoui contributed to this report.

#3142. HMH Holding (HMH) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Equipment delays and Middle East disruptions weighed on results.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

HMH Holding Inc. (HMH +3.56%) reported quarterly results impacted by delays in rig reactivations and ongoing disruptions in the Middle East, while maintaining a constructive outlook for 2027 deepwater activity. Management reported that equipment order intake was below expectations due to the timing of larger projects and customer capital discipline, which reduced the absorption of the company's global cost base. Despite these near-term headwinds, the company is preparing for a projected increase in offshore activity by procuring long-lead materials and expanding its service footprint through the acquisition of Deepwater Riser Services. The company is managing a multiyear strategy to grow its presence in the North American land market and expects increased floater utilization to drive recurring demand for spares and repairs as rigs transition back into operation.

Operator: Good morning, and welcome to HMH Holding, Inc. Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Call and Webcast. [Operator Instructions] As a reminder, conference call is being recorded. I would now like the call to turn over to David Bratton, SVP Finance. Please go ahead.

David Bratton: Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us for HMH's third quarter results. Joining me today are Eirik Bergsvik, our Chief Executive Officer; and Tom McGee, our Chief Financial Officer. Before we begin, we would like to remind you that this conference call may include forward-looking statements. These statements, which are subject to various risks, uncertainties, assumptions, could cause our actual results to differ materially from these statements. These risks, uncertainties, and assumptions are detailed in this morning's press release as well as our filings with the SEC, which can be found on our website at investor.hmhw.com. We undertake no obligation to revise or update any forward-looking statements or information, except as required by law.

Management's statements may include non-GAAP financial measures. For reconciliations of these measures, please refer to our earnings release and our SEC filings. Following our prepared remarks, we will open the call for your questions. I will now turn the call over to Eirik.

Eirik Bergsvik: Thank you, David, and good morning, everyone. During the third quarter, our results were impacted by several near-term timing and market headwinds, including rig activation delays, continued disruptions in the Middle East and the timing of certain large equipment orders. Despite these pressures, the underlying market remains constructive with increasing deepwater investments supporting activity growth into 2027, and we remain confident in the opportunities ahead of HMH. The timing of equipment orders also impacted cash flow during the quarter. In anticipation of expected demand, we intentionally procured long lead materials ahead of purchase orders to shorten delivery lead times, improve our cost position and ensure we are ready to execute as these opportunities convert.

We continue to maintain our cost base through this temporary slowdown in equipment activity, which reduces the pace of facility cost absorption and working capital liquidation but preserves the capacity we believe will be needed as activity increases. We also continue to invest strategically in our long-term growth. On September 21, we announced the acquisition of Deepwater Riser Services, expanding our riser service footprint and further strengthening HMH's position in the deepwater market. Taken together, while timing-related headwinds have affected our near-term results and cash flow, we remain confident in the underlying demand environment and believe the actions we are taking position HMH well as we move into 2027. Moving now into the financial highlights.

Orders for the quarter were $191 million, representing a book-to-bill ratio of 1.1x in the quarter. Total revenue for the quarter was $171 million and adjusted EBITDA was $38 million. Looking at revenue composition. Spares revenue declined 2% year-over-year to $57 million, reflecting prior quarter's reduced order intake. Quarter-over-quarter spares orders were up 7% year-over-year, mainly driven by increase in Europe, offsetting the reduced Middle East demand. Service revenue in the quarter was $97 million, driven by repairs and digital technology. Importantly, service order intake increased 16% year-over-year, driven by repairs and field services.

Product order intake and revenue remained subdued in the third quarter with order intake of $16 million, revenue of $17 million, reflecting the timing of larger equipment orders we mentioned previously. Turning now to the broader drilling market and what we see developing as we look toward 2027. Following a very strong first half of the year, offshore contracting activity moderated during the third quarter. In the floater market, however, we view this more as a matter of timing than a fundamental change in the outlook. Several tenders remain active across key offshore basins with some awards taking longer to formalize. Importantly, year-to-date floater contracting remains well ahead of last year.

Through September, approximately 110 rig years have been awarded globally compared with 59 rig years during the same period in 2025. This distinction between the pace of new contract announcement and underlying future activity is important. While contracting activity has moderated during the second half, the outlook for 2027 remains constructive. A number of rigs have already secured future work and will be undergoing contract preparation, shipyard work, and mobilization ahead of those programs. And we see this clearly within the HMH installed base. Additionally, the recent announcement from RigCo regarding financing of reactivation of 4 rigs, including 2 harsh environment semis with HMH equipment is a positive indicator of investment in the market.

To be clear, these are long-term investors putting capital into expanding offshore fleet. The number of HMH key floater currently on contract is broadly stable compared with recent quarters. However, that measure does not fully reflect activity developing beneath the surface. Several HMH equipped units are currently being prepared or mobilized for future contracts, creating a meaningful expected increasing activity as we move into 2027. This is particularly relevant for HMH: bringing a rig back into operation after an extended period of inactivity generates activity ahead of the actual drilling contract through preparation, inspections, equipment refurbishment, shipyard work and mobilization. Once these rigs begin operating, they also expand activity installed base, supporting recurring demand for HMH products and services.

As we finish 2026, we expect activity across our HMH key floater fleet to be broadly in line with 2025 levels. Looking into 2027, however, we see a meaningful step-up in activity. Approximately 85% of our expected base case 2027 activity level is already supported by firm customer backlog or contractual options for 2027. This provides a strong foundation for growth even before considering additional contract awards. Importantly, we do expect further contracts to be awarded to HMH-equipped floaters. Based on our current review, we, therefore, expect HMH's key floater activity to increase approximately 10% to 25% year-over-year in 2027, with particular strength in the second half of 2027.

The range reflects the timing of contract commencements, option exercises and additional awards that remain to be secured. The key message for HMH is that the number of rigs operating today does not yet reflect the activity level we expect in 2027. As these units transition from stacked status through preparation and mobilization and ultimately into drilling operations, we believe that increasing activity should translate into growing opportunities for HMH. In particular, a larger active installed base should support increased consumption of spare parts, together with additional field service, repairs and maintenance and equipment upgrade opportunities during 2027. The broader floater fundamentals remain supportive as well. At the end of September, global committed floater utilization stood at approximately 86%.

And within the harsh environment segment, committed market utilization was approximately 89%. Beneath the near-term contracting cycle, we also continue to see healthy investments in future offshore developments. Global offshore greenfield investment commitments for 2026 are projected at approximately $142 billion with a significant pipeline of projects extending beyond 2026. Turning briefly to our equipment and project business. Order intake has been below our expectations during the last 2 quarters. This has primarily been driven by timing. Some drilling contractors have secured contracts later than we had anticipated, reducing the availability, lead time and operational white space to execute larger equipment upgrades.

At the same time, we have seen certain larger projects and upgrade decisions move to later periods as customers maintain a disciplined approach to capital deployment. Importantly, we have not seen these opportunities disappear; rather, the timing of the associated order intake has shifted to the right. We continue to see a healthy pipeline of equipment upgrades and larger project opportunities across our installed base. As customers gain greater visibility on future drilling programs and suitable shipyard and preparation windows become available, we expect this to create opportunities to progress these projects. We, therefore, view the recent lower order intake primarily a timing issue rather than change in the underlying opportunity set for our equipment and our projects business.

Turning to the jack-up market. The picture remains more challenging. Global jack-up contracting is running below last year's level with approximately 146 rig years awarded through September compared with 195 rig years during the equivalent period of 2025. The Middle East continued to be an important contributor to this weakness with additional Saudi Aramco rig suspensions during the quarter and further delays to tender activity. For HMH specifically, deterioration in Middle East activity has continued to affect our business. Based on our current expectation, we estimate that lower activity in the region will negatively impact our 2026 order intake by approximately $50 million to $60 million.

While we see pockets of improving jack-up activity elsewhere, these have not yet been sufficient to offset the broader year-on-year decline in global jack-up contracting. As a result, we remain cautious on the near-term outlook for this segment. Turning to our land business. I would also like to highlight an encouraging development in North America. Over the past years, we have been executing a multiyear strategy to expand HMH's presence in the North American land market. This has included investments in our facilities, including our new larger facility in Odessa, additions to our product portfolio and broader efforts to strengthen our offering and position HMH closer to our customers. We're now beginning to see those investments translate into results.

Although this business remains relatively small for HMH today, we are seeing a significant growth trend across both equipment and service revenues in the North American market. As our equipment presence expands, we also see an opportunity to build associated services and aftermarket business over the life of that installed equipment. This creates the potential for the growth in equipment sales today to support a larger recurring revenue opportunity over time. We are, therefore, encouraged by the momentum we are seeing, and we believe it can become an increasingly relevant contributor to HMH's growth over time.

Consistent with our disciplined capital allocation strategy, we believe these opportunities will enhance our capabilities, expand our market presence and create meaningful long-term value for shareholders. Tom McGee: Yes. I think you've seen the preparation, largely speaking, and we would -- barring a major project order like a new build something, a massive new build project, we would see inventory really more being released Q1 and Q2 next year. And that's really what we've set up for.

Bumshik Kim: Got it. And just shifting gears, you mentioned several additional strategic opportunities beyond Deepwater Riser. I think we want to go ahead and grow the business, and our bias is to do that and take advantage of the assets that are out there at attractive rates and increase the scale of the business.

Operator: At this time, I would now like to turn the conference back over to Eirik Bergsvik for closing remarks. Please go ahead.

Eirik Bergsvik: Thank you all for your support and participation on today's call, and we look forward to updating you on the fourth quarter results. Thank you.

#3141. How Smart Glasses Detector Apps Work, and How Much You Can Trust Them

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Detector apps can identify Meta’s glasses and similar devices by their Bluetooth signals, as long as they’re switched on, nearby and broadcasting.

Bluetooth devices announce themselves to nearby phones with short broadcast signals, which is how your earbuds show up when you open your phone’s Bluetooth menu. Smart glasses do the same thing, and apps such as Zuckoff listen for signals that match known models, then send an alert when one turns up nearby.

It’s a clever workaround for glasses designed to blend in. How useful it is depends on what you want it to tell you: The app can detect that a pair is close by, but not whether it’s recording. Still, that’s more notice than most people get today, especially if they haven’t spotted the glasses’ built-in LED indicator

Here’s how those apps work, what they reliably catch and what they miss.

Zuckoff, whose name takes a direct jab at Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, has joined a small ecosystem of apps such as Antizuck Smart Glasses Scanner and Nearby Glasses that offer similar functionality — letting you know when someone has smart glasses activated and how close the device is, although they can’t tell you specifically whether someone is actively recording or using AI to pull up information. The apps detect approximate device proximity by sweeping local Bluetooth frequencies to locate vendor IDs, system identifiers and hardware signatures associated with smart glasses.

As Zuckoff’s website notes: “Glasses advertise loudest while powering on, pairing or leaving the case. Once paired to their owner’s phone, they can go quiet, so silence is not proof that nobody is recording, and a detection is not proof that anyone is. Signal strength gives a rough distance and no direction at all.”

Zuckoff’s developer, Pawel Szydlowski, said he was already working on projects that used Bluetooth to detect nearby devices and discovered the tech could be applied to smart glasses. “It’s just the same technology wrapped in a different paper,” he said in a video chat with CNET.

Recent reports have shown that smart glasses are being used for everything from bullying in schools to viral videos with unwitting subjects who don’t know they’re being recorded.

Since it launched in early August, the Zuckoff app has gotten 2,000 sign-ups, and Szydlowski is beta-testing an Android version he hopes to make available on the Google Play Store. The app also has a premium version for $10 a year that can run continuous detection checks in the background when the app isn’t in use.

But a booming ecosystem of DIY modifications and third-party hardware hacks is also giving smart glasses wearers unprecedented stealth by allowing them to disable the activation lights, either by bypassing the capture LEDs or by patching software to suppress system notifications.

Tech journalist Joanna Stern hosted a video showing the process in which a local hacker removed the LED light from her Ray-Ban Meta glasses for $100, allowing the wearables to secretly record without notice.

Detecting active smart glasses in public or private spaces adds a new layer of security awareness, but it raises an obvious dilemma: What do you actually do with that information? Once a detector app alerts us that smart glasses are nearby, it seems our only choices are to either leave the space or ask the wearer to remove the glasses.

Uttara Ananthakrishnan, an associate professor of information systems at the University of Washington who studies the societal impacts of technology, says we’re still figuring out the social norms around wearables like smart glasses. It’s impossible to know whether the person filming will behave responsibly, and the question of consent gets even thornier if children might be captured on video or in photos.

“Until we develop clear mechanisms to balance seamless innovation with consent, these devices will continue to turn everyday public spaces into zones of surveillance anxiety,” she said.

The Even G2 smart glasses don’t have a camera for recording photos or videos. They can pair with a separately sold R1 control ring that works as a fitness tracker.

For instance, Even Realities’ G2 smart glasses don’t include a front-facing camera at all. Instead, the Even G2 devices, released in late 2025, focus on providing the wearer with information and acting more like a personal assistant.

“We made the decision from the beginning that smart glasses don’t need to have cameras on them in order to be useful,” Even Realities CEO Will Wang told CNET in an email. “We believe something worn on your face should respect not only the person wearing it, but everyone around them.”

The G2 devices don’t record externally, a design choice Wang said gave the company a unique challenge. “Leaving the camera out also pushed us to think differently about what actually makes smart glasses useful day to day, rather than assuming more sensors automatically make a better product,” he said.

Wang said there’s room in the smart glasses market for different approaches to features and functionality, and that buyers may want to make trade-offs for devices they’ll wear on their faces. But Wang noted that the rise of smart glasses detectors indicates that social acceptance is an issue the industry needs to consider.

Over the last several months, smart glasses have been getting cheaper. And with more models and companies jumping into the fray, the demand for surveillance detectors is likely to grow — that is, unless Big Tech and wearable companies radically change their devices to make them invisible to detector apps.

Szydlowski said his hope is that, in time, Zuckoff won’t be needed at all. He pointed out that the ability to detect nearby Apple AirTag devices eventually became part of the operating systems on iOS and Android devices. If consumers pressure manufacturers and their governments to make smart glasses easier to detect, it would be “the perfect solution” to make his app obsolete, he said.

#3140. Which Foldable Phone Has the Best Battery Life? We Put Them to the Test

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

From Apple's iPhone Duo to Samsung's and Motorola's foldables, we tested how today's most popular book-style and flip phones hold up under pressure.

For years, foldable phones haven’t exactly been praised for their battery life. However, that’s starting to change.

Because of their unique design, foldables have traditionally struggled to match the battery life of conventional slab phones. Their massive displays, space-consuming hinge mechanisms and limited room for heat dissipation all present challenges. But battery technology has improved in recent years, with some of the newest foldables benefiting from higher-energy-density silicon-carbon batteries and more power-efficient processors. Even slim phones like the Galaxy Z Fold 8 can last all day, showing that you don’t have to sacrifice practicality for a sleek, innovative design.

Still, foldable phones remain a niche category, even with a major player like Apple entering the market with the iPhone Duo. But they offer an appealing alternative for anyone looking to break away from the sameness of more traditional slab phones. And with battery life being a key consideration when choosing a new device, it’s important to know which phone can keep up with all your scrolling, streaming and snapping without constantly reaching for a charger.

We’ve dug into CNET’s extensive smartphone lab data to find out which foldable phone in 2026 delivers the best battery life. Because book-style and flip phones differ in design and screen size, we’re separating the results to provide a more accurate comparison.

Here’s how devices from Samsung, Apple, Google and Motorola stack up.

This year, CNET has reviewed and tested five book-style foldable phones: the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8, Z Fold 8 Ultra, Motorola Razr Fold, Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold and the Apple iPhone Duo. These devices are phone-tablet hybrids, with designs ranging from taller, narrower builds to squatter, passport-style designs. (We didn’t include Samsung’s Galaxy Z TriFold because of its unique design.)

Apple’s $1,999 iPhone Duo may be late to the foldable game, arriving seven years after Samsung’s first Galaxy Fold ushered in the modern era of foldable phones. Still, given Apple’s strong brand loyalty and mainstream appeal, the Duo has generated considerable buzz.

And there’s another reason Apple’s first foldable deserves attention: its battery. The iPhone Duo achieved the highest average score in CNET’s testing among book-style phones. It’s a testament to its dual-cell battery design, which is standard in foldables, and the efficiency of the A20 Pro chip powering the device.

To test a phone’s battery, CNET runs a 3-hour streaming video test and a 45-minute endurance test that includes watching videos, scrolling through social media, playing a game and joining a video call. Both tests take place on the foldable phone’s inner screen, starting with a full charge and while connected to Wi-Fi.

The iPhone Duo had the highest remaining charge after the 45-minute endurance test, finishing with 99%. It ended the 3-hour streaming test with 84%, placing it just below the Razr Fold, Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Z Fold 8 Ultra in that category. That average gives the Duo, which has a 4,883-mAh battery, the number-one place in our foldable battery tests.

Not far behind is the Razr Fold, Motorola’s first book-style foldable. This phone has a whopping 6,000-mAh silicon-carbon battery, which helped it earn one of the top spots in our battery testing.

Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8, which is the company’s first palm-size foldable phone, just barely tops the more standard-size Z Fold 8 Ultra. Both phones are the thinnest in this ranking, which makes their results even more impressive. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 measures 4.5mm thick when unfolded and 9.7mm when folded, and has a 4,800-mAh silicon-carbon battery. The Z Fold 8 Ultra is 4.1mm thick when open and 8.9mm when closed, and it has a 5,000-mAh silicon-carbon battery.

Close behind the competition is Google’s Pixel 11 Pro Fold, which has a 4,806-mAh battery. Like the other phones, including the iPhone Duo, it performed relatively better in the endurance test than in the streaming test. That suggests these devices handle shorter bursts of use well but can take a more noticeable battery hit during prolonged activities like video streaming. Even so, they should easily power through a full day of mixed use, whether you’re watching movies, scrolling through social media or taking photos.

Overall, every book-style foldable we tested demonstrated strong battery results. Beyond the numbers, our hands-on experience suggests you can get through most days without constantly worrying about your phone’s battery level. Be sure to check out CNET’s in-depth reviews for more on the everyday experience using each of these phones.

Some people may prefer the more nostalgic design of a flip phone. Motorola revived its iconic Razr brand for the smartphone era, and now has a handful of devices at varying price points to choose from. Samsung’s Galaxy Z Flip 8 is another pocket-friendly choice.

These clamshell devices have less space for a battery than larger foldable and slab phones. Still, Motorola’s and Samsung’s battery specs are nothing to sniff at.

This year’s $800 Motorola Razr has a 4,800-mAh battery, the $1,100 Razr Plus has a 4,500-mAh battery and the $1,500 Razr Ultra has a 5,000-mAh battery. Meanwhile, the $1,200 Z Flip 8 has a 4,300-mAh battery. Every one of these phones uses a silicon-carbon battery to squeeze more power into a smaller design.

Impressively, the baseline Motorola Razr got the best average score in our battery testing of clamshell phones. It also had the highest result in CNET’s 3-hour streaming test among its peers and tied with the much pricier Razr Ultra in our battery endurance test. The Razr Ultra, Galaxy Z Flip 8 and Razr Plus are in close succession.

Interestingly, the flip phones aren’t that far behind their book-style counterparts in our testing. One key advantage is that their smaller cover and inner displays require less power, helping them keep pace with larger foldables.

The results are also a testament to how battery technology is progressing, with the mobile industry increasingly shifting toward high-density silicon-carbon batteries, which can pack more capacity into tighter dimensions. This means that regardless of whether you choose a book-style or clamshell foldable, you can be assured that your battery won’t leave you in the lurch as you go about your day.

From the newest foldables like the iPhone Duo and Pixel 11 Pro Fold to flip phones from Motorola and Samsung, you no longer have to sacrifice battery life for a more versatile mobile design. Today’s devices can comfortably get you through a full day of swiping, scrolling and snapping photos, even with larger screens to power.

In fact, when ranked among all the phones CNET tested this year, including non-folding options, the iPhone Duo sits among the top five performers, with the iPhone 18 Pro Max taking the top overall spot.

That’s especially important given that a major part of a foldable phone’s appeal is the ability to switch between two displays. You can quickly send a text on a smaller screen, then move to a larger one to watch a movie, for example. That versatility requires a battery capable of handling more intensive tasks like streaming and gaming, as well as extended activities like browsing and working across multiple displays.

And while the iPhone Duo and Motorola Razr topped CNET’s foldable battery tests, the other phones we evaluated weren’t far behind, highlighting just how competitive battery life has become across the leading brands. Ultimately, choosing the right foldable will come down to other factors, including camera performance, design and price.

Our testing data, combined with real-world experiences shared in our in-depth reviews, illustrates just how far foldable phones have evolved. They’re no longer just a novelty; they’ve become increasingly practical devices in their own right.

#3139. CoreWeave credit default swaps hit distress levels as investors sour on AI debt

CoreWeave's credit stress continued to spiral on Thursday amid a broader sell-off in AI-related names.

CoreWeave — a so-called neocloud company — has taken on more than $51 billion of debt and obligations to finance its AI infrastructure build-out. It's now facing a rebellion from stock and bond investors as concerns mount about AI overspending and debt levels.

Yields on CoreWeave debt have continued to climb, with the yield to maturity on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 reaching 15.78%. Bond yields move inversely to prices. Meanwhile, the spread on its five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default, at one point soared above 1,140 basis points. It last stood at nearly 1,038 bps — a 16% week-over-week jump and 164% higher than a year ago.

Credit concerns are spreading into AI equities too. CoreWeave's stock dropped during trading Thursday before recovering and closing 5.94% higher. The moved followed Wednesday's 15.5% nosedive.

Other neocloud stocks were under similar pressure. Nebius also sank before climbing higher to close 1.29% and and Iren ultimately ended the day down less than 1%.

Anxiety about AI overspending is also spreading. For instance, shares of Micron Technology and Advanced Micro Devices sold off following a big sell-off in South Korean chip stocks. Micron closed up 1.87%, while AMD fell 1.5%.

While AI debt worries have been rising steadily, investors have suddenly grown skittish about the underlying finances of companies borrowing heavily to buy chips, build data centers, and rent out computing power.

Coreweave's credit default swaps are one place to see that stress.

Credit default swaps are contracts where buyers pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. The spread widening in CoreWeave's CDS means investors view the debt as riskier.

The market is "basically saying 'no mas' to AI debt without operating cash flow support," the Evercore ISI trading desk said.

A spread level of 1,000 basis points or above is generally a sign of credit distress, said Gavan Nolan, executive director of fixed income pricing at S&P Global Market Intelligence.

No one is questioning whether demand for CoreWeave's services is real, since the company has contracts with all the big hyperscalers, Nolan said. The question is whether the cash flows will ultimately arrive.

"It's obviously heavily negative free cash flow at the moment, and it needs that cash flow to arrive really to justify all the capex that it's spending," Nolan said.

CEO Mike Intrator dismissed the market moves on Wednesday, according to a memo obtained by CNBC.

"When you are building a new type of technology company there will be periods of time when the market misunderstands and acts irrationally," he wrote. "We are confident in our backlog which more than supports all of our debt obligations."

The backlog is over $100 billion, with around two-thirds of it with investment-grade counterparts including Microsoft, Meta, IBM and Caterpillar, Deutsche Bank said in a note Thursday. The firm reiterated its buy-rating on the stock Wednesday, calling the dislocation a buying opportunity.

"The problem is this kind of concern can prove to be a self-fulfilling prophecy, and risks triggering broader issues in other AI-related names," said Jim Reid, global head of macro and thematic research.

Domino effects may already be happening. Oracle's five-year CDS spread also spiked this week. It was last at 282 basis points, a roughly 10% increase in one week.

"A downgrade from its BBB rating would risk pressuring IG-only investors into forced sales," Reid said.

Democrats won big in the midterms, but mortgage rates have bigger forces to reckon with.

Mortgage rates fell again this week, extending a gradual slide that began well before Election Day.

The average rate on a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage fell 13 basis points to 7.05% APR in the week ending Nov. 5, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.) We calculate our weekly average using daily APRs recorded over the past five business days.

Homebuyers’ budgets are feeling the pinch from high mortgage rates, steep home prices and a shortage of listings. On the campaign trail, candidates from both parties promised to make homeownership more affordable. But solving that problem is like untangling 20 years’ worth of Christmas lights from your attic. Yank on one strand, and three more tighten.

“Jumpstarting the housing market relies on a calmer geopolitical environment and bond market in the short run and more housing supply plus a more dynamic labor market in the long run,” Jake Krimmel, senior economist for Realtor.com, said in an email.

A shift in political power won’t erase those challenges overnight. Here's what's driving mortgage rates right now — and where a Democratic Congress might have some pull.

How that affects mortgage rates: The relief of one less uncertainty is giving rates some breathing room.

Election results have cleared up one big unknown for investors. With Democrats controlling Congress and Republicans holding the White House, markets are bracing for the reality that any major spending bills could face roadblocks.

Political gridlock isn't always popular, but weirdly, investors sometimes welcome it. When a divided government limits new spending, the government may need to borrow less than expected — which could turn down the heat on mortgage rates.

But there’s a catch. That same gridlock could make it harder to pass laws to help bring down housing costs.

How that affects mortgage rates: Heavy borrowing from the government and tech companies adds upward pressure to the bond market, where mortgage rates take their cues.

When the government spends more than it collects in taxes, it borrows the difference by selling Treasury bonds. When there's lots of debt for sale, investors may demand higher returns, called yields. Mortgage rates tend to follow the yield on the 10-year Treasury note.

The new Congress still faces a mountain of government debt. What they choose to do about it can ripple through the economy to affect your monthly mortgage payment.

“Sound fiscal policy, rather than deficit-financed spending and standoffs over budgets and the debt limit, can help keep rates in check,” Andy Winkler, managing director for housing and infrastructure policy at the Bipartisan Policy Center, said in an email.

Meanwhile, Big Tech companies are borrowing a boatload of money to build AI data centers. To get the cash, they issue corporate bonds, giving investors another place to put their money. More bonds flooding the market can push Treasury yields higher, taking mortgage rates along for the ride.

But how long can the AI building boom last? Voters across party lines pushed back against data centers in the midterms. Even if lawmakers pump the brakes on new construction, a slowdown in tech spending doesn't guarantee cheaper mortgages.

How that affects mortgage rates: Wartime disruptions to global oil supplies can fuel inflation, pushing borrowing costs higher.

The unpopular war in Iran likely added to the voter frustration that helped fuel Democrats' midterm victories. Higher energy costs can hit household budgets in multiple ways: at the pump, through pricier goods that need to be shipped, and through higher interest rates on loans (including mortgages) as inflation heats up.

“A resolution would likely improve oil supply, helping to ease price pressures and potentially providing relief for mortgage rates,” Krimmel said.

A Democratic Congress could push for a different approach to ending the war, but it can't make Iran agree to a deal.

Meanwhile, stubborn inflation from the Iran war has raised the prospect of another Federal Reserve rate hike at its Dec. 8-9 meeting. Futures traders now put the odds of a quarter-point increase at more than 80%, according to CME FedWatch. The Fed doesn't set mortgage rates directly, but investors anticipate its decisions — so mortgage rates often move before the Fed does.

If buying a home makes sense for your budget now, there's little reason to wait just because Congress changed hands. Buyers can sometimes score lower prices in winter, when sellers are more willing to negotiate. But with today’s mortgage rates hovering above 7%, higher borrowing costs can eat into those savings, so it’s important to compare mortgage lenders to get the best rate.

For longer-term hope, look to the bipartisan 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which became law this summer. This legislation shows lawmakers can, in fact, work together to make meaningful progress on housing affordability.

“Even with divided government, lawmakers and the administration can build on that common ground to further boost housing production, preserve existing affordable homes, and help families struggling with high housing and utility costs,” Winkler said.

But new homes take time to build, and your house hunt doesn't have to follow Congress's calendar. Your homebuying budget and local market conditions matter more than the next political headline.

#3137. Google’s AI Mode Will Soon Show Ads Even in Your Follow-Up Questions

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Ads will start appearing in AI Mode’s follow-up answers in the US as Google expands AI Mode ads to more countries.

Sponsored results will soon appear in responses to follow-up questions in Google’s AI Mode in the US. Google announced the change, along with plans to show ads in AI Overviews and AI Mode to more people, after reporting that AI Mode searches generate less revenue than traditional searches.

The company says sponsored product listings in AI Mode already get clicked about as often as organic results. For publishers, the change adds paid competition inside AI answers, which a Pew Research Center study last year found already make people less likely to click through to websites.

You’ve probably seen how this works: Type a question into Google, and an AI-generated summary often appears at the top of the page. That can mean fewer clicks on the ads below, which underpin Google’s core revenue.

Now, the tech giant is expanding how and where we see ads when using AI Mode during searches. Google is scaling ads in AI Mode to 10 new countries (including Australia, Canada, India, Kenya and Singapore), with plans to launch in Brazil, Mexico and the UK later this year.

In the US, Google is launching what it calls “multiturn ads,” allowing ads to appear directly within follow-up queries in AI Mode when a search or conversation has “commercial relevance.” Take, for example, if you start a search with “How does a smart fridge work,” and follow up with “What are the best-selling smart fridges?” You could then see refrigerator ads in sections labeled “sponsored.”

Google said that “multiturn ads” can better target what a user wants in a product because AI Mode gathers more information during a back-and-forth conversation. Ads can also appear on initial AI Mode queries, not just after follow-up questions, and sometimes ads won’t appear at all if there doesn’t appear to be purchase intent, according to Google.

But as Google relies more on AI Mode and AI Overview, there’ll be less reason to click on content links “below the fold,” meaning content that sits out of view until a reader scrolls down a web page.

Lily Ray, a well-known SEO expert and founder of Algorythmic, told CNET that it’s going to become harder to use Google to find articles from preferred publishers and articles you want to read directly from a website. “You’ll have to dig deeper and look outside of Google’s products,” Ray said via email.

According to Ray, Google’s AI tools aren’t designed to give you the exact link you’re looking for. Still, you don’t have to rely on AI Mode or AI Overviews to get search results. You can also scroll down to the search results the old-fashioned way or use a web filter to use Google as a list of links. She also recommends setting up your favorite publications as “preferred sources” (instructions here) so you can see more of those pages cited in your personalized results.

“Unless you’re satisfied with AI answers directly on Google, you’re going to need to start evolving your own search behavior to find the websites you’re looking for,” Ray said.

Google is still the largest search engine in the world, accounting for nearly 90% of the global search engine market. In fact, the company said its year-over-year query volume growth in the third quarter was the fastest over the past five years.

But beginning with the launch of AI Overviews in May 2024, Google’s reliance on AI has slowed advertising.

The impact has been even more devastating for online publishers — ranging from major newspapers and digital media sites to brands and trade associations — driving an unprecedented decline in website traffic. AI Overviews now appear on nearly half of Google search queries, with a corresponding 61% drop in raw traffic volume to other pages. Google is effectively scraping publisher information, summarizing it and satisfying the user before they leave the search results page. That’s why it’s often referred to as the “zero-click” crisis.

“AI Mode and AI Overviews answer questions directly in Google’s interface, so there’s less reason for people to click on publishers,” Ray said.

AI Overviews are summary boxes at the top of a traditional search results page, while AI Mode is a conversational interface designed for ongoing dialogue and research. You can access AI Mode directly by selecting the AI Mode button at the far right of the search bar on the Google home page, or by selecting AI Mode in the horizontal menu near the top of other Google pages.

When you use AI Mode, you won’t get an AI Overview or a long list of links to other websites offering more information. Instead, AI Mode provides “more advanced reasoning and ways of interacting” with a conversational approach. For instance, if I use AI Mode and ask, “Where can I see the northern lights?” I get a map and a list of various locations with pros and cons for each. In regular search mode, I get an AI Overview at the top and, below that, pages of links to websites related to my query.

Ray said that with more ads, there’s going to be an even greater decline in organic click-through rates — in publishing speak, that’s the percentage of people who actually click on a natural, nonpaid search engine result, out of the total number of people who simply saw the headline on the page. Not only will the AI text answer your question, but Google will now aggressively route you toward advertisers rather than publisher links.

“Like many things in Google Search, it means that if you’re not participating in Google Ads, it’s going to be harder and harder to get that traffic organically,” said Ray.

Last month, we issued $400 million of senior notes due 2033, further strengthening our funding flexibility. Rakesh will talk more about this shortly. We also were able to achieve our eighth quarter in a row of deleveraging, supported by the strong adjusted EBITDA generation I mentioned earlier. When combined with our level of buying this quarter, this benefited our cash flow profile for Q3. Our cash flow will naturally fluctuate based on the level of portfolio investments in a given quarter.

When higher returning purchasing opportunities are more limited, we can generate more cash flow. When there are significantly more attractive portfolio opportunities, we have the flexibility to reinvest that cash at returns we believe will create long-term shareholder value. As it relates to our capital allocation strategy, our priorities remain unchanged. We continue to prioritize portfolio purchases that meet our return thresholds, investments that improve our operating performance and opportunistic share repurchases depending on valuation and balancing portfolio purchases with leverage. Turning now to operations, technology and data. Our team has made great progress in developing our U.S. operating capability over the past few years, but we have more work to do.

We have built up offshore capabilities, introduced external debt collection agencies and focused on our U.S. P&L. We have also embarked on a major technology transformation. As I've said many times, cost discipline remains a core operating principle. The actions we took over the past year to simplify the organization, reduce corporate and overhead costs and improve efficiency are beginning to show up in our financial results. As Rakesh will go over in more detail, operating expenses during the third quarter declined, enabling our adjusted EBITDA to continue growing even as we invest in legal and in technology.

The rollout of our cloud-based omnichannel contact platform in the U.S. during the quarter is off to a strong start and is already improving agent productivity and customer engagement. Our data migration to the cloud in the U.S. also remains on track for completion by the end of the year. We are moving billions of documents and a lot of data into the cloud, which will streamline our processes and provide for faster insights and decision-making. We also continue to make progress modernizing our legal, core and data platforms. The legal IT investments, in particular, are worth mentioning.

We're in the process of developing a significant upgrade to our legal collection capabilities, one that will benefit from the rapid advancements in AI. These investments will improve our systems, enhance our processes, improve efficiency and enable greater coverage in the states we operate in. We expect our IT modernization investments to be less than $10 million over the next few years as we work with partners who themselves are leveraging AI for software and system development. AI is also becoming an increasingly important component of how we operate. We have multiple pilots and projects underway across the U.S. and Europe to drive productivity, improve processes and increase cash collections.

As an example, these initiatives are helping us enhance document processing and improve customer engagement. I would point out that we are being very cautious in terms of direct customer interactions with AI. Finally, under people and culture, we continue to build a more agile, accountable and performance-oriented organization. We recently celebrated our 30th anniversary, a milestone made possible by the dedication and hard work of our employees around the world. We were also encouraged by the strong participation and engagement reflected in our annual staff survey, which reinforced the strength of our culture during a period of significant transformation.

Our team understands the need for change, and they are really a leaner and more efficient organization with a great culture. Overall, I am pleased with the progress we're making. We have strengthened our funding position, reduced costs, grown adjusted EBITDA to near record levels, lowered leverage, advanced our technology capabilities and continue building a stronger foundation for long-term growth. With that, I'll turn the call over to Rakesh to discuss our third quarter financial results in more detail.

Rakesh Sehgal: Thanks, Martin. We purchased $229 million of portfolios during the quarter. In Europe, portfolio volumes continue to trend higher towards pre-COVID levels, and we expect that trend to continue in Q4. Our global diversification and disciplined capital deployment focusing on net returns provides the flexibility to direct capital towards the most attractive opportunities globally.

Total operating expenses were $200 million for the quarter. As we work through the remaining backlog of accounts, we expect annual legal collection costs to begin declining and to be lower in 2027 than they are in 2026. This is based on our current buying outlook and is subject to change. Moving below the operating line. Net interest expense was $64 million for the quarter, relatively flat year-over-year. Net leverage at quarter end ticked lower to 2.6x, down from 2.67x last quarter and from a peak of 2.87x in the third quarter of 2024. This marks our eighth consecutive quarter of deleveraging and reflects the combination of growing adjusted EBITDA, stable borrowings and disciplined capital deployment.

As we've said before, to the extent we see good investment opportunities, we may capitalize on them, which in some quarters may result in an uptick in our leverage. However, our objective over the longer term continues to be to move towards the mid-2x area as outlined in our PRA 3.0 strategy. Turning to funding and capital allocation. Given the current rate and market environment, we are pleased that the recent bond issuance further extends our debt maturity profile, which remains well staggered. Finally, we continue to view opportunistic share repurchases as part of our overall capital allocation strategy to drive shareholder value.
