#3123. Green Plains (GPRE) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

A tax credit deal and record yields lifted this producer's quarter.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Green Plains Inc. (GPRE +2.95%) reported record quarterly results driven by improved operational execution and the expansion of its low-carbon platform. Management stated that the company successfully executed an agreement to monetize 45Z clean fuel production tax credits, providing a clear path to convert tax credit receivables into cash. The company achieved 95% platform utilization and record ethanol and corn oil yields while advancing strategic projects to lower carbon intensity. Management indicated that the current financial position allows for disciplined capital allocation focused on asset safety, debt reduction, and high-return organic growth opportunities.

Operator: Good afternoon, and welcome to the Green Plains Inc. Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] I will now hand the call over to your host, Will Joekel, Vice President of Investor Relations and Treasurer. Please go ahead, Will.

Will Joekel: Thank you, and good afternoon, everyone. Welcome to the Green Plains Inc. Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call. Joining me on today's call are Chris Osowski, President and Chief Executive Officer; Ann Reis, Chief Financial Officer; and Imre Havasi, Senior Vice President of Trading and Commercial Operations, together with the other members of our senior leadership team. The accompanying slides are available in the Events and Presentations section of our website. Before we begin, please note that during today's call, we will be making forward-looking statements, which are expectations, projections and statements about future events. These statements reflect current assumptions and are subject to risks and uncertainties that could cause actual outcomes to differ materially.

Please review the risks described in today's earnings release, our remarks on this call and our Form 10-K, Form 10-Q and other SEC filings. Green Plains does not undertake any duty to update any forward-looking statements. With that, Chris, I'll turn the call over to you.

Chris Osowski: Thanks, Will, and good afternoon, everyone. This is an exciting time for Green Plains. We delivered exceptional third quarter results with a record $118 million of adjusted EBITDA, more than double our prior year results and more recently reached a major milestone with the execution of an agreement to monetize our 2026 45Z clean fuel production tax credits. The significance of this quarter goes well beyond record adjusted EBITDA and the benefits of 45Z. We are operating better and creating more value from the assets we already own. Together, those factors are strengthening our earnings power and giving us greater flexibility to invest in the business and pursue opportunities that can create long-term value for shareholders.

What makes the third quarter particularly important is how we delivered those results. While market conditions were favorable, the quarter also demonstrated the tangible benefits of the investments we have made in our people, assets and processes. Platform utilization recovered to approximately 95%, production increased by 14 million gallons sequentially, ethanol and corn oil yields reached record levels and energy usage per gallon improved year-over-year. Those improvements translated directly into financial results. Consolidated crush margins improved approximately $0.11 per gallon sequentially, and the majority of that improvement came from plant performance, commercial execution and other factors beyond the commodity environment. Nowhere was that improved execution more evident than at Madison.

Following the extended downtime in the second quarter, the plant not only recovered but achieved the highest quarterly ethanol production in its 15-plus years of operation. I said last quarter that we will not be skipping leg day, and that's exactly what I meant. We're putting in the work to come back stronger. That is precisely the culture we are building at Green Plains and what operational excellence is intended to deliver. When challenges arise, we identify them, address them and emerge stronger. The stronger base business performance is only one part of the earnings and cash-generating opportunities we've built at Green Plains.

During the third quarter, our low-carbon platform generated $65 million of 45Z production tax credit value, net of discounts and associated costs. Higher qualifying production and improved capture performance have expanded the value generation across the platform, supporting another increase in our full year outlook. We entered 2026 expecting approximately $188 million of carbon EBITDA and are now on track to deliver approximately $230 million to $250 million for the full year. Looking ahead to 2027, we currently expect at least $250 million of EBITDA from our low-carbon platform. We ended the quarter with $160 million of cash and $210 million of production tax credit receivables that our monetization agreement provides a clear path to convert into cash.

Together, that is approximately $370 million of cash and tax credit value that we can put to work while maintaining balance sheet strength and flexibility. Our capital allocation framework remains consistent, clear and disciplined. First, we'll continue to invest in the safety, reliability and competitiveness of the assets we already own to drive performance and unlock additional value. Second, we will direct a portion of our cash flow towards reducing debt and strengthening our balance sheet while preserving financial flexibility. Third, we will pursue opportunities, both organic and outside of our platform, which can accelerate value creation and generate attractive risk-adjusted returns for shareholders.

We have attractive opportunities within the platform today and also have the flexibility to evaluate opportunities outside of the platform where we believe Green Plains can create more value as the owner. In every case, the standard is the same. We need a clear path to attractive risk-adjusted returns and long-term value per share. As all of our projects compete for capital, from time to time, we expect to be buyers of our own shares as well, and it may be one of the highest cash flow accretive options available. With that, I will turn it over to Ann to go through our quarterly financial results in more detail.

Ann Reis: Thanks, Chris. Our third quarter results reflect the improved operating execution Chris discussed with better base business economics and a significant contribution from our low-carbon platform. Revenue for the third quarter was $496 million compared with $508 million in the prior year period. The 2.5% decline primarily reflected lower ethanol volumes associated with the sale of the Obion plant, which offset underlying revenue growth from higher ethanol and renewable corn oil volumes across our continuing operations and higher weighted average selling prices. Net income attributable to Green Plains was $85 million or $1.03 per diluted share compared with $12 million or $0.17 per diluted share in the third quarter of 2025.

Adjusted EBITDA for the third quarter was $118 million compared with $53 million in the prior year period and $93 million in the second quarter. The quarter included $65 million of 45Z production tax credit value, net of discounts and expenses, while the base business generated $53 million of adjusted EBITDA. The consolidated ethanol crush margin increased to $123 million or $0.70 per gallon from $60 million or $0.30 per gallon over the prior year. Agribusiness and Energy Services adjusted EBITDA was $6.3 million compared with $6.7 million last year. One of the most important aspects of our performance this quarter was the significant improvement in our ethanol production results.

Gross margins increased by approximately $0.07 compared to the third quarter of last year and were also higher than the second quarter of this year. Record quarterly ethanol and corn oil yields improved production utilization, lowered operating expenses per gallon and a strong commercial execution all contributed to the improvement. Hedging impacts were negligible as financial crush positions were a positive contributor in the quarter, but were offset by mark-to-market hedge losses associated with our future physical corn purchases. The key takeaway, as Chris discussed, is that the majority of the improvement came from operational performance, commercial execution and other factors beyond the market crush environment. Turning to carbon.

As Chris discussed, the agreement to monetize the 2026 tax credits was signed during the fourth quarter. As of September 30, we had approximately $210 million of 45Z tax credit receivables on our balance sheet based on production in the first 3 quarters of the year. We will convert approximately $140 million of those receivables into cash during this quarter, and we expect to monetize our third and fourth quarter production in the first half of 2027.

The agreement provides for the transfer of a minimum of $250 million worth of tax credits and a maximum of $325 million, with an option for the buyers to purchase an additional $30 million dependent upon our total generation of 45Z tax credits in 2026. To be clear, these amounts represent the gross face value of the tax credits to be transferred, not a dollar-for-dollar contribution to adjusted EBITDA. Cash proceeds reflect the agreed transfer discount, while our 45Z related adjusted EBITDA is net of both discounts and associated operating expenses. Adjusted EBITDA from the production of 45Z tax credits increased during the third quarter due to higher qualifying production and the improved capture performance.

At Madison, improved ethanol yields lowered the plant's carbon intensity enough to qualify for a more favorable 45Z credit tier, generating approximately $6 million of additional tax credits during the quarter. We also recently announced the implementation of our Farm Forward incentive program at our Nebraska facilities, which provides another opportunity to lower the carbon intensity of qualifying gallons through recognized farming practices. For qualifying gallons, these practices can further reduce feedstock CI and increase 45Z credit value. Based on the combination of Farm Forward and other CI-lowering initiatives across our platform and continued operational improvements in the plants and sequestration assets, we expect to generate at least $250 million of carbon-related EBITDA in 2027.

Our focus remains on maximizing qualifying production, improving capture efficiency, optimizing pathway economics and converting the resulting credit value into cash as efficiently as possible. Turning to expenses. Total SG&A was $27 million in the third quarter, down approximately $2 million or 9% from the third quarter of 2025. On the balance sheet, we ended the quarter with $160 million of cash and cash equivalents and $478 million of total debt. As Chris mentioned, we have in excess of $370 million between our cash balance and production tax credit receivables, positioning us to invest in the business and pursue attractive opportunities while maintaining balance sheet strength.

Capital expenditures were approximately $12 million during the quarter, bringing year-to-date capital expenditures to $29 million. Cash flows from operating activities were $47 million through the first 9 months. Cash conversion in the first 3 quarters was affected by the build in production tax credit receivables ahead of monetization, which, as discussed, are now being converted into cash with the monetization agreement in place. Taken together, the stronger performance of our base business and the increased visibility to 45Z monetization expands the range of capital allocation opportunities available to Green Plains. As Chris mentioned, our first priority remains supporting safe, reliable and competitive operation of our assets.

We will maintain balance sheet flexibility and continue investing in high-return opportunities within the existing platform. Beyond that, we will selectively evaluate strategic opportunities where we can leverage our expertise in operational excellence, carbon capture and sequestration and our scale to create value. Any investment will need to meet a high bar for strategic fit, risk-adjusted returns and long-term per-share value creation. Where appropriate, buying back our own shares will compete against those opportunities under the same risk-adjusted return framework. We are operating from a stronger financial position, but our standards for deploying capital have not changed.

We intend to remain disciplined and selective with a focus on investments that can strengthen the long-term earnings power of Green Plains and create durable value for shareholders. With that, I will turn the call over to Imre to discuss our commercial performance and market outlook.

Imre Havasi: Thanks, Ann. As Ann mentioned, we saw improvement in our realized margins during the third quarter, and I want to spend a little time on what drove that performance. The board crush margin is an important reference point, but it is only one component of our realized economics. Our actual results reflect how we operate and commercialize across the business. We entered the third quarter with good physical corn and corn oil positions. We continue to have success managing our corn basis, optimizing our product mix, while improved plant performance allowed us to capture more value across the platform. Corn oil was a good example.

Demand remained strong during the quarter, and we benefited from both our commercial position and record yields across the platform. Our Ultra-High Protein business also performed well with stronger demand. Values have improved from the second quarter, which contributed nicely to gross margins. When you put all of those pieces together, it helps explain why our realized results were stronger than the headline industry indicators alone would suggest. That differentiation is important because it gives us more ways to create margin than simply relying on changes in board crush and spot values. Ethanol industry production remains elevated, but so does demand.

Domestic blending continues to provide a solid baseline, while export activity remains an important source of support for the market. International demand has been supportive throughout the year and continues to provide an outlet for U.S. production. Brazil remains a key market to watch. The interplay between sugar economics, domestic ethanol demand and production decisions continue to influence global ethanol trade flows and export opportunities for U.S. producers. On the corn side, the market continues to focus on harvest results and final crop size. While expectations remain for a large U.S. corn crop, demand from exports, feed usage and ethanol production continues to absorb a meaningful portion of the supply.

We continue to manage grain procurement activity and maintain a disciplined approach to both physical positions and risk management. Looking ahead, the fourth quarter has started off well. While industry margins remain below the levels we experienced during portions of the third quarter, our outlook for base ethanol profitability remains constructive. We continue to benefit from many of the same factors that supported third quarter performance, including strong plant reliability, favorable corn procurement positioning, solid corn oil economics and continued operational execution across the platform. As a result, we currently expect fourth quarter gross margins to remain above historical averages and continue to support strong profitability from the base business.

While market conditions can change, what we're seeing today gives us confidence that many of the operational, commercial and financial achievements during the third quarter are carrying forward in the fourth quarter. In closing, we remain focused on the factors we can control, optimizing our physical positions, managing risk, maximizing the value of our products and working closely with our plant teams to capture the benefit of higher yields, greater reliability and lower cost. Q3 demonstrated how those capabilities can differentiate our results even when the broader market indicators don't tell the entire story. With that, I'll turn it back to Chris.

Chris Osowski: Thanks, Imre. As we close, I want to leave you with 3 takeaways from the quarter. First, the third quarter validated our operating strategy. Operational excellence is translating into stronger operating and financial performance. We're getting more from the assets we already own and importantly, we're not done improving. We see more opportunities to improve ethanol yields, recover more corn oil and increase carbon capture performance, further strengthening the earnings power of our existing assets. Second, the execution of our 45Z monetization agreement validated our low-carbon strategy. We have demonstrated our ability to generate meaningful carbon earnings and convert that value into free cash flow. And that leads directly into the third takeaway.

We're now well positioned to put the capital to work. The combination of stronger base business performance and improved visibility into 45Z cash flows gives us greater capital allocation flexibility. We can accelerate reinvestment in high-return projects across our existing platform, maintain balance sheet strength, evaluate strategic opportunities and consider additional ways to create value for shareholders. Ultimately, the real opportunity is how we deploy that capital to further strengthen our earnings power and create long-term value for shareholders. At Central City, we already operate a highly efficient plant and the projects already underway provide a pathway to take carbon intensity even lower.

With additional reductions in natural gas use, continued improvements in plant efficiency and the benefits we expect from Farm Forward, Central City is on a path to net negative carbon intensity. Those gallons will generate approximately $1 per gallon of gross 45Z credit value. At York, we're advancing the low-energy distillation project designed to lower energy consumption, improve plant efficiency and reduce carbon intensity with front-end engineering work progressing. At Wood River, construction of additional grain storage is moving forward with the project on track for startup in early 2027 with key electrical tie-ins having just been completed. This investment will strengthen local grain procurement and operating flexibility, helping the plant manage input costs and support more consistent production.

We are also advancing oil recovery projects across the platform, having just finished commissioning new corn oil separation equipment at Shenandoah and engineering a similar project at Wood River. These are repeatable, high-returning investments designed to capture more value from each bushel. This fits squarely within our capital allocation framework, reinvest first in high-return opportunities that improve the competitiveness and the earnings power of the assets we already own. We will continue to evaluate opportunities against the same standards we've established, strategic fit, compelling risk-adjusted returns and the ability to create long-term value per share. The bar will be high. We are evaluating growth opportunities, but we are not going to overpay.

We need to see a strategic fit, a clear path to attractive returns and a compelling reason why Green Plains is the right owner. If an opportunity doesn't meet those standards, we have other attractive ways to deploy that capital. We have more options today than we have had in a long time, and we're going to be very thoughtful on how we evaluate them. We are operating better, generating more cash and entering 2027 with greater flexibility to invest in the business and create value for all Green Plains stakeholders. I want to thank our employees across Green Plains. Their commitment and execution are what has made this possible.

We accomplished a lot this quarter, and we should be very proud of that. But we're not done. We see more opportunities in front of us, and we're going to keep pushing to get better. We'll celebrate the progress and then get right back to building. With that, we'll turn the call over to the operator for questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Your first question comes from the line of Kristen Owen at Oppenheimer.

Kristen Owen: Chris, it's been just over a year since you took on the role. And I just have to start by acknowledging what a year you've really had. It's just been tremendous to see the execution. I know it takes a team, but I just wanted to acknowledge that. So against that backdrop, can we start with just sort of the base ethanol business? I mean you've done a lot to reinvest in the platform, ensure that you're getting the operating metrics there. If we were to extrapolate out, and I'm thinking about this without the 45Z credits, like how do you think about the overall run rate EBITDA of the base business today?

And maybe just relative to where it was 3 years ago, 4 years ago, like how do you think that baseline has moved? And then I'll have a follow-up.

Chris Osowski: Well, thanks for the acknowledgment, Kristen. And as you mentioned, it takes a team to get the results that we're getting. And I definitely appreciate everyone at Green Plains who's contributed a lot to improving our business. As it pertains to the run rate base business, I think it's really a question of what we've done over the past couple of years to get the Green Plains assets performing at a best-in-class level. And when we say we hit record yields for ethanol and oil in this quarter, those are real numbers, and that is real measurable results. And we have line of sight into 2027. We're basically planning to have our best year ever.

We expect ethanol yields to improve. And when ethanol yields improve, it's much easier to get better protein yields and oil yields. And the projects we have in flight right now, they have the ability to incrementally improve EBITDA in the tens of millions of dollars on an annualized basis on the go forward. But once again, the team is firing on all cylinders and really focused on executing these projects to get those results in 2027.

Kristen Owen: Great. So then now let's layer on the carbon credit piece of this. You saw a nice step-up here sequentially in carbon credit EBITDA. Obviously, you had a little bit better operating rates. But maybe can you help us in terms of what's contributing to that strength? And as it relates to the Farm Forward program, is there any sort of catch-up that we should expect on that or incremental CI reduction on a go-forward basis? Just help us think about how that contributes to the CI score overall.

Chris Osowski: Okay. So I'll cover the incremental improvement on carbon performance, and then I'll hand it off to Ann to talk a little bit about Farm Forward. Effectively, we have a team that is -- now has almost a year of operating the carbon sequestration equipment under their belt. And I think the relationship we have between our operations group and Tallgrass is only getting better and the communication is getting better, and we're learning how to operate the equipment even more efficiently than we did earlier in the year. And we have a line of sight to that improving into 2027.

At the same time, when we run these plants at high utilization rates and high yields, all of the carbon intensity factors improve. So it's kind of like a synergistic result. When all the wheels are turning, we are able to produce more gallons at a lower CI score. We're able to dilute fixed cost amongst more volume and the whole business economics improve.

Ann Reis: Yes. And I can touch a bit on Farm Forward. So we're really excited about this program and being able to roll it out. It's something we've been working on for a while, but really just needed the policy attached to it for us to be able to have full confidence to roll it out. We're starting with our Nebraska facility, the whole concept of walk before you run. So we're making sure everything is going to work well there, which we're already seeing good sign-ups even with the farmers still in the fields and harvesting. We're getting a lot of interest and a lot of great questions.

The program that we've rolled out will help add premium to the bushels that are brought in anywhere from $0.05 to $0.25 a bushel depending on what the farmer CI score is. And it will go through verification and validation. So as of right now, we're not really in a place to be able to say exactly how much additionality we're going to get from the Farm Forward program, but we'll be able to talk more to that in future quarters as we start to get the results in and start to get the CI scores and the farming practices and the information from the farmers.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Matthew Blair from TPH.

Matthew Blair: On the very strong results. Chris, I wanted to ask about capital allocation. Thanks for outlining your priorities. But I was wondering if you could put maybe a few numbers around 2 of the components. You mentioned that you're looking to reduce debt. I believe that at one point, Green Plains had a target for 2x net leverage. You're obviously a lot better than that today. But are there any dollar figures in terms of the target for debt reduction in 2027? And then you also mentioned organic opportunities or organic spending. I think growth CapEx might be around maybe $20 million or $25 million this year. Is that a good number for 2027?

Or do you think it would go up materially?

Chris Osowski: Okay. I appreciate the question. And when it comes to debt reduction, of course, we have plans in place to take care of some convertible debt in early 2027. But as it pertains to growth CapEx, we would expect that $20 million to $25 million number to bump up into 2027.

We have line of sight to numerous projects that are very low in terms of technical risk that will help improve both the base business, but then also capitalize on 45Z opportunity, one of which is the project we are just wrapping up, getting close to wrapping up in Wood River for an additional 4.5 million bushels of grain storage, which we are looking to replicate in other locations and the next location would be Central City.

Which has a synergistic benefit for the business because it allows us to take advantage of peak arrival pressure during harvest and capture more bushels directly from the farmers, which then also has a synergistic effect as it pertains to the Farm Forward program and lowering the CI score of the plant. So we have a strategy around our overall grain storage assets and we'll look to deploy that in 2027. On top of that, we have additional improvement projects within the fleet to further reduce natural gas consumption and extract more oil per bushel.

And I mean, we have great line of sight to significant improvements in oil yields that we would expect to be able to execute on in 2027.

Matthew Blair: Sounds good. And then could you talk a little bit more about the environment you're seeing so far in the fourth quarter? I think there was talk that margins are below certain points -- current margins are below certain points of Q3. But in general, if the quarter ended today, do you think you would be a little bit below Q3 profitability? And any other moving parts that you could touch on would be great.

Imre Havasi: Yes. This is Imre. I'm going to take that question. So as I mentioned in the prepared remarks, the quarter started out well, of course. But Q4 generally is a softer quarter as seasonality is starting to kick in with domestic demand, driving demand lower than for the rest of the year. So I think that we cannot avoid this year. Those weaker demand numbers are starting to show up. But you can expect that pretty much every year. Again, lower ethanol demand, a little better DDG values, somewhat softer corn oil values for the same reason. But what -- maybe I want to highlight a couple of things that are specific to this year.

Of course, corn futures dropped significantly. We've all witnessed a very significant sell-off, and that is helping crush margins, both crush margins. Export sales are robust. They are going to be -- we continue to see very strong export demand in Q4. And natural gas cost is low. So we have certain components of this consolidated crush margin that are offsetting some of the seasonal pressures. One thing to watch, though, is corn basis. Harvest is getting delayed. Prices have fallen so much that the farmer is now a reluctant seller. So we got to be a bit careful here how we finish the year, Q4 going into Q1 in terms of physical corn availability.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Pooran Sharma from Stephens.

Pooran Sharma: I just wanted to maybe get your comment you alluded to strong export demand, but maybe wanted to get your sense as to how much visibility you have into continued momentum in '27? Are there particular markets that we've made gains in or maybe are planning to make gains in that make this momentum more sticky as we go through the next [indiscernible]?

Imre Havasi: Yes. This is Imre, again. Thanks for the question. Yes, we do expect exports to move even higher than current levels. I mean if you go back '24, we exported a little over 2 billion gallons, '25, 2.3 billion, a little north of 2.3 billion. We're going to probably end the year at somewhere between 2.4 billion and 2.5 billion, and our forecast for next year is north of 2.6 billion. The demand is out there. There's some -- of course, the same suspects, Canada, the EU and of course, South America and the Far East. The interesting thing is that export volume has grown quite significantly, but it has grown proportionately.

So in terms of the market share of that export volume hasn't really changed. Canada is still taking 35%. The EU has grown a little bit, about 25%, 30% if you throw in the U.K. So we expect those share percentages to remain relatively stable and expect some growth in Asia and perhaps South America. Not sure about Mexico. They are taking some, but there may be an opportunity there as well. But just in general, we're expecting another, let's just say, 200 million gallons of growth in exports to pretty much the same destination, but some incremental opportunities in -- outside Canada and the EU. Brazil is uncertain. They took some in January.

We're currently cheaper on a FOB basis than Brazilian ethanol. That may be in play also for Q1, especially as sugar prices are where they are today, and they will probably process more sugarcane for sugar than ethanol in Q1, early Q2.

Pooran Sharma: That's very helpful. And -- just for my follow-up, Chris, you kind of alluded to it and hear you on the don't skip leg day message. But you hit 95% utilization this quarter. I think in the past, you've hit quarters where that's kind of higher. As we get out of spring and fall maintenance, do you see opportunity for that number to get sequentially higher in 4Q? Or how should we think about utilization?

Chris Osowski: Well, I mean, for our fleet of plants, we just in the last month, executed fall outages in 5 of the locations safely and efficiently. And the team is always focused as part of continuous improvement on tightening that window of downtime. So I'm looking at Trent Collins across the table here, who is our Head of Operational Excellence in our -- leading our operations team who is driving that improved performance. But as far as Q4 goes, we would expect to be in that mid-90% utilization rate.

And as a general rule for operations, whatever the nameplate capacity of an asset is, we view that 95% is kind of our benchmark for what we expect best-in-class to be, and that's what we want to operate all of our assets to that kind of a standard. So we feel pretty good about where we're at. We do have additional projects that are in the works for 2027 that could not necessarily -- unlock a little bit of capacity, but really more focused on improving yields and lowering OpEx that will help improve that number potentially.

Pooran Sharma: Appreciate the detail. Congrats on the results and the outlook.

Operator: Your last question comes from the line of Ben Mayhew from BMO Capital Markets.

Benjamin Mayhew: Congratulations on the really strong quarterly performance and string of strong performances to date. My first question has to do with the CI levels of your existing asset base. And I'm wondering how much runway you have on improving your existing asset base CI level? And what type of capital investment would be needed to maximize your asset-wide CI score across your plants over time? Like is this a multiyear investment time line? Or is this stuff that can be pulled forward more over the next year or 2? I'll stop there.

Ann Reis: Ben, this is Ann. I'll maybe start and then let Chris kind of chime in with some additional CapEx that we're looking at. But overall, we haven't given specific scores for each plant because they really are -- each one is different and unique depending on where they're located and how they've been constructed and what other pieces of equipment that are associated with the facility. I think just in general, if you wanted to try to do a rough calculation, what they start with is a 50 and then we're taking off 6 points for the iLUC penalty being removed. And we've talked about how we buy RECs to offset our electricity usage. So that's roughly another 6 points.

And then there's other different pieces like the sequestration, right, that some facilities have and others don't. So you can kind of back into some rough scores that way. The Farm Forward program is now going to create a different level of calculation that will be dependent on what growing practices and how much farmer-originated corn that we can receive at each facility, which is why the capital improvements such as adding the storage to Wood River and some of the other ones that we've talked about is so important because it allows us to take more farmer-originated corn. There's definitely -- we've talked about the net negative score at Central City that we're looking towards.

So each facility, we're looking at closely to see what is -- what makes the most sense from a capital perspective. We want to make sure that what we're putting in and we're getting the returns out of it. And we've got a window here with 45Z. We don't have an expectation that it's necessarily going to be extended in the same format that it is today. So really, everything we want to be able to accomplish and see the returns quickly. But also for perpetuity, if we can see these projects that reduce our natural gas or reduce our electricity, that's something that's going to be great for the entire platform even beyond 45Z.

Chris Osowski: Yes. Just to add maybe a little bit to what, Ann, answered there. With the 5-point rounding adjustments, we have line of sight to hitting those type numbers in each of our locations and really focused on getting Central City to that net negative level. And then we'll work on even in parallel, the rest of the location to try to maximize the opportunity and reduce the overall OpEx in our plants. And I can say with certainty that we're working as efficiently as we can to quantify the total CapEx of these projects and then get them executed in parallel. But as we've mentioned in previous calls, we want to do all of these things with absolute discipline.

We want to measure twice and cut once and make sure that what we are putting in is going to work effectively, and it's going to be providing value for the long haul.

Benjamin Mayhew: Got it. That's very helpful. And then just for my follow-up question because a lot has already been covered. I guess I'd be interested in hearing your thoughts on from a policy perspective, now that the midterms are behind us, like how are you thinking about 2027 and some of the opportunities for the biofuel industry versus some of the risks? I'd just like to get your quick thoughts on that and maybe as investors, what we should be looking out for?

Ann Reis: Yes. Thanks for the question. Obviously, top of mind for a lot of folks right now. The thing that we've always said and continue to fully believe is that ethanol is really bipartisan. So it's applicable both sides of the aisle. And we've had -- we do have great relationships and we'll continue to have really great relationships with all legislators that are within the different states that we have assets. There's some new ones, obviously, there is the results of this week definitely mix things up a bit in some areas. And we're excited to build those new relationships.

And for the ones that maybe aren't as familiar with ethanol, we always see that as an opportunity for us to go and share our story and why we believe they should be very bullish on ethanol and help us as far as driving policy and protecting the farmers.

Operator: We have reached the end of the Q&A session. I will now turn the call back to Chris Osowski for closing remarks.

Chris Osowski: Thanks, everyone, for joining our call today and your continued interest in Green Plains. We look forward to giving you another great update next quarter.

Operator: This concludes today's call. Thank you for attending. You may now disconnect.

#3122. The United Explorer Card Is Great if You Fly Basic Economy

Basic economy tickets come with plenty of restrictions, but holding the right credit card is my top trick for avoiding some of them.

As airfares remain high, that basic economy fare might look more tempting than ever. Saving $100 on a round-trip domestic flight could mean more money for hotels, dining or other experiences at your destination.

I’ve flown my fair share of basic economy flights, which come with restrictions like being unable to select a seat, earning no award miles and boarding last. You also can’t make changes or cancel your itinerary without paying a hefty fee, and — specific to United Airlines — you can’t bring a full-size carry-on on board.

But as a United frequent flyer, I have a secret to share with you: Holding the United℠ Explorer Card (annual fee: $0 intro for the first year, then $150) lets you avoid several of those basic economy restrictions.

Right now, new United℠ Explorer Card applicants can receive this welcome offer: Earn 70,000 bonus miles after you spend $3,000 on purchases in the first 3 months your account is open. Plus, earn 10,000 bonus miles when you add an authorized user in the first 3 months your account is open.

Most major airlines no longer let you earn points or miles on basic economy fares. United is an exception, though — assuming you hold the right credit card.

Eligible cardholders, including those who have the United℠ Explorer Card, earn at least 3 miles per $1 spent on United basic economy tickets, excluding taxes and select fees. That’s half of what a standard economy ticket earns for cardholders (6 miles per $1), but it’s better than zero. If you have elite status, you’ll earn more.

Those miles are in addition to the 3 miles per $1 you earn on all United purchases when using your United℠ Explorer Card.

With the card, your miles can become more valuable. That’s because cardholders get at least 10% off award tickets that are operated by United or United Express. If you have United status, that discount gets bumped up to at least 15% off.

With the credit card, you have access to priority boarding in Group 2. That means you’ll be able to board earlier compared to the rest of the basic economy passengers in Group 6, making it more likely you’ll find space for your carry-on bag.

Now, you might be thinking: Wait a minute… Basic economy doesn’t allow you to bring a carry-on bag. Let me explain how that works.

United enforces its full-size carry-on restriction based on your boarding group. Group 6 passengers can't bring a full-size carry-on.

Because the credit card gets you Group 2 boarding, you essentially skip that restriction.

Premier members — who board in Group 2 or earlier — are also exempt from the full-size carry-on restriction when flying basic economy.

If you don’t want to deal with the hassle of a carry-on bag, you can opt to check it instead.

As long as you pay for your ticket using your United℠ Explorer Card, you’ll be able to check your first bag — and your companion’s first bag — for free when traveling on United. (If you’re booking an award ticket, make sure to use your card to pay for the taxes and fees.)

Keep in mind that if the first flight on your itinerary is operated by another airline, that airline’s baggage rules would apply and you would have to pay for your bag.

Of course, holding the right United credit card only gets you so far.

With basic economy, you’ll still need to pay a fee to change or cancel your ticket, and you won’t be able to select a seat for free.

Ultimately, whether basic economy is a good deal depends on a few factors.

If your plans might change, pay up for standard economy. Otherwise, the penalty to change or cancel will end up costing you more than you saved.

Another thing to consider is whether you’re willing to sit in a middle seat. You might be fine with it for a few hours, but what about a long-haul flight to Asia? Everyone’s threshold is different, so you’ll need to decide whether the middle-seat gamble is worth it.

If your plans are firm and you don’t mind a potential middle seat, booking a basic economy ticket can be a solid way to save money. Just book with a United card like, the United℠ Explorer Card, to avoid the biggest downsides.

#3120. There's No Rulebook For AI In Compliance Yet—That's Not Permission To Skip Explainability

Madhu Nadig is co-founder & CTO of Flagright - building the AML compliance infrastructure for Financial Institutions.

The Federal Reserve, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation replaced 15-year-old model risk guidance with SR 26-2. The guidance is expected to be most relevant to banking organizations with more than $30 billion in assets, and is not itself a prescriptive AI rule. Yet, one footnote has wider implications for banks experimenting with AI: Generative and agentic AI models are outside the guidance’s scope because they are novel and changing rapidly.

That carveout could be misread as permission to wait for regulators to finish writing the rules. It is not.

The same footnote directs banks to use their existing risk-management and governance practices to determine appropriate controls. Federal Reserve Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman later said that banks are already relying on existing frameworks and that other governance practices are expected to support generative and agentic AI adoption. Earlier in the year, the U.S. Treasury released a Financial Services AI Risk Management Framework, adapting the NIST framework to the operational, regulatory and consumer-protection realities of financial services.

While the industry does not have a complete AI-specific supervisory playbook, it does have a clear direction, namely that accountability cannot be deferred until the guidance catches up.

Explainability is often treated as the answer to AI risk. It is necessary, especially when an AI system influences an alert, investigation or regulatory filing, but it is not sufficient.

A generative model can produce a fluent explanation that sounds convincing without proving that the explanation faithfully represents how the output was produced. In a financial crime workflow, a well-written rationale is not evidence that the conclusion is accurate, complete or consistent with policy.

The more useful standard is whether an AI-assisted decision is auditable, reconstructable and contestable.

Those capabilities require more than a model description, but instead require controls around the entire workflow.

Risk does not come from the words “generative AI” or “agentic AI” but from what the system can access, recommend and do.

A tool summarizing a public policy document should not face the same controls as an agent reviewing transaction data or drafting a suspicious activity report. Institutions should classify each use case by materiality, data sensitivity, customer impact, regulatory impact and degree of autonomy.

One practical distinction is between assistive systems that retrieve or summarize information, advisory systems that recommend an action and agentic systems that can execute steps or call other systems. As authority and consequence increase, so should testing, approval requirements and monitoring.

For consequential workflows, institutions need an evidence trail that covers the system, not only its final answer. Subject to appropriate security and retention controls, that record should include the model and version used, system instructions, relevant input data, retrieved sources, permissions, human review and final action.

This matters because AI systems are not static. Without versioned records, an institution may be unable to explain why two apparently similar cases produced different outcomes.

Traceability also changes the quality of human review. An analyst cannot meaningfully challenge an output if the evidence behind it is hidden or if the system presents a conclusion without showing its sources.

“Human in the loop” is not a control if the human merely clicks approve. Reviewers need the information, authority and time to challenge the system.

High-consequence actions should have explicit approval gates. Agentic systems should operate with defined tool permissions, transaction and rate limits, escalation paths and an immediate way to suspend execution. Institutions should also decide which actions the system may never take without human authorization.​

Model benchmarks rarely reflect the conditions of a live compliance operation. Validation should measure the performance of the full workflow, including data retrieval, policy interpretation, analyst interaction and downstream actions.​

The relevant question is not simply whether the model performs well, but whether the combined system remains reliable for its intended purpose and whether failures are detected before they become decisions.

Using a third-party AI product does not transfer accountability to the vendor. Banks need enough visibility to understand how the product behaves in their use case and how changes could affect that behavior.

Due diligence and contracts should address model and feature-change notifications, data use and retention, subprocessors, security controls, evaluation methods, audit evidence, incident notification, service continuity and rollback options. Institutions should also test vendor claims against their own data and risk profile rather than treating a general benchmark as validation.

This does not require vendors to disclose every line of proprietary code, but it does require them to provide enough evidence for a regulated customer to govern the outcome.

The wrong response to regulatory uncertainty is to freeze useful AI projects. The other wrong response is to deploy them through scattered pilots with no common controls, and both approaches create delay.

A reusable governance layer makes adoption faster. When every new use case enters the same process for ownership, risk classification, evidence capture, permissions, testing, human oversight and incident response, teams spend less time reinventing controls and more time evaluating whether the use case creates value.

The regulators’ carveout is not an accountability gap. It is a warning against forcing rapidly evolving systems into a checklist designed for a different class of technology. Future guidance may change the details, but the durable questions are already visible: Who owns the system? What decision can it influence? What evidence does it use? What can it do? How is it tested? Who can stop it? Can the institution reconstruct what happened?

Financial institutions that can answer those questions will be better prepared for whatever guidance arrives next, and they will be better prepared to deploy AI responsibly now.

#3119. Starwood: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Starwood's $800 million 2026 resolution target would clear over 40% of its nonaccrual real estate, while the board weighs whether the dividend can stay.

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 6, 2026, Starwood (STWD -1.25%) reported distributable earnings, a non-GAAP metric measuring cash available for dividend payouts, of $0.41 per share excluding realized losses. Shareholders can't ignore how effectively the commercial mortgage lender recycles capital from older loans into higher-yielding investments. Three things management said stand out.

Starwood resolved $254 million of nonaccrual loans, which are nonperforming loans where interest collection is in doubt, and real estate owned, which refers to foreclosed properties on the balance sheet. Cleaning up those legacy positions allows management to recycle capital into fresh loans with higher interest rates.

Starwood increased its Current Expected Credit Losses (CECL) reserve, an accounting buffer for expected bad loans, by $369 million because of rate-driven macroeconomic models. Management noted that the stock's current discount to undepreciated book value, or net asset value, implies severe loss rates that don't match real-world asset sales.

Third-quarter distributable earnings came in at $0.41 per share, falling short of the quarterly dividend payout of $0.48 per share. Management plans to review the payout ratio, which measures dividend payments against earnings, with the board to preserve liquidity until loan resolutions restore earning power.

Commercial real estate conditions are healing as construction slows and property supply declines across major markets. Starwood relies on its massive scale, energy infrastructure lending platform, and non-real-estate earnings streams to cushion the impact of higher interest rates. Executive focus centers on optimizing borrowing costs and executing steady asset resolutions.

A deep liquidity pool of $1.1 billion lets the business manage pre-2023 loans for long-term recovery rather than forced short-term sales. Reinvesting repaid capital into high-yielding new loans positions the portfolio to rebuild distributable earnings as credit market friction eases.

#3118. We Write About Saving Money; Here’s How We Trick Our Brains Into Doing It

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

Even personal finance writers and editors need psychological hacks to save money. Here are the tips we use, and why they work.

While staring at the Container Store cart on my phone at 11 p.m., I did something for the first time that I’d read about a hundred times. Instead of spending $200 on more organizational boxes that I categorically did not need, I transferred that amount to my savings account.

Normally, my willpower is no match for the very real psychological phenomenon called present bias: Our brains light up more when we’re rewarding our current selves than our future selves.

Research has also shown that you imagine your future self almost like a stranger — it’s tougher to care about that stranger than about who you are right now. But that night, I saw near-future-me using that $200 on next summer’s vacation. I wanted the vacation more than the boxes. So I abandoned my cart.

I had managed to use a psychological savings trick: Find a goal that helps you envision your future self. With this epiphany in mind, I asked some of my fellow Nerds to share the savings habits they’ve put to work in their own lives. Perhaps reading these can give late-night you some saving inspiration.

Kimberly Palmer, senior writer and spokesperson: I let nonessential items sit in my online shopping cart for at least 24 hours before buying them. It definitely makes me realize I don't need a lot of them! I also informed my children of this rule, and it has helped cut down on their requests — or at least they know they have to be patient.

Karen Gaudette Brewer, head of content: Fellow let-it-sit-in-the-cart person here. I wait for notifications that something's at least 30% off before I make any moves. Ideally, 40% to 50% off.

Julie Myhre-Nunes, managing editor: When I browse online, I add an item to my shopping cart and wait 24 to 48 hours. After that, I either decide it’s a waste of money/an impulse purchase and delete it from my cart (or forget about the cart altogether), or I decide I want it and make the purchase — it’s the former 99% of the time.

Why it works: “Waiting 1 to 2 days allows me to take the emotion out of purchasing. I no longer succumb to marketing or sales, and instead make spending decisions based on what my family and I actually need or can use.” — Julie again, eloquently making the point for me.

Caitlin Constantine, managing editor: My one real shopping weakness is books, and I’ve found I can get a very close approximation of that feeling without spending an outrageous amount of money by going to the library, wandering around the stacks to see what books might look interesting, and checking out a bunch of them. Even if I don’t end up reading them, I’m still helping the library with circulation numbers, so I see it as a win-win.

Spencer Tierney, senior writer: Plus one to Caitlin Constantine’s “my one real shopping weakness is books.” If I want an older or smaller book, I'll try to find it at one of four libraries I belong to on Libby, the library e-book reader app. (The Libby waitlist for new books can take months, so I have to account for that.)

Why it works: There’s no secret here: It’s nice to get free stuff. You might be surprised what the library has to offer, like movies, magazine subscriptions, games, classes and theater tickets.

Pamela de la Fuente, managing editor: We always tell people to automate savings, and I do in my high-yield savings account, but Dasha Kennedy, the woman behind “The Broke Black Girl”, told Elizabeth Ayoola on the Smart Money podcast that you should invest, even a little bit every week or so, for future you. So I just set up a small recurring deposit to my robo-advisor.

Why it works: You only have to make this decision once for your future self, not over and over again. And if you do it early enough, you could avoid being part of the 41% of Americans who wish they had started investing earlier, according to a 2026 NerdWallet survey.

Athena Cocoves, managing editor: To cut down on food delivery, I started cooking when I feel like it instead of when I’m supposed to. I exercise free will and make soup at 10 p.m. It sounds more obvious than it feels, and it's made a big difference in my budget. And it'd make an even bigger difference if I wasn't also rewarding myself with fancy spices and vinegars, but a girl's gotta splurge somehow.

Ryan Brady, lead writer: My wife takes advantage of a T-Mobile freebie that gives us a discount for DoorDash deliveries. She uses it to buy groceries from Aldi instead of takeout. Aldi is far from us. Publix is right across the street, but more expensive. So this saves us money on the actual items and also helps us not impulse buy (as we often do when we're in-store shopping).

Why it works: You don’t need to call on willpower if you can avoid the situation that tempts you to spend money.

» Read more: Strategies to save on groceries that actually work

Kenley Young, managing editor: I use credit cards for most purchases to get those sweet, sweet rewards, but there's a lot in this article that I've also taken to heart.

I've started using library resources more, and it's saving me money on things like monthly subscriptions.

I've negotiated down several monthly bills, too: refinanced my car loan, got cheaper homeowners insurance, opted for a little less auto coverage in exchange for a lower premium, and haggled online with everyone from Xfinity and SiriusXM to my local newspaper until they all gave me a discount.

Plus, I've opted for some home improvement projects with the expectation that my utility bills would be lower. A plumber finally fixed our toilet, which has led to lower water bills, and I even installed solar panels.

Lastly, my analog skill (playing live music) has become a steady side hustle. I play eight to 10 gigs a month, where (on top of my baseline rate) I also get tips, free food and beer.

Why it works: Because you’re Kenley and you put in a lot of effort.

But you don’t need to be Kenley to find a savings habit that works for your personality, your financial situation and even your musical talents. You just need to experiment. Pick the strategy that speaks to you most, and test it out. Which one are you going to try first?

#3117. This Janus Henderson fund manager owns CoreWeave debt — here's why he's sticking with it

CoreWeave can overcome the market's skepticism about its debt.

That isn't the consensus view — some Coreweave debt remains deeply distressed with yields above 15%. But Coreweave should power through this tough stretch, according to John Lloyd, global head of multi-sector and corporate credit at Janus Henderson.

"It's a little bit of overreacting," Lloyd tells CNBC, referring to the sell-off in Coreweave bonds, which have tanked along with its equity.

Lloyd owns Coreweave 9.75% bonds due in 2031 in the firm's Multi-Sector Income Fund. The yield to maturity on the debt is now 15.97%, a more than 70% jump since its issuance in April. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.

"Bond prices are lower, spreads are wider, yields are wider, and I don't see a huge fundamental change in the ecosystem right now that would warrant that, other than their higher cost of financing, which I think they can get creative with," Lloyd added.

CoreWeave has taken on a massive amount of debt to fund its data center buildout. The company has roughly $51.6 billion in total debt, including about $35 billion in notes, bonds and loans.

The market is getting nervous about how CoreWeave will be able to keep financing its data centers, and at what cost. Its stock has tumbled 20% over the past week, while the spread on its five-year credit default swaps is nearly 1,081 basis points — lower than earlier in the session but up 13% week over week. Spreads of 1,000 basis points and above are generally a sign of credit distress.

CoreWeave shares moved roughly 2% higher on Tuesday, after tumbling over the past several days and hitting a 52-week low earlier in the session. Its bond yields and spreads remain highly elevated.

Lloyd believes the selloff is a bump in the road for the neocloud company.

The market has been spooked by the jump in Treasury rates, which pushes up funding costs for companies, he explained. The focus largely turned to companies like CoreWeave that have refinance risk when rates move higher, he said.

CoreWeave leverage is high with a debt-to-equity ratio of 702%, up from 290% a year ago. Moreover, CoreWeave will spend an estimated $36.4 billion on capital expenditures this year against Ebitda of $7.5 billion, according to consensus estimates.

Revenue and Ebitda will ramp up next year, hitting $26.5 billion and $16.7 billion respectively, analysts estimate. But capex will hit $47.9 billion, indicating the company may need to finance its data center buildout with more equity issuance and/or debt.

Lloyd isn't necessarily worried about CoreWeave's ability to finance its capital expenditures, despite the fact that its capex outweighs its free-cash flow.

"Next year … they're going to be generating operating free-cash flow that'll support some of that capex need," he said.

The company can also turn to other methods of funding, like more GPU financing, which will allow it to borrow against its graphics processing units or rental contracts, he noted. In addition, CoreWeave could ask its biggest customers — including Microsoft, Meta Platforms and OpenAI — to increase their prepayments, he added.

"They can probably get creative enough where they don't even need to come to the high-yield market," Lloyd said.

The company also doesn't have any near-term maturities, which means it isn't facing a refinancing risk anytime soon, he added.

Meanwhile the supply/demand dynamic should remain tight across the AI compute landscape. Overall adoption rates within the ecosystem are running above consensus demand curves, he said. Add to that a bottleneck in supply, with chips and memory power sold out, and it's a nice set up for CoreWeave.

"All data point to the business model functioning very, very well," Lloyd said. "CoreWeave is one of the best-in-class at getting data centers up and actually running them," he added, noting that CoreWeave's financials have been improving throughout the year.

Another turning point could come if Anthropic goes forth with an IPO, expected in November, followed by OpenAI. Successful IPOs for the frontier labs could soothe market nerves and help support the neocloud operators.

"You just need more of those data points where people become more comfortable with the AI demand side," Lloyd said.

CoreWeave still needs to convince markets it can handle higher market rates and get through the financing bottlenecks.

Lloyd sees the company making it, albeit with some bumps along the way. The bonds should recover, he says, "just not in that straight line."

#3115. How IPv4 Became An Asset Class Most Technology Leaders Still Misread

Vincentas Grinius is a tech entrepreneur and cofounder of IPXO, with a focus on internet infrastructure and sustainable digital innovation.

The internet ran out of new IPv4 addresses years ago. The regional registries that allocate them exhausted the pool between 2011 and 2020, depending on the region. Yet the world kept connecting billions of new devices, and it still runs, overwhelmingly, on the same 4 billion IPv4 addresses it has always had.

That gap between fixed supply and rising demand did something quiet yet consequential. It turned a block of numbers into a traded asset with a real, moving price. Address space is now bought, sold and leased on a secondary market most people outside the field have never heard of. Yet most technology leaders still treat it the way they always did, as free plumbing somewhere in the network stack.

That blind spot is getting expensive. If your business runs on distributed infrastructure, address space is a line item that behaves less like a utility and more like a scarce input you have to manage. It is not infinite, and it is not a simple commodity either. The pool cannot grow; IPv6 has been arriving for two decades without displacing IPv4 for most traffic, and the value of what already exists is real. In my years working in this market, I have watched capable teams misjudge it in the same few ways.

The most common mistake is timing. Acquiring address space and putting it to use are two distinct problems on two different clocks, and leaders routinely conflate them.

Acquisition is a capital problem. With a budget and a willing seller, a sizable block can change hands in a few weeks. Deployment is an operating problem. A block earns nothing while it is owned. It earns only when it is routing traffic for a real workload, and getting there requires provisioning, building routing reputation and clearing the hurdles that come with reputation-sensitive resources. That does not speed up just because you spend more. A team that budgets for the fast clock and plans around the slow one ends up with idle inventory and a timeline that slips by quarters.

The second mistake is treating price as a one-way bet. For most of this market’s history, prices rose, and much of the early narrative assumed they always would. They did not. Prices fell over the past couple of years as the largest buyers pulled back, then steadied. Anyone who underwrote address space as a guaranteed appreciation learned that the income it can generate, not the number on the screen, is what carries the case.

This is closer to real estate than to a commodity. Value comes from use over time and a gradual lease-up as the space is deployed, not from holding a static thing and waiting for it to be worth more. Block size matters, too. Large and small blocks sit in different price ranges and have moved differently. The asset is not a uniform thing.

There is one more factor that never appears in a price quote but quietly determines whether a purchase was smart. Address space is administered by five regional registries, and in some regions, a national layer sits on top. The rules vary widely. Some regions allow addresses to move freely. Others impose multiyear holding periods, restrict transfers or leave leasing in a legal gray zone. Two blocks can carry the same price yet be very different assets once you try to use or move them. A cheap block from a restrictive regime can be the more expensive choice.

None of this makes IPv4 inherently good or bad to hold. It makes it a real asset with real characteristics, and the error is treating it as anything less. In practice, that means a few shifts. Put address space on the managed-asset list, not the plumbing list. When you acquire, diligence the regime under which a block sits as carefully as the price. Plan capital and timelines against the slow deployment clock, not the fast acquisition clock. And weigh leasing against owning honestly because for many operators, using address space without carrying it on the balance sheet is now a rational choice rather than an exotic one.

While the industry spent a decade fixated on the application layer, the address layer beneath it became a scarce, priced, actively traded resource. Organizations that recognize this and treat their addresses accordingly will be better positioned to make sharper infrastructure and capital decisions than those still counting on plumbing to be free.

#3114. Nvidia Stock Falls Below $180: Is It a Bargain Buy?

News of a relationship involving a possible Chinese spy and CEO Jensen Huang has resulted in Nvidia's stock falling sharply.

After years of tremendous gains, 2026 is proving to be a much more challenging one for chip giant Nvidia (NVDA -4.32%). Heading into this week, the stock has been flat, and news that CEO Jensen Huang has been involved in an affair with a Chinese spy has sparked new concerns about governance and potential government repercussions.

The stock has been struggling mightily of late and may soon hit a new 52-week low. Is Nvidia really in trouble, or is the market overreacting, and could this instead be a great buying opportunity for investors?

Prior to this week, the big concerns around big tech were that the recent midterm election results might result in greater pushback on data centers and artificial intelligence (AI) spending as a whole. If that happens, then Nvidia, whose chips are front and center in AI development, could see its growth rate fall significantly.

Now, however, there are also concerns that Huang's relationship with a Chinese spy might open up a whole new can of worms. The tech company is looking into the matter, and there may be possible blowback from the government as well, which has been highly restrictive of the types of chips that can be sold to China.

While there's no doubt that Nvidia's business has experienced tremendous growth due to AI, the market appears to be pricing in greater uncertainty and risk ahead. The big question for investors is whether these risks are exaggerated, and if the stock is worth buying at these reduced levels.

Due to Nvidia's decline in value and impressive growth, it's now trading at a forward price-to-earnings multiple of just 12, which is based on analyst expectations. It's an incredibly low price tag for such a top growth stock. However, it also depends on the company continuing to grow at a fast pace.

There's some risk here due to that, but overall, I'm not overly concerned about the spying scandal. Any mistake Huang may have made was likely just that -- a mistake; not something worthy of a serious reprimand from either the government or the company itself.

Buying the stock on this decline in value could be a great move for long-term investors, as Nvidia's chips remain in high demand and with fantastic margins, the business still looks poised to be a top stock to own for many years to come.

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

TL;DR: Mortgage rates dropped today, but inflation data could shake things up next week.

With the midterm elections behind us, mortgage rates are continuing their gradual slide this month. One factor is a sell-off in tech stocks, which can send investors toward the relative safety of bonds and help push mortgage rates lower.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage ticked down to 6.96% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is five basis points lower than yesterday and 11 basis points lower than a week ago. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.)

Meanwhile, a stronger-than-expected jobs report could slow that slide by reinforcing expectations for another Federal Reserve rate hike in December.

And a reminder: While the economy never sleeps, markets are closed on the weekends. The rates you see Friday are unlikely to change much (if at all) until Monday.

Here are the average APRs we're seeing today, as well as movement over the past month for context:

As for what’s next: Tomorrow’s jobs report, showing October data, could potentially nudge mortgage rates in either direction. To understand the link between jobs data and mortgage rates, keep reading below the video.

» Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

The recent slide in mortgage rates might reverse course if next week’s inflation data comes in hot.

This week, the Nerds are watching the October Consumer Price Index, which comes out on Tuesday, Nov. 10. CPI is one of two key measures of inflation, which the Federal Reserve aims to keep in check relative to the strength of the labor market. (The Fed looks more closely at the other data set, the Personal Consumption Expenditures Index, which comes out Nov. 25.)

Right now, the labor market is looking pretty darn healthy: The October jobs report, released today from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, showed U.S. employers added 165,000 jobs in October, far more than economists expected, and unemployment edged down to 4.1%.

Raising the federal funds rate is the Fed’s main tool for bringing inflation down, but rate hikes are only on the table when the labor market is strong enough to handle it. Right now, it’s looking fairly likely that the Fed will approve a rate hike when the committee meets Dec. 8-9. The Fed doesn't set mortgage rates directly, but an anticipated rate hike can put upward pressure on mortgage rates, which respond to investors’ expectations for the economy and Fed policy.

Still, a jump in mortgage rates isn’t a sure thing. October’s inflation data will capture the effect of the Fed’s last rate hike, which came in the middle of September. If that worked as expected and inflation shows signs of slowing, mortgage rates will be less affected.

Refinancing might make sense if today’s rates are at least 0.5 to 0.75 of a percentage point lower than your current rate (and if you plan to stay in your home long enough to break even on closing costs).

With rates where they are right now, you may want to start considering a refi if your current rate is around 7.46% or higher.

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

If you're looking for a lower rate, use NerdWallet's refinance calculator to estimate savings and understand how long it would take to break even on the costs of refinancing.

» Time to refi? Compare refinance rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates.

If the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a new home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy.
