#3112. In The Age Of Abundant AI, Context Is The Competitive Advantage

Michael Amori is CEO and cofounder of Virtualitics. A data scientist and entrepreneur with a background in finance and physics.

Over the last several months, the conversation about large language models (LLMs) has focused on capability: which models are most advanced, which proof points matter and which companies are moving too fast. The AI race has largely been framed as a race for better technology.​

Those questions still matter, but a fundamental shift is underway within the enterprise as AI capabilities become increasingly accessible through cloud providers, software platforms and enterprise ecosystems. Much of the dialogue treats all AI use cases the same when they can be fundamentally different.​

AI, in general, is becoming abundant and increasingly accessible, but AI with context remains scarce.​

For most organizations, the challenge has shifted from obtaining intelligence to applying it effectively, considering an organization’s unique data, workflows, policies, governance and institutional knowledge.​

As AI becomes more widely available, intelligence will become less differentiated, and competitive advantage will be derived from the context a model operates within. The ability to transform intelligence into trusted decisions and measurable outcomes will define the next era of enterprise AI.​

Enterprise decisions rarely depend on information alone.​ Operational priorities, regulatory requirements, risk tolerance and years of accumulated expertise shape them. AI can surface insights and generate recommendations, but without context, it may struggle to know which factors matter most.​

Consider a supply chain leader evaluating a potential disruption. An AI model may identify the issue and summarize the data, but the decision requires context. Which program is most critical? Which trade-offs align with business objectives?​ The model provides intelligence, but context determines how to turn insight into action.​

At Virtualitics, we see this in complex operational environments where decisions depend on connecting maintenance history, parts availability, scheduling constraints and organizational priorities. AI agents help surface trade-offs and explain recommendations while keeping final judgment with the people responsible, made possible by the data, knowledge, governance and expertise surrounding the model.​

Organizations building sustainable AI advantage invest in capabilities well beyond the model.​ Four elements define what I believe will become a context advantage:

The most valuable enterprise data often sits inside the firewall, where LLMs alone can’t reach it.​ Operational records, maintenance histories, customer interactions and domain-specific datasets give organizations perspectives that generic models don’t have.

As AI capabilities become a level playing field, unique data becomes increasingly valuable, often determining the quality of AI outcomes.

Every organization holds expertise that exists beyond formal documentation.​ Experienced operators understand nuances and decision criteria that no database can capture. They see patterns others miss and understand how decisions affect broader outcomes.

Capturing this knowledge may be one of the biggest opportunities in enterprise AI. Combined with institutional expertise, AI moves organizations beyond automation and toward organizational intelligence.

Trust remains foundational to enterprise AI.​ Leaders need confidence that recommendations align with priorities, regulations and policy, with transparency into how they were generated.

Context includes the governance that guides how AI operates and how outputs are evaluated. Without it, intelligence can scale faster than accountability.

No organization has every source of expertise, data or technology needed to maximize AI outcomes, which is why strategic partnerships are becoming critical to context advantage. They connect LLM capability with the domain expertise and operational realities to make it useful.

For example, we recently announced a strategic collaboration with OpenAI to bring frontier models into Iris, its agentic AI for readiness. The goal is to combine advanced reasoning with the readiness, personnel, material and sustainment context behind mission-critical decisions.

The same logic applies across our broader ecosystem. Partners in cloud, technology, integration and services help customers connect complex data with AI, implementation support and specialized expertise, expanding the context available and increasing the odds that insight becomes action.

In the next phase of enterprise AI, the advantage will belong to those who assemble the richest ecosystem of data, expertise and partnerships around it.

As leaders evaluate AI investments, five questions are worth asking:

• What unique context exists within our organization that competitors can’t easily replicate?

• How effectively can AI access trusted enterprise data?

• Are we capturing institutional knowledge before it becomes siloed or lost?

• Which partnerships strengthen our AI ecosystem and improve decision quality?

• How do we ensure AI recommendations reflect our priorities, governance and business objectives?

These questions move the discussion beyond model selection toward long-term value creation.

The first phase of enterprise AI was about access, as organizations raced to adopt and deploy new models.​ The next phase will look different.

As AI becomes more abundant, advantage will increasingly come from the context organizations build around it. Data, expertise, governance, workflows and partnerships become the ingredients that turn AI outputs into trusted decisions and measurable outcomes.

Models will keep improving, and access will keep expanding. However, the lasting advantage will belong to the organizations that build the richest context around the most advanced AI.

#3111. How To Communicate The Value Of Complex Tech To Buyers

The more sophisticated a technology product is, the harder it can be to explain to buyers who aren’t familiar with the technical language behind it. Lean too heavily on technical details and you risk losing their interest, but oversimplify and you may undersell what makes the product valuable.

Getting the balance right matters: Nontechnical buyers need to understand what a product can do and why it’s worth considering, even if they don’t need to know exactly how it works. Below, Forbes Technology Council members share ways tech companies can make complex products understandable without losing the nuance that sets them apart.

We put value in the buyer’s terms, anchoring every presentation in their data or like-for-like use cases they know well, and then we spell out the time or money saved, growth impact, or projected NPS gains. Compliance with SOC 2, ISO 27001/42001, and GDPR reassures without overwhelming. We avoid AI model internals and technical deep dives. It’s tempting to put an “AI expert” before customers, but buyers are evaluating how the product helps them; AI depth can confuse, not reassure. - Keith McFarlane, Globality, Inc.

Tell the story before sharing the specs. We never teach developers “Hello World.” We explain why a technology exists, then have them build something they instantly get, like their own AI assistant. Buyers are no different. Show them the problem the product was born to solve and let them build one real thing with it, and the technical depth will finally make sense. - Phil Kwok, EasyA

Forbes Technology Council is an invitation-only community for world-class CIOs, CTOs and technology executives. Do I qualify?

Most users and customers care more about outcomes than the underlying technology. That’s why we lead with tangible customer benefits, which naturally spark curiosity among both technical and nontechnical audiences. This creates an opportunity to engage more deeply and explain the technology in a way that is accessible without oversimplifying its value. - Sachin Khanna, IQSIGHT

Focus on relatable, industry-specific storytelling that centers around product outcomes rather than how the product works to achieve those outcomes. Most products are built around solving a specific pain point. Speak to that pain point and purpose first, and position the product as the clear solution using case studies and ROI stories. Technical education can come later in the buying journey once a customer has bought into the value. - Mark van Berkel, Schema App

Show them the moment they missed. We don’t open by explaining how our models read video. We show a buyer the TikTok that was driving the conversation about their brand while their dashboard showed nothing. Lead with an outcome they’d recognize from their own week, and let the technical depth answer the “how” when they ask. - Ofer Familier, dig

Hide the complexity, not the value. Buyers don’t need an architecture lesson. They need to see how the product changes the way they work. Show them a real workflow, what becomes easier and what they can now accomplish that wasn’t practical before. Complexity should be absorbed by the technology, not passed on to the customer. - Hugh Cumming, Vena Solutions

Describe the outcome you own, not the task or technology. A nontechnical buyer does not need to understand harness architecture. They need to know which outcome or task it will handle and how they will verify it. Then show it by running a demo on the buyer’s real workflow. - Aidan Guo, Attention Engineering

In my experience as a user-centric product leader, the best tool companies can use to help make complex products understandable is to provide real-life use cases that make sense to nontechnical buyers. Demonstrating the possibilities that can be unlocked by your product through these examples really helps clients imagine the future with your product integrated in their flow. To level up, uncover a novel use case that the client never even thought of. - Mugdha Gogte

Write for the AI that will explain your product first. Many nontechnical buyers now ask ChatGPT or Gemini what a product does before they ever talk to sales. If your product content is vague, the answer flattens you into a generic category. Publish specific, plain-language pages on who the product is for, what it replaces, its limits and the proof behind it. AI will simplify you both ways; make sure it keeps your product value. - Mohammed Razem, Vardot

Visual metaphors help companies translate their value for nontechnical buyers. It turns “look at this cool tech” into smaller moments that invite further exploration. The tip of the iceberg will be the leading value, but it won’t be all of the value. It’s hard to make peace with that and let it be as a technologist. We tend to want to show all of the value, like an infomercial. - Diane Weaver, Baryons Inc.

One method I use to explain the technical to the nontechnical is analogies. It was very helpful when I was a CIO during my previous agency’s transition to zero-trust architecture. I explained to them how traditional cyber network solutions were designed as a castle and a moat. Implementing zero trust makes it so that even if you get across the moat, you still need the keys to get in and around the castle. - Jim Tunnessen, GOVERNBOX.ai

Anchor the product in a single customer outcome, then layer the technical depth behind it. Lead with the problem the buyer already feels and show the result in their terms, like hours saved or risk reduced. Let a concrete example carry the explanation, and keep the details available for anyone who wants to go deeper. - Monisha Somji

Design your message for the second conversation, not the first. A nontechnical buyer rarely decides alone. They have to repeat your pitch to a CFO or board who never sees the demo. Test every message by asking the buyer to explain it back. Where they stumble is where your story breaks. Give them language they can own, and the full value travels intact. - Ivan Kan, Hackindia

One way is to describe the change, not the product. Nontechnical buyers don’t need to know how it works to know what it’s worth. Show them the day their life gets easier, the worry that goes away, and the thing they can finally do. They’ll remember the moment they realized they could stop trying to hold everything together. The depth should remain available for anyone who wants it; it just isn’t the lead-in. - Anila Siraj, OpsBridge Advisory

The best way to explain a complex product is to get outside of the product team. Brainstorm with marketing and test the language with people across the company who aren’t in technical roles to see where they get stuck. If they can’t explain the value back to you, it’s a sign the language needs to change, not that the customer needs to learn more jargon. - Todd Fisher, CTM (formerly CallTrackingMetrics)

Show, don’t tell. Instead of expecting nontechnical buyers to care about your technology choices, show them the product in action. Then, show them the specific outcomes they’ll achieve if they use the product. Ideally, these outcomes should be well-documented and involve real testimonials. Boring nontechnical buyers with technical and process content is an anti-pattern, and we should avoid it. - Michael Quoc, Product.ai

Showcasing how tech solutions fit into daily life can be an effective approach; consumers have little time and short attention spans. Using clear, direct storytelling to demonstrate how a product can improve their lives—without oversimplifying its use, but keeping the message honest and clear—can resonate directly with their emotional side. - Nino Letteriello, FIT Group

Nontechnical buyers quickly tune out when presented with abstract feature lists or complex architecture diagrams. Instead, focus on showing the tangible difference in an employee’s daily routine by comparing their current manual process with the new streamlined workflow. Demonstrating that clear “before and after” makes the business value obvious without needing to explain every technical detail under the hood. - Neil Lampton, TIAG

#3110. BlackRock's Rick Rieder sees 'historic' opportunity in high-quality bonds

Investors may be wary of the volatility hitting parts of the bond market right now, but they have an "historic" opportunity to grab attractive yields in high-quality credit, Rick Rieder, BlackRock's chief investment officer for global fixed income, told CNBC in an exclusive interview.

Hypothetically, it's now possible for investors to build a diversified portfolio that yields more than 7% with less than three years of duration and an average credit quality of A-, he said. Duration is a measurement of a bond's price sensitivity to fluctuations in rates, and issues with shorter maturities tend to have lower duration.

"Not only is it historic in that these yields are where they are, but the only time these yields are ever here is when there's some problem, like an economic problem or default problem," Rieder said in an interview about his fourth-quarter outlook, released Wednesday.

That isn't the case now, where the economy remains strong, he said. "So you don't really have to worry about defaults of any significance."

While Rieder didn't specifically identify the credits in the aforementioned portfolio, the iShares Aaa - A Rated Corporate Bond ETF (QLTA) has a 30-day SEC yield of 5.68% and an effective duration of 6.48 years — higher than Rieder's low duration focus.

The iShares Flexible Income Active ETF (BINC), which is managed by Rieder, has a 5.66% 30-day SEC yield and three-year effective duration, but its portfolio extends beyond investment-grade credit.

Rieder sees the best opportunity right now in investment-grade corporate bonds — which he pointed out he hasn't said "in a really long time." Investment grade bonds are rated AAA through BBB- by S&P and Fitch, while Moody's rates them Aaa through Baa3.

That includes hyperscaler bonds, which have flooded the market with issuance this year as they ramp up their AI infrastructure. Alphabet, Amazon, Meta Platforms and Oracle have issued a total of about $228.4 billion in bonds year to date, as of Oct. 20, according to LSEG.

"They're very low leverage. They have tremendous amounts of cash flow coming in," Rieder said of the hyperscalers in general. "You're now getting to buy these entities which are higher quality, paying you a very attractive yield to get it."

Rieder's iShares Flexible Income Active ETF has upped its allocation to investment-grade corporates to 14.3% of its portfolio. In July, that stood at 8.5%.

That said, investors need to be patient and sit tight since rates could still move higher from here, he advised.

"Your starting point is by far your best barometer of what your return is going to be," he noted. "So if you get seven and a quarter, maybe you get eight, maybe you get six, but ... if your holding period is a year or longer, you're going to get that yield."

Caution should also be exercised outside of investment-grade credit, which requires more selectivity and deep research, he warned. That includes AI names.

"There's parts of the data center supply that's not hyperscaler guaranteed or hyperscaler backed," he said. "That we've been more cautious around, and we'll continue to be."

The bond market, particularly high-yield credit, has been rocked as investor concern grows over the massive amount of debt some companies are taking out to fund their artificial intelligence build-out.

Junk-rated CoreWeave has become the poster child, seeing its stock drop, bond yields jump and credit-default spreads widen. Oracle, which is sitting in the lower end of investment grade and is seen as a bellwether on the broader AI market, has also taken some hits.

Rieder is also keeping an eye on the Federal Reserve, which is expected to raise its federal funds rate again in December to combat inflation. The market is currently pricing in a nearly 90% probability that the central bank will hike at that time, according to the CME Group FedWatch tool.

The money manager expects that to happen, although he does not agree with it. Higher rates are hurting parts of the economy, like housing, while not having much of an impact on other areas — such as tech companies' capital expenditures, which have become a big driver of growth, he said.

"They're not borrowing off the overnight funds rate," Rieder noted. "There's a lot of floating rate finance in housing, credit card, auto loan finance, and you're seeing those areas already under pressure."

Instead, the market is and will continue to price the AI supply coming into the market, he added.

Rieder sees a number of possible risks ahead, including rising levels of government debt across the globe. In the United States, the budget deficit has grown to $2 trillion for fiscal 2026.

"The more the central banks raise the rates, the cost of debt to these to already indebted governments is something we've got to be careful about over time," he said.

Bond supply coming from AI companies should also be watched.

"With the amount of supply that's coming — data center, hyperscaler — there's some crowding-out effect that's taking place," he said. "With government rates moving higher, that is something that we just got to keep an eye on."

In the meantime, Rieder would just continue to reap the rewards of high investment-grade yields "and smile a lot," he said.

#3109. Here's the Average Social Security Benefit at 62 vs. 70

Waiting until 70 costs you eight years of payments, but the monthly boost often makes up for it.

The average 70-year-old collects $850.28 more per month than the average 62-year-old. As of December 2025, the most recent data available from the Social Security Administration (SSA), that difference amounts to an annual income gap of $10,203.36. These figures show how much the timing of your claim influences the size of your checks.

The SSA bases your benefit on your highest 35 years of earnings, which it adjusts for inflation before applying its primary insurance amount (PIA) formula. Social Security is designed to replace about 40% of pre-retirement income. Most retirees need a much higher replacement rate to cover their costs.

A 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) will take effect in 2027. The figures in the table below don't include it yet. That adjustment will add about $51 per month for 62-year-olds and $82 per month for 70-year-olds, on top of these averages.

These averages assume a full retirement age (FRA) of 67, which is the standard for anyone born in 1960 or later. Your FRA is the age at which you receive your unreduced benefit. Claiming before or after that date will permanently change your monthly payment.

Filing at 62 locks in a permanent 30% reduction if your FRA is 67. If you wait past your FRA, you earn delayed retirement credits. These credits are worth 8% per year you delay, for a total increase of 24% by age 70.

Earnings histories also drive the gender gap. At 62, men average $1,572.83 per month, and women average $1,285.50, a gap of $287.33. By age 70, men receive $2,529.62, while women receive $2,024.08, resulting in a monthly difference of $505.54.

According to the SSA, men at age 65 are expected to live about 18 more years. Women at the same age are expected to live about 21 more years. These figures are population snapshots and don't account for your specific health or personal circumstances.

While these population averages show a wide spread, your individual payment depends on your highest 35 years of earnings and the exact age you choose to file.

Claiming Social Security at age 70 isn't inherently better than claiming at age 62. It depends on your finances and your life expectancy.

You might do better applying early if you have a short life expectancy or if you're unable to work and don't have the personal savings to cover your living expenses independently. You might get a smaller lifetime benefit by doing this, but that's better than falling into debt.

Those with average or above-average life expectancies who can afford to cover their living costs on their own for a while often walk away with a larger lifetime benefit by delaying their Social Security application until their FRA or beyond.

It's worth weighing the pros and cons of both choices before you decide what's right for you. Feel free to change your mind down the road if you need to. Just make sure you adjust your retirement plans accordingly.

For more on how Social Security affects your retirement, see this guide.

#3108. Gaining Financial Control Requires More Than Just a High Income

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

Income is one factor to feeling financially in control, but your approach to managing your money is crucial, too.

Earning more money can boost your feeling of financial control.

Nearly 9 in 10 (89%) Americans with a household income of $100k-plus say they feel in control of their day-to-day finances compared with 62% of Americans with a household income of less than $50k, according to NerdWallet’s October 2026 Financial Resilience Index survey conducted by The Harris Poll.

But getting a raise or a higher-paying job isn’t a surefire way to feel in control. Pairing your paycheck with good financial habits is a more robust approach.

Nearly 4 in 5 (78%) Americans feel in control of their day-to-day finances, according to the survey. That’s up from 73% in September.

There’s no single external measure for what makes someone feel in control of their finances. If you swap financial positions with someone else who feels in control, for example, there’s no guarantee you would feel the same way.

That said, a person who lives comfortably with what they have and who has the ability to withstand unexpected expenses has a good chance of feeling in control.

Americans with lower household incomes are much more likely to feel a lack of control in their day-to-day finances compared with those with higher household incomes.

That may seem intuitive. Someone with a high income is more likely to be able to cut back on luxuries, such as dining or vacations, when the costs of groceries and healthcare rise. Someone whose income is lower might not have expenses to cut.

However, that narrative is an overgeneralization.

If feeling in control of your finances depended entirely on having a high income, you might expect to see a much higher share of Americans with low incomes who feel they aren’t in control of their day-to-day finances.

But in fact, the majority (62%) of Americans with a household income of less than $50k do feel in control of their day-to-day finances. At the other end of the income spectrum, it’s clear that money doesn’t automatically result in feeling in control: About 1 in 10 Americans (11%) with a household income of $100k+ say they don’t feel this.

A high income alone won’t offset spending more than you earn, and it isn’t a substitute for an emergency fund. Good financial habits are an important component of financial control, too. They may look like:

Preparing for an emergency: Car repairs, medical bills, broken appliances: There are plenty of expensive emergencies that can pop up, even if you’re doing everything right. One-third (33%) of Americans don’t have enough cash on hand to cover an unexpected $1,000 expense if it popped up this month. Those who have an emergency fund can avoid relying on credit.

Managing debt: Monthly expenses that exceed income indicate a shaky financial footing — not great for developing a feeling of control. Nearly 2 in 5 Americans (38%) say they’ll have to rely on credit to manage expenses in October. Managing debt goes beyond paying your credit card bill each month. For example, if you get the maximum car loan or mortgage that lenders approve, a large portion of your paycheck is committed to debt payments. Keeping your overall debt load low gives you flexibility if your situation changes in the future.

Avoiding expensive mistakes: Saving money takes time. Spending it can happen quickly. A separate recent NerdWallet study found that 3 in 5 Americans (60%) say they’ve spent money on something expensive and later regretted it. Luxury items, gambling and vehicles topped the list of regrettable purchases. Pump the brakes on avoidable expensive purchases. For any big buy, take a day or two to mull over your options, especially if you have outstanding debt or if your emergency fund is low. Considering spending decisions carefully is another way to feel more in control.

The feeling of control is likely to emerge over time. Build momentum by making progress on one tangible financial goal — saving money or paying down debt, for example — before adding another.

Yes, Americans across a range of incomes report feeling in control financially. But it would be glib to suggest that this demonstrates that the feeling of financial control can be flicked on like a light switch, if only people tried harder.

There are plenty of reasons why the road to feeling in control can be arduous. Family obligations, medical concerns, affordability issues and limited opportunities can all present real obstacles, even for those who strive to practice sound financial habits along the way.

#3107. Can Your Callers Reach You? A Regulator Will Want The Evidence That Says So

Liam Dunne is the Co-founder and CEO of Klearcom, a global leader in customer call path testing & real-time contact center optimization.

When a regulator looks at your voice channels, like interactive voice response (IVR) and toll-free numbers, it ultimately comes down to one thing: When someone needs to reach you, can they, and can you prove it?

Most contact center leaders I am in contact with can explain who owns the agents, the platform and the workforce plan. Ask, though, who owns the customer’s phone line, from the carrier to the last word of the call, and the room goes quiet. Someone points to IT, and someone else points to the carrier. That answer holds up okay until a regulator dials the number to actually check it.

Credit where credit is due. Compliance teams have grafted through cyber resilience, data protection and third-party risk programs. The voice channel tends to get left out of that work because it’s treated as plumbing. Yet in pharmaceuticals, banking and healthcare, it carries some of the most regulated conversations a business has, and more of them are now answered first by AI agents. A call doesn’t have to fail for a call to fail, and very few organizations can show which of their calls did.

Medicare’s 2026 Star Ratings still score health plans on whether a caller who needs an interpreter or TTY can get one on the phone. In April, CMS finalized a rule that drops that measure from 2028. The caller’s need stays where it was, though, and plans lose one of the few outside checks on their own phone lines. It’s like taking the smoke alarm down because there hasn’t been a fire in a while.

My company runs test calls into enterprise phone lines across more than 100 countries, and what we find rarely matches what an organization believes it has. When a U.S. health insurance customer of ours recently tested close to 200 of its numbers, 17 calls failed to connect, and four more played a leftover test recording where the menu should have been. That’s roughly one in 10 lines where a member could have rung and gotten nowhere.

In pharmaceuticals, the stakes get higher. U.S. rules give drug makers 15 calendar days to report a serious, unexpected adverse event to the FDA, as do the MHRA and the European Medicines Agency. In March, the FDA warned a major drug maker over patient deaths it hadn’t reported in time. That clock only starts once the company hears about the case. A call that never connects starts no clock at all, and if an AI agent mishears the caller or never passes the case to a person, the company is still on the hook.

On phone lines a life sciences customer of ours runs in China, nearly 15% of test calls failed to connect or played the wrong message. The problems clustered around the emergency option a trial doctor would use after a serious reaction. The team got stuck in and fixed it, but every caller who hit a failure in the meantime dropped out of the record.

The worst failures look all okay from the inside. For another customer, a toll-free number in Belgium stopped connecting while the desk behind it answered normally when dialed directly. Every internal check passed. Think of your car’s brakes: The dashboard tells you they should work, and the person standing behind the car tells you whether they do.

Banking regulators have been pretty clear on this: Hand a service to a supplier and the accountability stays with you. In March, U.K. regulators finalized a single framework for reporting incidents and material third-party arrangements, and the FCA’s first annual review of operational resilience flagged firms claiming they could recover from any scenario without evidence of testing anything severe enough. That’s marking your own homework.

A single call can pass through a carrier, an aggregator, a contact center platform, an IVR menu and an AI agent, each reporting on its own leg of the journey while nobody is watching the whole journey. Last month, a major U.K. bank apologized after an outage left customers unable to use its app, online banking, phone or chat lines.

A couple of years back, we saw a financial services customer of ours U.S. service lines starting to tell callers the call center was closed. The outsourced provider had stopped taking the calls and never said a word. They told us they wouldn’t have known without our human-verified alert.

Four habits can separate calm organizations from the ones left scrambling the jets.

Firstly, name one owner: a single person accountable for the voice channel from first ring to last word, across every supplier. Second, rank your lines, and hold those with a regulatory obligation, such as adverse event, fraud reporting and card blocking lines, to a higher standard.

Third, test like a caller. That means testing from outside your own systems and in-country, and where an AI agent answers, checking that it understands the caller, captures what it should and hands the call over to a person at the right moment. Finally, keep the record and retest after every change to routing, menus, platforms or AI models because that’s when things quietly break.

AI agents add another layer because a call can connect perfectly and still go wrong in the conversation. A recent Gartner survey reported by CMSWire found customers still expect a route to a person whenever a company puts AI on the line. Nobody has fully cracked that across every language, accent and edge case, us included, and it’s where most of our work is focused.

So, can someone reach you when they need to, and are you able to prove it? Leaders who can open a record in response will find that conversation a lot shorter.​

#3106. Biotech stocks are surging. How investors can play the new drug innovation boom

Moderna gave investors a scare as its stock plunged on Thursday. But it's still one of the hottest biotechs this year. And it's hardly alone – the sector is on a roll and looks poised for more gains.

The iShares Biotechnology ETF (IBB) is up 24% through October 23, building on a 28% gain in 2025. Two dozen of the ETF's 233 holdings have more than doubled year-to-date. Moderna leads the pack with a 587% surge — even after an 18% decline following a leak of clinical data for its cancer vaccine (which was actually positive).

Analysts say a new biotech cycle is underway, fueled by clinical trial results, M&A activity, and promising technologies such as genomics, mRNA — and AI.

"We're in the midst of a powerful innovation cycle," said John Hall, portfolio manager of the T. Rowe Price Biotechnology ETF. "What's super exciting is we're seeing newer modalities start to make it to market." Companies "understand the disease biology better," he adds, and that could ultimately lead to more novel drugs making it to market.

Investors are excited about technologies like mRNA and genomics, along with a steady stream of new drug approvals. The FDA approved about a dozen novel biologic drugs in 2025, out of 46 approvals in total. Roughly 66 novel drugs are in the pipeline for FDA approval, including potential blockbusters like Moderna and Merck's cancer drug for melanoma, and a next-generation obesity drug from Eli Lilly.

Analysts say AI could also lead to more approvals as companies deploy the software to speed up drug development.

"Biotech is a phenomenal application for artificial intelligence and machine learning," says Piper Sandler analyst Ted Tenthoff. "You can set up exciting predictive models that, frankly, can do things that we've never been able to do in the space in terms of novel drug discovery."

Granted, the industry is recovering from a fallow period. The sector's last strong performance was during the Covid era when ultra-low interest rates encouraged investment in early-stage drug developers, and mRNA vaccines fueled a revenue surge for companies like Moderna, Pfizer and Biontech.

The sector then went cold as many early-stage companies fizzled. Demand for Covid vaccines evaporated, and surging interest rates put a chill in IPOs and M&A.

The risks haven't evaporated – this is still a sector whose products take years to develop, resulting in far more failures than successes. But analysts say the outlook is healthier now. While that's reflected in strong performance and richer valuations, there's still good reason to invest.

Recent clinical trial results are stoking excitement that novel drugs in the works could tackle some of the toughest problems in medicine.

Moderna and Merck's melanoma drug, for instance, uses mRNA to trigger an immune response in patients, targeting tumors that have been surgically removed and genetically analyzed. It's not a preventive vaccine, but it uses a similar immunology mechanism and showed a 42% reduction in cancer recurrence or death (used in conjunction with Merck's cancer drug Keytruda).

While the Phase 3 results disappointed Wall Street, oncologists say the outcomes were still highly positive. And they see the technology as a potential game changer, ushering in an era of personalized treatments for cancers. Moderna and Merck have said they aim to submit the drug for FDA approval and get it launched in 2027.

Inflammation treatment is another promising area. AstraZeneca and Amgen recently released positive Phase 3 results for another use for their drug Tezspire, an injectable approved for nasal polyps and asthma. In clinical trials, it showed that it successfully relieved swallowing symptoms and healed microscopic and visual tissue damage in patients with severe throat inflammation.

Roche, meanwhile, notched a win after the FDA approved its drug Enspryng, a therapy to treat rare inflammatory and autoimmune diseases. It became the first and only at-home injection for adults with thyroid eye disease.

Obesity drugs are also advancing beyond the first generation of GLP-1s. Eli Lilly's retatrutide, a "triple agonist" targeting three different hormone receptors, cleared two more clinical trials over the summer. The drug produced 28%-30% weight loss at the highest doses in the study, Lilly said. The company plans to submit the drug for FDA approval in the first quarter of 2027.

Much of the innovation isn't just happening in drug-making – it's also in areas like gene sequencing, mRNA, and high-tech instruments.

Illumina has more than doubled this year. The DNA and gene sequencing company is seeing accelerating demand for its NovaSeq X high-end sequencing platform. Pharmaceutical companies including Bristol-Myers Squibb, Merck and Kura are working with Illumina to develop precision oncology solutions.

Another big winner is 10x Genomics, up more than 300%. The biotech firm offers its lab instruments to help scientists research cancer, immunology and neuroscience. The company's Atera platform is helping produce data sets to train AI models, a process that helps accelerate personalized therapies.

On the AI front, companies are using the technology for more efficient drug discovery, says Shreefāl Mehta, president of Guidant BioTherapeutics. Using AI, "you can now bring a drug to clinical trials with less capital. More investment is also going into companies that are demonstrating that," he said.

Global AI in drug discovery will grow from a $20 billion market in 2025 to more than $160 billion by 2035, according to forecasts by Towards Health, a research and consulting firm.

One other catalyst for the sector could be M&A. Dealmaking for biopharma hit $134 billion in the first half of 2026, up from $112 billion for all of 2025, notes Jeet Mukherjee, biotech analyst at BTIG. That's a positive signal, indicating more drugs in development are showing clinical promise.

It also helps that Big Pharma has a "patent cliff" ahead. Products representing $180 billion of revenue will lose exclusivity by 2030, according to research firm RTW Institute. Companies with looming expiries "are looking for novel products and innovative products to put into their pipeline," Mehta says.

GLP-1 blockbusters have also left some companies flush with cash for acquisitions. Eli Lilly alone has completed 10 acquisition deals in 2026 worth $25 billion.

ETFs can capture the investing theme, though they aren't all alike. The iShares Biotech ETF is one of the lower cost funds. It tracks a market-cap weighted index of biotech stocks, led by companies like Gilead Sciences, Amgen, Vertex Pharmaceuticals, and Moderna.

The State Street SPDR S&P Biotech ETF holds stocks in equal weight, offering more exposure to small- and mid-cap names. Its top holdings are Moderna, Natera, Twist Bioscience and Halozyme Therapeutics.

Piper Sandler calls Illumina and 10x Genomics the "primary infrastructure plays" in the life science arena, saying their technologies are "driving the next generation of precision medicine."

Piper analyst David Westenberg has a buy rating and $305 target on Illumina, implying 14% gains from recent prices around $267. He has a hold rating on 10X with an $80 target, above recent prices around $70.

Twist Bioscience is another name to consider. The company makes customized synthetic DNA and sells DNA sequencing tools. Twist has partnered with Eli Lilly's AI and machine-learning platform and linked up with Anthropic in August to start testing its AI model, Claude, for protein development.

Twist isn't expected to turn an EPS profit until 2029, according to consensus forecasts. But revenue is expected to go from $572 million in 2027 to $833 million in 2029. Analysts have an average target of $168 on the stock, implying 21% returns from recent prices around $138.

In the small-cap space, Piper Sandler's Tenthoff likes Monte Rosa Therapeutics, a pioneer in protein degradation that selectively destroys disease-causing proteins.

The firm has partnered with Novartis to develop a drug for inflammatory conditions and autoimmune diseases. The companies announced a Phase 2 clinical study in September for an autoimmune disease treatment, which has been "triggering milestones to Monte Rosa," Tenthoff said.

Tenthoff has a buy rating and $37 target on the stock, which recently traded around $10.70.

Also in the small-cap arena, BTIG's Mukherjee recommends Faeth Therapeutics.

The biotech is developing a novel two-drug regimen to treat breast cancer and other tumors. The regimen "has the potential to address safety and dosing limitations of another recently approved drug for breast cancer," he says. And it could become "a mainstay of the future breast cancer treatment paradigm and other cancers."

Faeth is a clinical-stage company that has yet to bring a drug to market. Yet the stock is up 93% year-to-date on positive clinical trial results, trading around $18. Mukherjee has a $55 target on it.

Kymera Therapeutics is worth considering too. The company is developing an oral version of the blockbuster drug Dupixent (made and co-developed by Regeneron Pharmaceuticals and Sanofi). Dupixent is an injectable, however, and oral agents "are frequently preferred by patients," Mukherjee says. "The drug has the potential to not only take share from patients taking Dupixent for numerous immunological diseases but also expanding the market to those not taking systemic biologic drugs," he tells CNBC.

Kymera has said it doesn't expect a patent fight over Dupixent because its drug is distinct, not a biosimilar or biologic copy.

T. Rowe's Hall also likes Kymera for its potential "to unlock disease targets that have been classically considered un-druggable." The stock is the second largest holding in T. Rowe's Biotech ETF, accounting for 4.2% of the portfolio.

#3105. Universal Corp (UVV) Q2 2027 Earnings Call Transcript

Delayed tobacco shipments and Ingredients cost pressure weighed on quarterly profit.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Universal Corp. (UVV -4.73%) reported a decrease in second-quarter financial results, citing a delayed tobacco market cycle that pushed shipment volumes into the second half of the fiscal year. Management indicated that customer commitments remain aligned with full-year sales plans and that uncommitted inventory levels are within the target range. The Ingredients Operations segment recorded an operating loss during the period due to supply constraints in the apple market and higher raw material costs. The company is implementing a reorganization of its Ingredients business to improve operational efficiency and facility utilization. Management stated that emerging customer interest in additional tobacco volumes is being driven by concerns regarding potential weather impacts from El Niño.

Operator: Hello, everyone. Thank you for joining us, and welcome to the Universal Corporation Second Quarter Fiscal Year 2027 Earnings Call. [Operator Instructions] I will now hand the conference over to Wush Ma, Vice President and Treasurer.

Wushuang Ma: Good morning, and thank you for joining us. With me today are Preston Wigner, our Chairman, President and CEO; and Steve Diel, our Chief Financial Officer. During the course of this call, we will be making forward-looking statements that are based on our current knowledge and some assumptions about the future. These are representative as of today only. Actual results, performance, or achievements could differ materially from the anticipated results, prospects, performance, or achievements expressed or implied by such forward-looking statements, and we assume no obligation to update any forward-looking statements, except as required by law.

For information on some of the risks and uncertainties related to these forward-looking statements, please refer to the reports we file with the SEC and under cautionary statements regarding forward-looking statements in our current earnings press release. Finally, some of the information we have for you today may be based on unaudited allocations and may be subject to reclassification. Our comments today may also include certain non-GAAP financial measures. For details regarding these measures, including a reconciliation of these non-GAAP measures to the most comparable GAAP measures, please refer to our current earnings press release and other public materials. This call is being webcast live and will be available for replay on our website through February 5, 2027.

This call is copyrighted and may not be used without our permission. Other than the referenced replay, we have not authorized and disclaim responsibility for any recording, replay, or distribution of any transcription of this call. I would like to now turn the call over to Preston.

Preston Wigner: Thank you, Wush. Good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining us today. Our century of experience and market leadership have prepared us well to navigate the current tobacco market cycle, and we entered the second half of fiscal year 2027, encouraged by where our tobacco business stands. Our second quarter and first half results reflect the slower timing of tobacco shipments within the delayed oversupply cycle. During the quarter, we worked closely with our customers, stayed focused on tobacco quality and operational excellence and demonstrated the resilience of our company through challenging market cycles. As a result, our customer commitments remain in line with our full year sales plan.

And as of September 30, uncommitted inventory declined to 19% within our target range. We continue to expect shipments and financial results to be heavily weighted to the second half of our fiscal year, consistent with historical patterns. We also expect uncommitted inventories to reduce further during that period. At the same time, we are seeing emerging customer interest in additional volumes, driven in part by El Niño weather concerns. Together, these factors give us confidence in our outlook for the balance of the year. Turning to Ingredients. Our second quarter results continue to reflect market and cost challenges, while we took decisive steps to build the business for the long-term success.

We aligned the business and leadership around Fruit, Dry, and Taste solutions, which sharpens our commercial focus and supports efforts to improve facility utilization and operating efficiency. Our actions prioritize execution and support continued progress. We remain committed to this work as we manage the market and cost pressures that persist. We are confident in our strategy, and we believe the actions underway will strengthen the business and its contribution to Universal over time. I'll now turn the call over to Steve to review our financial results, after which I'll share a few additional thoughts.

Steven Diel: Thank you, Preston. Good morning, everyone. As Preston has mentioned, our results for the second quarter and the first half of fiscal year 2027 continue to reflect the slower start to the market cycle for our leaf tobacco business as well as market challenges for our Ingredients Operations. I will start by reviewing our segment financial summary. First, I'll discuss our Tobacco Operations segment. For the second quarter of fiscal year 2027, revenue was $534 million, down 19% versus the same quarter of last year. Segment operating income was $44 million as compared to $65 million for the same quarter of last year.

For the first half of fiscal year 2027, revenue was $972 million, down 17% versus the same period of last year. Segment operating income was $47 million, down 53% as compared to the same period of last year. Lower tobacco shipment volume was the primary reason for the variances. Due to the shift to market oversupply, customers made commitments and delivered shipping instructions later in this market cycle as compared to last year, and we expect full year results to be heavily weighted to the second half. Turning to our Ingredients Operations segment. For the second quarter of fiscal year 2027, revenue was $88 million, down 8% compared to the same quarter of last year.

The segment generated an operating loss of $2 million for the quarter as compared to an operating loss of $200,000 for the same quarter of last year. For the first half of fiscal year 2027, revenue was $174 million, down 5% as compared to the same period of last year. The segment generated an operating loss of $2.7 million for the period as compared to operating income of $1.5 million for the same period last year. The Ingredients segment continued to be impacted by market challenges, including persistent weakness in the consumer packaged goods industry, inflationary pressure, and high raw material costs. Supply constraints, particularly a tight apple supply market in the Pacific Northwest have also impacted our results.

On a consolidated basis, for the second quarter of fiscal year 2027, revenue was $622 million, down 18% from the same quarter of last year. Operating income was $43 million as compared to $68 million for the same quarter of last year, and net income attributable to Universal Corporation was $13 million as compared to $34 million for the same quarter of last year. For the first half of fiscal year 2027, revenue was $1.1 billion, down 15% from the same quarter of last year. Operating income was $45 million as compared to $102 million for the same quarter of last year.

And net income attributable to Universal Corporation was $8 million as compared to $43 million for the same quarter of last year. Regarding liquidity and capital structure. As of September 30, 2026, our net debt was $1.15 billion, approximately $82 million higher relative to the same point last year. The increase was mainly due to delayed timing associated with tobacco shipments during the first half of the year. Our liquidity availability, which includes cash and availability under our committed and uncommitted credit lines totaled approximately $945 million.

Over the last several years, we saw the leaf tobacco market progress through a historic cycle with very elevated green tobacco prices during our fiscal years 2024 and 2025, followed by extraordinarily large crop sizes in fiscal years 2026 and 2027. Navigating these market conditions required high working capital investments and drove increases to our debt and leverage levels as well as interest expense. Given the recent shift to oversupply and expected smaller crop sizes globally for the next growing season, we expect working capital usage to moderate. From a financial management perspective, we aim to take this opportunity to delever our balance sheet and reduce interest expense to support earnings per share and dividend coverage ratios.

Preston Wigner: Thank you, Steve. Looking ahead, we are well positioned to execute our plans and deliver results in the second half of our fiscal year. With shipments and financial results heavily weighted to our third and fourth quarters, we will continue partnering with our customers, focusing on operational excellence and demonstrating the market resilience we have gained through our century of experience. Our proven ability to deliver consistent cash flows from our core leaf tobacco business comes from that experience. We understand farmers, crop size and quality, and customer requirements. We know the value of robust agronomy and sustainability programs, and we know how to operate our company efficiently. Those strengths have been key to our success.

Together with our deeply experienced regional and local management teams and the advantages of our globally diverse operational footprint, they enable us to deliver the quality and quantity of tobacco our customers require regardless of market conditions. That kind of resilience is just as important to our investors as it is to our customers. Next November, Universal will proudly mark our 100th anniversary as a listed company on the New York Stock Exchange. That milestone is made possible by our history of managing through cycles and finding opportunities in the challenges. We're proud of our history on the stock exchange and of delivering value to our shareholders, including 56 consecutive years of annual dividend increases.

As we look toward this milestone, we're also building a foundation for the century ahead. That foundation rests on 3 pillars of our corporate strategy: maximizing and optimizing tobacco, growing ingredients, and strengthening our company for our next 100 years. Maximizing and optimizing tobacco relies on our resilience of our tobacco business and our ability to deepen our strategic partnerships with our customers. Growing ingredients requires us to advance our transformation and improvement initiatives with a focus on commercial execution, improved facility utilization and greater financial and operational efficiency.

And by proactively seeking opportunities for Universal to innovate and become more efficient and productive, including by advancing our sustainability programs and expanding our use of AI, we prepare our company for our next 100 years. Thank you again for joining us today. We'll now open the call for questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Your first question today comes from the line of Daniel Harriman with Sidoti & Company.

Daniel Harriman: I'll start out with 2 today and then get back into the queue. But firstly, obviously, the first half this year looks quite different from what it did last year, and you talked about that in the prepared remarks. But just overall, can you give us an idea of how we should think about a normal split between your first and second half of the year, just so that neither this year nor last year gets mistaken for the baseline? And then you talked a little bit about El Niño.

And I'm just curious if you could quantify maybe how big of a tailwind that could be if customers end up buying earlier to get ahead of next year's weather risk? And do you think it would help pull down your uncommitted inventory below the 19% that you reported?

Preston Wigner: I'll cover your first question first, and it's a good question. Normal is more challenging to define these days because of the impacts of supply and demand market cycles, the weather impacts and the other uncertainties that we've seen just since COVID. But if you smooth all that out over time, there is a general annual cyclical pattern to our business that shows that our sales and our results are heavily weighted to the second half of our fiscal year.

The first half of the fiscal year is the period in which we've got funds in the crop as we move through buying tobacco in large regions like South America and Africa, processing the tobacco and then starting to ship that tobacco sometime in the second quarter. And as a result of that, uncommitted inventory levels follow that commercial flow also. That second half of the year is focused on finishing processing which is primarily wrapping up in our third quarter and then shipping that tobacco to our customers, which occurs through the third and the fourth quarters.

And with that annual flow in mind, that's why our sales and results are heavily weighted to the second half of the fiscal year in a normal annual cycle. So your next question could be, so that's great. So what prior year should I choose as the baseline on which future performance should be measured? And I can't give you one because there isn't one. Any of those different factors I mentioned earlier are occurring each year. And some of those factors are occurring at the same time in years. In addition to that, which is really important for our business, quarterly and annual results can be impacted by shipment timing.

The timing of shipments generally follow the flow I just mentioned, but shipments can move between quarters and that mix of what's being shipped with different shipments having tobacco carrying different margins, that can also impact performance. And in those shipments, if they slip from the second quarter to the third quarter or the third quarter to the fourth quarter, they can provide movement quarter-to-quarter, but they end up in the annual results. So shipments that ship from the -- that slipped from the fourth quarter into the first quarter, which is what we call carryover tobacco in the industry. That can have an impact on the fourth quarter, but a bigger impact on the following first quarter.

And the reason the impact is bigger is exactly where I started with our normal cycle. Our first quarter is a quiet sales quarter. So more carryover or less carryover in the first quarter can create a large percentage swing in the results of the first quarter. So this year, for example, we had less carryover and a different mix of carryover in our first quarter than we did last year's first quarter. And this second quarter, everything was delayed due to the delayed market cycle. So we had less sales this quarter than we did last year's quarter.

That's the reason our first half results this year are different than last year based on our customer commitments today and the fact that we're in line with our fiscal year sales plan as evidenced by our reduction in uncommitted inventory level. That's why we didn't sell in the first half what we sold in the second half starting in our third quarter. So that's sort of the reason for the delay this year. That's why this year versus last year swings, why it's difficult to say how this -- our type of business is going to follow a normal cycle year-to-year. But overall, that normal cycle is heavily weighted to the second half of the year.

And then things that could also impact, which is your second question, those different market dynamics that I talked about earlier, how do they impact it? And El Niño is one and potential tailwinds with El Niño with this emerging interest from customers who are thinking about El Niño impacts. The impact of those additional sales opportunities, it's hard to judge today. We've seen interest from customers that are considering buying additional volume through the current crop inventories and hedge against those possible El Niño impacts. And although uncommitted inventories reduce, we do see opportunities to sell inventory that we have on hand in the second half and to support our customers' purchase plans and strategies.

But it largely depends on what customers need, what grades are available, and when they want to purchase it. And we'll be able to talk more about that in our next quarter. Because today, based on our experience and the estimated timing of El Niño impacts, we certainly understand how it can impact crops in our origins, which origins should experience wet conditions, which ones will have drought conditions, which stage of the crop is likely to be impacted, and how those factors could impact crop size and quality.

And we've seen these weather events before and our deep experience and strong regional and local teams give us that solid framework for how we plan with our farmers and with our customers, but we're just now entering the period where we can better and more accurately assess the actual severity of this El Niño and how it's going to impact the key origins we have around the world. So as part of our ongoing communications with our customers and as part of the service we provide to our customers, we have discussions about possible crop size and quality risks in the upcoming crop.

And during this quarter, we're going to continue those discussions with a more tailored perspective on what the likely impacts will be as we start to see them evolve during this month and next month. So with that in mind, customers who are interested will likely balance their desire to buy tobacco now against waiting to better understand the full impact on the crop and buy it later, but with the risk that the inventories on hand today might be sold to someone else by then.

And they also need to factor in the timing of when they want to receive that tobacco if they want to buy it, given their existing shipment plans for the large volumes we're shipping in the second half. So as we go through this quarter, we'll have a better sense of how that's playing out. There are tailwinds that we could see with additional sales this quarter, but it's a little early to say exactly what those could be, quantify them until we really understand what our customers are really going to do with that planning and coordination and collaboration with us.

Steven Diel: Daniel, this is Steve. Maybe to put a little bit of data around that question on the $1.74 last year versus this year, looking back last year with that number and then the year before, which was $1.46 through the first half, both of those were accelerated in light of what we would typically see. If you were to go back to 5 years before that, so fiscal 2020 through, say, fiscal 2024, you would see kind of first half EPS, adjusted EPS ranging from anywhere from $0.40 to $1.19. So kind of think about averaging a little over $1 a share. So this year has certainly seen that delayed activity in the EPS.

But yes, to your point, comparing to last year's $1.74 is not valid when you look back historically.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Ann Gurkin with Davenport.

Ann Gurkin: I would love to continue with a discussion in tobacco. So if we think about the back half, then how do we think about margin progression with increased shipments, hopefully improving mix? And is that potential increased sales volume with customers because of El Niño factored into your full fiscal year outlook at this point?

Steven Diel: Yes, I can address the margin question. I mean if you look back historically, gross profit percent of revenue has been inside of that 17% to 19% range. Our first quarter was below that a little bit. Second quarter started to get back into that range for the -- or get us back into that range for the first half. And we certainly see things trending to continue to be in that range. So we don't see any significant changes to the trending of gross profit margins.

Ann Gurkin: So in terms of tobacco operating margin, that was a little bit lighter in Q2 than I would have thought. So should I expect that to improve in the back half of the fiscal year tobacco operating margin?

Steven Diel: Yes. I would say our forecast now are some improvement to that margin as we run through all those volumes from the gross [ margin standpoint. ]

Ann Gurkin: Can it be comparable with what we saw in fiscal '26 for tobacco operating margin?

Steven Diel: Yes. I think our current forecasts are showing something comparable, again, within that kind of 17% to 19% range.

Preston Wigner: Yes. I think our overall sales plan in terms of volumes...

Ann Gurkin: That's for tobacco operating margin. 17% tobacco operating margin for the year.

Preston Wigner: Yes. I think as we go through the second half of the year and really ship the volume we've purchased and based on how well we've bought the tobacco in the origins in a really tough market and market conditions and how we have really partnered with our customers to get them the tobacco they need, and it's got to be at competitive prices. We have been we've been focused on trying to protect our margins and then protect our operating margins. And we should see that in the second half of the year.

I think as we go into the second half of the year, the 2 factors, one, your question about potential additional sales for El Niño and whether they're in our sales plan, there are opportunities that would be in addition to our sales plan. But again, it depends on the timing of when they want to buy that and whether they want to buy it. And then we see that going well. We do see opportunities. And then, of course, the other one, which you know very well, we've got a lot of experience moving large volumes of tobacco in the second half of the year.

So we're confident we can do it but we're also mindful of keeping an eye on port congestion, ship and container availability, and making sure we're really working closely with our customers to have a sales plan that meets their needs, but also doesn't -- it can mitigate those risks of those logistics delays. And we're not seeing incredible delays today, but we do have a lot of tobacco to move.

Ann Gurkin: Great. And then may I get a worldwide uncommitted leaf number right now, please?

Preston Wigner: Yes. The estimated unsold flue-cured and burley stocks were about 134 million kilos at September 30, which is a decrease of approximately 45 million kilos from June 30.

Ann Gurkin: Okay. That's great. And with the recent election in Brazil, do I need to read anything into that for the tobacco industry? Are there any changes I need to think about? Or any insight there?

Preston Wigner: I think for us, it's really more paying attention to the strength or the weakness of the real against the U.S. dollar. And as that real weakens against the U.S. dollar, that certainly helps us since we're dollarized, it helps us in managing our costs and having more attractive pricing for our customers. So that's -- I'd say we probably focus more on that. I don't see from that election other immediate impacts in Brazil.

Ann Gurkin: Okay. Great. And then SG&A for the year, I'm using between $300 million and $310 million. Is that a fair range still?

Steven Diel: Yes, that's still a fair range.

Ann Gurkin: And interest expense in the range of $70 million? Or should that come down now given your comments during the update?

Steven Diel: I think if you look at the year-to-date interest expense and trend that out, that's a pretty fair way to see it.

Ann Gurkin: Okay. Great. And then switching to Ingredients. So that -- those results look like they softened sequentially. So how should I think about the progression for results for the Ingredients segment for the balance of the year?

#3102. Enterprise Software No Longer Has Just One User

By Arnab Bose, Chief Product Officer, Asana.

​The rapid rise of AI agents has prompted predictions about the “death of the user interface.” As agents become more capable, it’s easy to imagine a future where work happens entirely through prompts and conversations. ​

However, that misses the bigger transformation underway. Enterprise software isn’t losing its interface. Rather, it’s gaining a second participant: the people doing the work and the AI agents helping to execute it.​

The user interface remains critical for collaboration, evaluation and human judgment, while the machine-readable layer allows agents to execute. That’s very different from saying the user interface is dead. It’s more accurate to say its job, purpose and function are changing.

For decades, enterprise applications were designed almost exclusively for one audience: humans. The focus has been on screens, workflows and dashboards to help navigate information and make decisions.

That’s no longer sufficient. Those same products must now also support AI agents that need to understand work, participate in workflows and execute tasks alongside people.

Therein lies the challenge: Agents don’t navigate interfaces the way people do. They need structured context on who owns what, how work connects and what decisions have already been made, as well as durable ownership, clear permissions, approval checkpoints and machine-readable representations of work. These are the minimum requirements for an agent to operate safely and usefully inside an enterprise system.

What we previously considered great human user experiences now need to be great machine experiences, too. This doesn’t mean abandoning the fundamentals of good product design but raising the bar for what it looks like moving forward. Agentic AI makes the core principles more important while expanding the number of participants the product must design for.

The reality is that good interfaces become even more valuable alongside even more capable AI agents.

That’s because humans still need to direct work, inspect it, correct it, make judgment calls and align with each other. Taste, prioritization and accountability don’t disappear just because an agent can execute specific steps.

Knowledge workers recognize this, too: Our research found that 85% of surveyed workers “believe all AI agent output should be reviewed by a human.”

As agents take on more execution, the opportunity is there for humans to elevate the role they play—from producing every output themselves toward evaluating alternatives, applying taste and judgment before deciding what exactly moves forward. Importantly, those decisions rarely happen in isolation. Enterprise interfaces need to give people space to evaluate agent outputs, comparing recommendations and applying collective judgment.

The role of the interface evolves from helping people understand, supervise and improve work already in motion to helping them evaluate and guide work that agents are carrying out.

One of the biggest misconceptions people have about AI agents is that they’ll change the way people interact with software by collapsing the interface for work into chat.

That’s not how serious work actually happens. People don’t run companies through prompts alone. They work through plans, approvals, timelines and shared context. That’s why even the leading AI platforms are moving beyond pure chat; they support artifacts, embedded apps, structured tools and hosted experiences.

Chat will matter, but it will matter as an entry point rather than the whole product. In enterprise software, the winning pattern will be natural language to initiate, structured software to coordinate and governed systems of record to track what happened.

Agents will make software more dynamic but not less structured.

Looking ahead, the biggest product challenge isn’t building more capable agents but ensuring every participant—human or AI—works from the same foundational understanding of the organization.

Our previous research has found that 73% of IT decision makers say AI initiatives fail or stall at least sometimes because AI lacks complete organizational context—including decisions, dependencies and prior work. Agents can’t execute effectively if the underlying system can’t tell them what matters, who owns what, what has already been decided and where work is blocked.

The reverse is just as important; people need visibility into the context informing an agent’s actions. If someone is expected to evaluate an output or make the final judgment call, they need confidence that the agent has considered the correct goals, dependencies and prior decisions in their output.

The solution is something similar to a “company brain”—a shared understanding of work that both humans and agents continuously contribute to and learn from. With this in place, every interaction begins from a stronger foundation than the last. Local intelligence becomes coordinated execution, and that shared layer will matter more than any individual chatbot or model.

Enterprise software, agents and people will all need to work off the same common ledger of work, ownership, status and intent. Without that, you get activity but not necessarily outcomes.

The future of enterprise software isn’t about chat replacing interfaces or agents replacing people. Instead, it’s about designing products that give agents the context required to execute while giving humans the visibility to evaluate that work with other humans and steer it toward meaningful outcomes.

Agentic product design is evolving from building a clever assistant to building the right underlying system for human-agent teams. The companies that succeed in the future will build products where humans and agents operate from the same shared understanding of work, with agents able to execute effectively and people equipped to apply the taste, prioritization and judgment that remain distinctly human.

Grid investments and industrial demand position the utility to capture sustained growth across its regional footprint.
