#3098. As AI Videos Terrify Hollywood, Is It Time To Hand IP Management To The Masses?

Saro McKenna is the CEO of Dacoco GmbH and cofounder of Alien Worlds.

​A viral clip of Brad Pitt and Tom Cruise fighting on a rooftop showed us where the hands have come on the clock with AI-generated content.

The hyperrealistic 15-second clip, created by Irish director Ruairi Robinson using a two-line prompt punched into Seedance 2.0, perfectly illustrated how easy it has become to produce Hollywood-tier content using artificial intelligence. And it raises a pertinent question: Is it time to hand IP management to the community?

Pitt vs. Cruise sparked the latest AI cause célèbre, with Deadpool scriptwriter Rhett Reese predicting (paywall) the tool would “cost jobs all over the place.” Inevitably, users were soon spinning up alternate endings for Game of Thrones and pitting Jackie Chan against Bruce Lee in a dispute over ketchup.

Predictably, Disney sent ByteDance a cease-and-desist letter claiming the Chinese company had hijacked its iconic creations “by reproducing, distributing, and creating derivative works featuring those characters.”

That sound? Pandora’s Box snapping open, and film studios and other stewards of intellectual property (IP) scrambling to preserve their cherished copyrighted works. The press release announcing the launch of Seedance vowed to let users “control their creations like a true director.” But what about other people’s creations?

ByteDance, which owns TikTok and Seedance, promised to strengthen safeguards to “prevent the unauthorized use of intellectual property,” but this reassurance rings hollow.

If ordinary users can access powerful AI tools to produce slick scenes that previously existed only in their imagination, they’ll do it. And they’ll go to great lengths to bring their favorite actors, characters and worlds to life—guardrails be damned. The AI content onslaught will cause headaches for IP stewards everywhere. Seedance 2.0 is one of many powerful tools that can deliver epic visuals at scale, fast. These tools won’t regress, they’ll improve.

As Anthropic co-founder Dario Amodei suggested, “Humanity is about to be handed almost unimaginable power, and it is deeply unclear whether our social, political, and technological systems possess the maturity to wield it.” As access to quality generative AI tools increases, a tsunami of content will be unleashed, and IPs could quickly spiral out of control. Which is why we should think hard about how best to manage and control IP in the AI age.

Communities ought to be empowered to take the IP management reins, not central actors who cannot possibly scale enforcement fast enough to manage, much less contain, the threat.

The fact that Hollywood’s big players were blindsided by Seedance proves just how good these tools are and how ill-equipped the old guard are to defend against them. So why would the community fare better? Well, if literally everyone has the power to create convincing cinematic productions featuring characters from the annals of film, gaming and literature, why wouldn’t you leverage the crowd to manage what’s considered “official”?

It’s analogous to trusting the community to enforce Bitcoin’s consensus rules. There is no executive branch upholding the blockchain’s trustworthiness. Rather, nodes (users) reject blocks that do not meet consensus rules and, in so doing, keep the network healthy. If a collective dissents, they can fork the network (see Bitcoin Cash).

We have come a long way from glitchy prompt outputs to Hollywood-level choreography, lighting and audio, so the idea that studio execs will bury the GenAI genie through cease-and-desist letters and copyright finger-wagging is unrealistic. It’s easier to envisage legal and ethical questions piling up as IP-busting videos roll off the production line.

If we assume that IP can no longer be centrally controlled given the sheer volume of AI content, how would a community-driven system work? Imagine we enter a phase in which the canon of, say, LOTR is contested and the average fan can’t discern real from fake. How do a community of IP stewards deal with that?

As mentioned, Bitcoin provides one possible template: If a fan wished to discern what was official, they could open a block explorer and cross-check the repository, just as users can probe the entire Bitcoin blockchain, locate transaction IDs, etc. Thus, a community could be tasked with enforcing established consensus rules determining what constitutes approved canon.

A community-led IP management model featuring built-in arbitration and on-chain voting could enforce rules without involving a central authority. In this model, contributors would be incentivized to vet work and decide whether it meets the canonicity threshold. Connecting community management to legal IP enforcement, in other words, while entailing a “social rejection” of non-canon activity.

In short, if the community owns the decision-making process, non-canon IP activity isn’t a threat: It’s either absorbed to be exploited legally or rejected, thereby creating a clear process to absorb quality content.

Of course, this just deals with official canon. Arguably, the ability to produce high-quality, copyright-breaking clips detracts from or cheapens an IP, even if viewers acknowledge the new works aren’t “official.”

Beyond the question of official canon lies a thornier issue: outright commercial exploitation. While communities may agree on what constitutes official lore, there’s nothing stopping individuals from wielding AI to generate output featuring famous characters that they later monetize.

When high-quality AI content can be produced cheaply and at scale, the line between fan expression and outright infringement blurs. The challenge isn’t just protecting canon; it’s preventing people from profiteering off supposedly protected IP. But what recourse do IP owners have? Are they relegated to being impotent spectators as an AI-powered imposter mass-produces an endless stream of simulacra, the very existence of which prevents their work from gaining traction?

There are no easy answers. AI is no longer feeding the creative process—it’s attempting a root-and-branch takeover. If we want to maintain some semblance of control and stave off content chaos, we must look to leverage the wisdom of the crowd—humans, not AI agents—and decide our own destiny.

#3095. Why Most Enterprise AI Spending Automates The Wrong Part

Co-Founder of Superlinked, building enterprise-grade open-source inference for production-scale Agentic AI search and document processing.

​After Superlinked narrowed its focus to a single open-source product, I had to rebuild our go-to-market engine with far fewer people. My first move was an obvious one these days: I pointed Claude at our existing outbound process and asked it to write more emails to more people.

It worked, in a way. We did send many more messages, but the total number of replies barely moved. We made the easy part of the process faster. The hard part—knowing who to contact and when—hadn’t changed at all.

Organizational inertia is real, and it’s hard to let go of a well-established and familiar process, but we had to. What follows is how we redesigned the process after the volume experiment failed.​​​

​Companies expect to roughly double AI spending this year to about 1.7% of revenue, according to BCG’s January 2026 survey of 2,360 executives. Yet, in PwC’s “2026 Global CEO” survey, only 12% of CEOs said that “AI has delivered both cost and revenue benefits,” and 56% said they’d “seen no significant financial benefit” so far. And McKinsey analysts reported in April 2026 (registration required) that 60% of respondents to its global survey “still have not seen enterprise-wide EBIT impact from their AI programs.​”​

From both sides of the table (as an operator today and a management consultant previously), I think most of this money buys speed on individual tasks. However, speed on one step rarely changes the outputs of the whole process. The bottleneck just moves somewhere else, and the faster step just piles work up in front of it.​

​When redesigning our outbound process, I focused on the desired outcome rather than which tasks AI could automate. The goal wasn’t to increase email volume but to reach engineers experiencing the specific problems we address, at the right moment.

That reframing exposed a constraint that a small team couldn’t remove. Many of the best buying signals were public: engineers describing their problems in GitHub issues on open-source projects adjacent to ours. Reading thousands of those threads every week wasn’t realistic for a human team, but for an AI agent, it’s routine.

The new process looks nothing like the old one. Agents watch for specific pain signals, match each person to a professional profile and reach out to them with a message tailored to their pain point. An ML engineer fighting memory crashes receives something different from a CTO worried about infrastructure risk. The old process started from a purchased list. The new one starts from evidence of a problem.

The redesign was more successful than I expected. Each response and even each ignore helps us identify which signals indicate genuine interest, improving targeting over time. For example, we initially targeted everyone who starred a relevant repository, but learned that stars indicated curiosity rather than usage. Those who filed issues were more responsive, so we shifted our focus accordingly.

​Process redesign doesn’t mean removing people altogether. It means being deliberate about where they bring most value. My first test is simple: How costly is a mistake, and can it be undone?

Scanning and scoring signals is cheap to get wrong and easy to reverse, so agents run it unsupervised. A first message to a senior leader at a target account is expensive to get wrong, so a person signs off on each one.

My second test often gets less attention than it should. How much effort does it take to check the AI’s work? If verifying an output costs more than producing it by hand, automating that step is a net loss.

Before a workflow goes live, I’m looking to answer four questions. How can the AI agent know it’s unsure? Who does it hand off to? How can we stop or reverse an action? How does a correction feed back into the process so the same mistake doesn’t repeat?

Early on, our pipeline reached out to the people most active in those issue threads. Several turned out to be the project’s own maintainers (often, direct competitors), answering questions rather than asking them. They were the last people we wanted to pitch to.

That incident taught us more about the design than weeks of smooth runs: The system couldn’t tell someone asking for help from the person offering it.

​If your AI investment isn’t (yet) showing in your P&L, avoid purchasing additional tools. Instead, select a critical process and clearly define its intended outcome. Then, redesign the process based on current AI capabilities, rather than sticking to the workflows that you inherited.

Expect the first redesign to be wrong, and keep human supervision where the consequences are significant. Importantly, treat their feedback as a design input rather than a bug to solve. Track how long it takes a person to check the agent’s work. If this time is trending down, the redesign is working.​

The biggest gains I’ve seen came from teams willing to throw the old process away. A faster version of last year’s workflow often produces last year’s results.​

#3093. Where Will XRP Be in 2030?

Future price targets for XRP need to take into account the growing importance of stablecoins.

For the year, XRP (XRP -4.80%) is down a dismal 37% and currently trades for just north of $1. At one time, this popular altcoin looked set to go stratospheric, and some investors predicted it might go to $10, $100, or even $1,000.

But that simply hasn't been the case. One potential catalyst for XRP in 2026 -- passage of the Clarity Act -- did not materialize. And now, with the Democrats having swept both the House and the Senate in the midterm elections, the brief era of pro-crypto regulation may soon be coming to an end.

That puts XRP's prospects very much in doubt. Here are three potential scenarios for XRP in 2030.

In the most favorable scenario, institutional demand for XRP takes off, and new use cases continue to emerge. To make that a reality, Ripple, the company behind the XRP token, has spent nearly $3 billion to create an end-to-end payment and liquidity network featuring XRP.

Some analysts have suggested that the Ripple payment network could eventually replace the SWIFT payment network. Wouldn't it be cheaper, easier, and faster to run everything on blockchain rails rather than a legacy network dating back to the 1970s?

That type of thinking led to some truly eye-popping price targets for XRP. Even Ripple got into the act last year, suggesting that as much as 14% of SWIFT's annual payment volume (roughly $150 trillion) would eventually run through the XRP blockchain ledger.

If that happens, then demand for the XRP token would be off the charts. According to Standard Chartered, the price of the XRP token could hit $28 by the end of 2030.

However, there are a number of flawed assumptions in the preceding scenario. For one thing, SWIFT is implementing blockchain technology of its own. That dramatically reduces Ripple's potential growth opportunities.

Secondly, stablecoins continue to eat XRP's lunch. Stablecoins have become a $300 billion industry and a popular means of moving money around the world. Even Ripple has seen the writing on the wall. In December 2024, it launched a stablecoin of its own, Ripple USD. In less than two years, Ripple USD has attained a market cap of $2.7 billion.

Given those two facts, the long-run price of XRP might turn out to be $1, which is almost exactly where it's trading right now. In short, XRP will become nothing more than a glorified stablecoin.

In early November, Ripple CEO Brad Garlinghouse delivered some fantastic news for XRP investors. He proclaimed that XRP and stablecoins are "complementary" and not "competitive."

With that in mind, I'm predicting that XRP will be able to grow at a 20% compound annual growth rate (CAGR), about on par with what you'd expect from an established tech stock. Provided that Ripple continues to support it, XRP could hit a price of $2.50 by the end of 2030.

#3088. When To Build Your Own AI Model (And When To Stop Kidding Yourself)

Eilon Reshef, cofounder and CPO of Gong, is a seasoned entrepreneur, executive and investor in the internet and software spaces.

We were running our own models at Gong long before ChatGPT became a household name. This was the era of transformer-based language models, the state of the art for natural language understanding before LLMs. We’d take these prebuilt foundation models, train them further on our domain and data and then deploy them for very targeted jobs.​

We called it fine-tuning. Academics called it transfer learning. Most people just called it a lot of work.​

I tell you this because it’s important context for what comes next: the hype around post-trained small language models (SLMs) and their very real practical potential.​

First, an important distinction: This isn’t about training a foundation model from scratch. For most product companies, that would be economic malpractice. It’s about taking an existing model and making it much better at a specific job through supervised fine-tuning, preference optimization, reinforcement learning, distillation or some combination of them.​

Fine-tuning is one form of post-training. I’ll use the broader term when that distinction matters.​

Most major AI providers offer a lineup of models that sits roughly on a diagonal: cheap and fast at one end, more capable and expensive at the other. The names differ, but the trade-offs don’t.​

The promise of post-training is that it lets you move above this line for a specific task. You can get higher quality than an off-the-shelf model at the same inference cost or comparable task quality at a lower cost.​

That doesn’t mean the smaller model is smarter overall, but that specialization can make it better at the specific job you need it to do. The real question is when that advantage holds and what it costs.​

Before we go further, I want to address something I keep hearing in investor conversations and startup pitches: “We fine-tune our own models, so we have a proprietary moat.”​ The reality is, no, you don’t.​

Fine-tuning is an engineering decision. It’s neither magic nor a competitive advantage on its own. Saying “we do post-training” to investors is about as distinctive as saying “we use a database.”​

What’s defensible is what compounds around the model: proprietary data, feedback loops, rigorous evaluation and the application layer, or harness, that connects the model to context, tools, workflows and systems of record.​

The learning system that fine-tuning or a generic agent framework creates is the true competitive moat, refined and improved by real-world use. It captures how work gets done, raises switching costs and makes the underlying model replaceable. Pitch the model work itself as the advantage, and the story eventually falls apart with investors or customers who look closely.​

Knowing when to fine-tune is hard. The decision comes down to four things: scale, task specificity, prompting as the baseline and negotiation leverage.​

Scale is the biggest factor. Post-training carries meaningful upfront costs. At millions of inference calls a month, the economics can work. At thousands, they usually don’t—especially once ongoing maintenance is included.

Task specificity is the next filter. Fine-tuning works best on narrow, repeatable tasks with a high quality bar. Think tagging customer conversations, emails and calls against a defined taxonomy, where the model must understand the domain and return the exact format the system expects.​

Prompting as the baseline means pushing prompt engineering as far as possible before committing to post-training. Strong system prompts, few-shot examples, the right context and strict output specs will go a long way.​ It’s also no longer entirely manual. Automatic optimizers can generate and test variations, raising the baseline before you change a single model weight.​

Too many teams skip this work and go straight to fine-tuning because it feels more “real.” Don’t do that. Exhaust the prompting path first.

Negotiation leverage comes with scale. If you’re big enough to consider fine-tuning, you’re probably big enough to push vendors on price, volume discounts or dedicated capacity. “Should we fine-tune?” may not be the right question. You should probably be asking, “Should we renegotiate our API contract?”

One prerequisite underlies all of this: evaluation. Build a representative gold set with human-approved answers, hold back some for testing and run every prompt revision, model upgrade and fine-tune through the same pipeline. Keep adding production failures and edge cases. Without strong evals, you can’t tell real product improvement from an overfit demo.​

Once the math works, scale is achieved and prompting is exhausted, be sure to understand the operational cost of post-training before committing:

1. The model has to run somewhere. Self-hosted or managed, it’s still more work than calling a frontier API. You now own uptime, scaling, monitoring, hardware, utilization and capacity planning.

2. Models age. A fine-tuned model reflects a snapshot in time. Months later, the base model has improved, data has shifted and new edge cases have appeared.

Post-training isn’t a one-time project. You need to collect new data, rerun evaluations, track drift and retrain as new failure modes emerge. That takes ongoing staffing and investment.

The overlooked cost of SLMs is keeping them competitive.

Post-training and SLMs are real, powerful tools, but they work best as engineering and business decisions, not marketing stories. The winners usually have scale, strong evaluations, good data and the discipline to keep maintaining the system.

We use both approaches. Some products depend on fine-tuned models, while others are better served by riding frontier improvements. The point is to let the trade-offs decide.

The practical rule is simple: Start broad, measure everything and specialize only when the task is stable and the economics justify it.​

#3087. Apollo to buy nearly 10% stake in Abu Dhabi-backed alternative asset manager Mubadala Capital

Investing giant Apollo Global Management is finalizing a deal to buy nearly a 10% stake in Mubadala Capital, the alternative asset manager subsidiary of Abu Dhabi's sovereign wealth fund, Mubadala Investment Co., according to people familiar with the matter who spoke on condition of anonymity.

The deal is expected to be announced later Monday morning, they said. Financial terms were not immediately known.

The transaction is significant on multiple fronts. It further advances Apollo's ambitions in Abu Dhabi often called the "capital of capital." The firm has spent the past 15 years building key strategic relationships there, with both the country's investment arm and its core leadership.

Apollo already has a multibillion-dollar partnership with Mubadala Investment Co., first established in 2022 and extended two years ago. At the time of that extension, Apollo said the agreement would strengthen the firm's Capital Solutions platform by enabling the firms to jointly source and provide customized debt and equity financing to companies worldwide.

In 2023, the institutions formed a $2.5 billion joint venture designed specifically to co-invest in global private credit opportunities over a five-year horizon.

For Mubadala Capital specifically — the region's only large-scale asset manager, advising and administering more than $755 billion in assets — the deal further advances its growth strategy under the direction of CEO Hani Barhoush, and its relevance on the global investing stage. It also marks an inflection point for the company's core alternatives business, which has grown to more than $60 billion.

John Zito, co-president of Apollo's Asset Management arm, and Barhoush have worked closely together over the past several years and, according to sources, their close-knit relationship and the success of prior partnerships led to talks of deepening ties. So did the belief that scale in the asset management business matters more than ever.

"Capital as a moat is a big thing," said one person familiar with the deal.

Importantly, the deal also continues a notable shift in the relationship between American investment firms and the Middle East. While the region, and Abu Dhabi specifically, has long been a sought-after source of capital, this deal further reverses that dynamic, with Apollo making a significant direct investment in the country and its investment vision.

Mubadala Capital's international offices include London, New York, Rio de Janeiro and San Francisco.

Apollo's investment in Mubadala Capital is similar to deals the firm has done with other asset management platforms, including Diameter Capital, Thoreau, Motive Partners and others.

Spokespersons for both firms declined to comment.

#3085. How to Invest in CXMT, the Chinese DRAM Company -- and Why You Might Not Want To

CXMT sounds like it should be the ticker for a Chinese Nasdaq memory stock, but it's not. Why is it so hard to invest in this company?

Memory stocks have become the beating heart of the artificial intelligence revolution. If you want to train up an AI system, you probably want some good graphics processing units (GPUs). Once you're ready to transition to agentic AI, central processing units (CPUs) are the chips for you. But no matter what you're doing in AI, from training a large language model (and ensuring it remembers what you taught it), to using a model you've built to answer questions (and hope it remembers the question), to performing tasks -- well, you're going to need memory chips for that.

According to Wall Street analysts, more chips than are currently being produced -- and more chips than will be produced next year.

In July 2026, a new Chinese memory company burst onto the scene with the aim of (1) helping to alleviate the deficit in global memory chips and (2) grabbing gobs of memory chip market share for itself, at the expense of Samsung (SSNLF +0.00%), SK Hynix (SKHY +4.26%), and Micron (MU +5.47%).

According to the latest data from The Wall Street Journal, these three memory companies "control more than 90% of the global DRAM market." And while the precise numbers ebb and flow from quarter to quarter, Counterpoint Research data largely confirm this, showing Samsung with a 38% share, SK Hynix at 25%, and Micron nearly tied at 24% at the end of Q2.

CXMT, only an also-ran just one year ago, more than doubled its share from 4% to 10% by the end of Q2.

CXMT is clearly a company on the move. WCCFTech clocked the company's Q2 revenue growth at a whopping 716%. On the day of its IPO, CXMT stock gained an astounding 466% and closed at a $487 billion market capitalization as investors rushed to buy the next big thing in DRAM.

Chinese investors, I should specify. Because as much as U.S. investors might want to get in on the ground floor at CXMT, too, they cannot.

You see, "CXMT" may sound a lot like a ticker symbol on the Nasdaq, but it's actually just the initials of the company's name when it went public: ChangXin Memory Technologies. Trading on the Shanghai stock exchange, it's basically impossible for U.S. investors to buy CXMT stock directly. And the only way to own it indirectly (to my knowledge) is to buy shares of the KraneShares China Technology & Semiconductor STAR 50 Index ETF (KSTR +2.55%), which boasts that it's "the only U.S.-listed ETF with direct ownership of CXMT."

So that's the good news: If you feel you absolutely, positively, must own a piece of China's hottest DRAM stock, well, there's a way to do that. But here's the next question: Should you want to?

Because there are at least two good reasons you might not want to buy the KSTR ETF and own a piece of CXMT.

Reason No. 1 is that it would be a really small piece. According to KraneShares, CXMT stock makes up less than 2% of KSTR's total investments. CXMT may be, as KraneShares advertises, "China's leading dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) manufacturer and ... the world's fourth-largest DRAM producer by capacity and shipments, with an estimated 7-8% global market share as of late 2025." But buying KSTR will only get you a toenail's worth of that market share.

And here's the worse news: That toenail may already be shrinking.

Counterpoint Research reports that after rising from 7% to 10% in Q2, CXMT's market share reversed, sliding to 9% in Q3. Largely, this is because the incumbent giants aren't taking CXMT's challenge lying down. Samsung in particular, says WCCFTech, is scaling up DRAM production and targeting the market for high bandwidth memory (HBM) chips sold to data centers.

CXMT also wants to enter the data center market, but its HBM chips aren't yet ready for prime time, with only 20% to 30% of HBM3E chips produced being usable. What's more, CXMT's customers are largely limited to other Chinese companies -- probably mostly PC- and mobile device makers -- that use lower-end, less expensive DRAM, resulting in a smaller market share (as measured by revenue rather than units shipped).

The longer this situation lasts -- with Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron increasing their share of more valuable HBM DRAM sales while CXMT is relegated to selling low-margin memory chips to electronics companies -- the harder it will be for CXMT to reach critical mass.

My advice: Forget about buying CXMT stock for now. Buy Micron stock at less than 4 times forward earnings instead.

#3082. How Much Of Last Quarter’s Code Can Your Team Explain?

Soumendra Mohanty is the Chief Strategy and Innovation Officer at Tredence Inc.

It’s easy enough for large organizations to add agent tooling for their developers and mark the productivity gains. You’re invoiced for generative output; you make the business case based on hours saved. But there’s a second part to that transaction: all the review time that those developers will consume from colleagues whose calendars were already full.

Over the past two years, in particular, I’ve watched some versions of this cycle play out across enterprise delivery organizations. Thanks to the generative power of AI coding capabilities, the volume needing review outstrips the capacity available to provide it. This gets resolved by senior engineers approving changes faster than they can follow them.

As a result, code merges with an assumption that someone understood those changes. Then the cost surfaces months later, when an incident review asks why, to which nobody can provide a good answer. Too often, this is because the decision was made by a model and approved without enough scrutiny.

Agile is designed for a world where the scarce input is engineering hours. Standups, story points and the sprint itself all exist to extract more shipped software from a fixed supply of human time. Agent tooling makes generation hours abundant.

What remains is the number of hours in a week during which an experienced engineer can trace the logic of a change rather than skim it for red flags. Today, that number governs how fast an organization can safely ship. Few planning systems record it anywhere.

• In its 2025 report, Google’s DORA program put AI use among tech professionals near 90%, with about 30% of respondents saying they trust the output little or not at all. The same research found higher AI adoption moving throughput and delivery instability in the same direction.

• Stack Overflow’s 2025 developer survey says two-thirds of developers named “almost right, but not quite” as their leading frustration with AI output; 45% reported that debugging AI-generated code takes them longer than writing it themselves.

• A randomized trial by METR, in which 16 experienced open-source developers worked through 246 real issues, found that it took 19% longer when using AI tools (yet after the experiment, the developers had estimated that AI made them 20% faster).

In a word, adding tooling expands the queue. It’s understandable that, when looking at a review backlog, an executive’s response is to add capacity. In fact, that instinct may compound the problem. Each additional seat raises the volume of change requiring review, while adding nothing to the queue’s ability to perform it.

And of course, the people who can clear that review queue are the ones that most organizations have the fewest of. Senior review time isn’t procured on a quarterly cycle; it doesn’t scale with the licensing budget. Doubling generation capabilities is not the same as doubling review-capable engineers.

So how can organizations build a verification layer that sits inside whatever delivery framework they already run?

Estimate the hours per week your senior engineers can give for careful code review. That is, the kind of review in which engineers follow a change through the system, rather than skimming it for what stands out. Set that figure against the volume of change your teams now produce. Organizations that run this exercise often find a much bigger gap than they expected.

More likely than not, delivery estimates are already part of your planning sessions. Verification capacity belongs right beside them. When the two figures diverge, it reveals a decision about headcount, scope or risk appetite that would otherwise arrive as a later incident.

Uniform review across every change will exhaust the people doing it. Teams under that kind of review tend to reduce review to formality. Instead, review effort should track what breaks when the change is wrong.

Authentication, payment paths, data deletion and anything that touches customer records should earn full manual review by a named owner. Internal tooling and prototypes less so, and they should be labeled clearly enough that they don’t migrate into production unexamined.

Tagging a codebase this way is architecture work. Have an architect assign the tag, store it with the code and treat permissive tagging as the expensive error that it is.

Whatever your current system is, every merged change already carries a name attached. The question is whether that person can explain the logic, side effects and dependencies. Best not to scramble for those answers during a security review, or at three in the morning after an incident. Regulatory exposure resolves to a human being, so your delivery system should be able to show which one and on what basis.

Engineering judgment used to accumulate slowly, through years of writing code and living with the consequences. In the era of agentic AI, that apprenticeship is compressing. Organizations handling it well are putting junior engineers on verification work deliberately, paired with someone who can explain what they’re looking at. Organizations leaving this to chance are drawing on a supply of senior judgment that’s not currently being replenished.

We call this AVID: Agentic Verification and Iterative Delegation. It is a working methodology built around four values:

2. Judgment budgets over unlimited delegation

4. Blast-radius awareness over uniform review

None of these four values requires new tooling or reorganization. Taken together, they take verification from something that happens when there is time to something that appears in the plan. This will be critical in an era where organizations will need to account for what they’ve built. That capacity has to be budgeted like any other.​

#3077. Five Principles For Turning AI Agent Adoption Into Measurable Impact

Dr. Chih-Han Yu is the CEO and co-founder of Appier, an AI-native agentic-AI-as-a-service (AaaS) company.

​AI agents are moving from pilots into everyday business operations. According to McKinsey’s The State of AI in 2026 survey, 40% of respondents at organizations with more than $1 billion in annual revenue said they were scaling AI agents in at least one business function, up from 27% a year earlier. Yet among all respondents, the share reporting that AI contributed positively to their organization’s EBIT held at 37%, essentially unchanged from 2025.

Adoption is rising, but enterprise-level impact has yet to follow at the same pace.

In my experience, this gap is often less about the technology itself. Today’s models are highly capable, and many enterprises have already done the hard work of getting agents into their workflows. What often lags is how those agents are operated once they’re in place: how strategic goals are set, how decisions are checked, how tasks are assigned and how systems improve over time.

Scaling agentic AI, in other words, depends as much on how it’s operated as on how widely it’s adopted. Here are five principles I believe enterprises should build around.

Every AI deployment should begin with a clear answer to one question: What is this meant to achieve? Revenue growth, customer conversion, cost reduction and productivity improvement each call for different metrics and different timelines.

Without that clarity, teams tend to measure what’s easiest to see, such as activity, usage or the number of agents deployed. Those numbers can rise steadily while business results stay flat. It’s far more useful to agree on the outcome and the evaluation criteria before deployment, so AI is judged on what it delivers rather than how busy it looks.

This also makes later decisions easier. When the goal is clearly defined, it’s much simpler to tell whether an agent should be expanded, refined or retired.

Once the goal is clear, the next question is how reliably AI can do the job. As agents take on more decisions, they should be designed to assess their own capability and confidence, and weigh potential risks before acting.

In enterprise settings, small errors can have meaningful consequences. A mispriced offer, a misrouted customer request or an incorrect data entry can ripple through downstream systems. That’s why checking only the final output isn’t enough. Organizations should evaluate AI decisions at critical points across a workflow and put guardrails in place where the stakes are highest.

An agent that knows when to pause, flag uncertainty or hand a task back to a person is often more valuable than one that always produces an answer.

Knowing AI can handle a task is only half the equation. The other half is deciding which model or agent should handle it.

Applying a single model to every scenario is simple but rarely optimal. A quick classification task and a complex, multistep analysis have very different requirements. Model routing, which directs each task to the most suitable model, helps match capability to need. For more complex work, agent orchestration allows multiple agents with distinct roles and expertise to work together, much like a well-structured team.

The aim is fit, not firepower. The most powerful model isn’t always the right one, and the right one may change as tasks and models evolve.

For agentic AI to create lasting value beyond one-off automation, it needs to get better over time. That means feeding context, user feedback and the results of previous actions back into how agents make future decisions.

Many deployments still treat each task as a fresh start. The agent completes the work, and whatever could have been learned from the result is lost. Building feedback loops into workflows from the beginning lets systems improve with use, under appropriate human oversight, rather than depending entirely on periodic manual updates.

This is where much of the long-term value can come from. An agent that improves with every cycle compounds its value. One that doesn’t stay at the level it launched with.

Efficiency matters more as agentic systems grow more complex. Multistep reasoning, repeated model calls and interactions between agents all consume compute, and those costs can climb quietly as usage scales.

The goal isn’t to minimize resource use for its own sake. It’s to deliver consistent outcomes without using more than the task requires, matching models and compute to the job and reviewing costs regularly as real usage data comes in.

These SCALE principles reinforce one another. Strategic goals and metrics tell you what to measure. Calibrated confidence helps AI know when to act and keeps it reliable. Adaptive model selection makes it effective. Learning helps it improve, and efficient resource use keeps that improvement sustainable.

There’s a common assumption that as AI becomes more autonomous, it will need less management. I believe the opposite is true. The more decisions and actions AI takes on, the more sophisticated enterprises need to be about how they govern and operate it.

Autonomy alone isn’t the measure of success. What matters is whether AI can be operated reliably and efficiently, and whether its business impact keeps growing over time.​​​

Management narrowed the 2026 earnings guidance range and expanded the five-year capital plan by $1.5 billion to accommodate customer growth and reliability initiatives. The company reported the completion of the 1.2 gigawatt Orange County Advanced Power Station and moved forward with more than 1,000 miles of planned transmission lines, primarily in Louisiana and Texas.

#3072. Lakers’ Luka Doncic sitting out against Pistons with back ailment

DETROIT — Luka Dončić wasn't available for Sunday's road game against the Pistons.

The Lakers ruled the superstar guard out five hours before tipoff because of low back tightness.

Luka Doncic missed his second game of the season with back tightness. AP Photo/Mark J. Terrill

He entered Sunday listed as questionable because of the ailment before the team revealed he wouldn't play.

Sunday was the second game of the season Dončić missed through the team's first 11 games, with both absences coming amid back-to-back sets.

Cade Cunningham entered Sunday leading the Pistons in scoring and assists. Getty Images

The Lakers will play the Hawks at State Farm Arena in Atlanta on Monday to conclude their back-to-back set. Dončić's status for the matchup against the Hawks likely won't be known until Monday afternoon.

He also sat out of the Oct. 28 road win over the Clippers because of back tightness after playing in the Oct. 27 home loss to the Trail Blazers.

Dončić entered the weekend leading the league in scoring, averaging 40.1 points to go with 7.8 rebounds, 7.7 assists and 1.7 steals in 36 minutes per game.

Luka Doncic missed the matchup between the league's best offense (Lakers) and defense (Pistons). AP Photo/Mark J. Terrill

He's scored at least 40 points in four straight games and six of the last seven games he's played in.

Dončić was the lone Laker not available against the Pistons.

Third-year guard Bronny James and rookie wing Cameron Carr rejoined the team for the road trip after playing in the Coachella Valley Lakers' season-opening win on Friday.

The Pistons remained without Jalen Duren because of a strained right hamstring. The team said on Sunday that the All-NBA center will be reevaluated in two weeks after being cleared to begin on-court activities.

#3071. The 4 Dimensions Of Scoring AI Risk: Why ‘Probable’ Must Always Give Way To ‘Proven’

Imran Aftab, CEO and Co-founder, 10Pearls—driving AI innovation and creating meaningful opportunities that make an impact.

​Enterprises have poured tens of billions of dollars into generative AI, but only a small fraction of organizations report measurable impacts on profits. The vast majority of AI projects are stuck in pilots, proofs of concept or ungoverned experimentation that fails to earn the trust needed to scale across an organization. ​

This happens because AI is often deployed before it’s proven to be entirely ready and secure. Stanford University’s 2026 AI Index highlights findings from the AI Incident Database (AIID), which found that the number of AI incidents jumped by 55% between this year and last. Yes, there are more AI projects being deployed, but those accelerated rollouts also conflate “probably” with “definitely.”

Risk is not black and white across every AI system and model. It needs to be a score, built from named dimensions, that decides exactly how much autonomy a system earns. That score has to hold up in front of a board of directors, regulators, customers and, of course, engineers.​

Leaders must be able to confirm whether AI passes the following checkpoints before giving the green light. Ensuring AI is provably safe across these dimensions is at the base of a robust strategy that minimizes vulnerabilities, for business and tools alike. ​

Can a wrong decision be undone? A drafted email that’s human-reviewed before sending is fully reversible, but a recorded credit refusal already acted on is not. The less reversible the action, the further the use case moves away from autonomy and toward mandatory human oversight. ​

In my experience, this is the dimension boards are least prepared to weigh. For instance, research from Deloitte shows that 66% of boards still have limited-to-no knowledge of AI. Running blind on the real-world impact is a dangerous environment in which to make high-stakes calls. ​

What is the regulatory exposure, and does every AI decision and action comply with all relevant regulations?

Regulatory demands are increasing. Under the EU AI Act, the Article 50 transparency obligations and the AI Office’s enforcement powers over general-purpose AI have been activated, with penalties potentially reaching up to the tens of millions. Stringent regulatory exposure is now a live liability.

​Finally, can the AI’s reasoning actually be produced, explained and defended on demand? Auditability is now a central pillar of any AI strategy, and board oversight is a leading indicator in this regard: 31% of organizations still report AI is not on the board agenda at all. That suggests there is no formal mechanism in place at a third of companies for anyone at the top to ask for evidence before something goes wrong.

​These four dimensions should be combined into a composite score, which then guides the architecture and level of autonomy for the use case. Sometimes the risk score is high enough that the best answer is no AI at all. But that’s not a failure; it’s the process working precisely as it should. ​

The score routes every use case into a pattern that matches its risk. This ranges from full autonomy for low-risk, high-volume work to a blend of human oversight and AI outputs, to a human-only workflow for the most severe of risks. Testing depth follows the same score, scaling from lighter-weight functioning checks to independent audits and documented explainability for highest-risk systems.

​It’s where scored governance starts paying for itself instead of just protecting against downside, particularly as the majority of organizations approach the strategic or embedded stage of AI. Reaching that stage and actually extracting repeatable commercial value, however, are two different achievements, and only a small chunk of organizations seem to be closing that gap.

Boards, regulators and customers trust decisions that are explained and defended. That trust cannot be won through decisions where “probably” was the default.

Fortunately, organizations are rising to meet that expectation. The share of organizations with no responsible-AI policy fell from 24% to 11% between 2024 and 2025, while AI-specific governance roles grew 17%, per that same Stanford University AI Index report.

​What has not caught up is enforcement and accountability. Surprisingly, even as regulators are cracking down on any ambiguity around accountability, per a 2025 survey by McKinsey, only 28% of organizations give their CEO direct responsibility for AI governance, and 17% to the board. That gap is where we’re still seeing firms accept “probably fine” as the threshold for successful AI, and it is what scored and evidenced risk closes. ​

Winning with AI is not about aggressive adoption or being over-cautious, but being able to show exactly why each AI decision was made and who is accountable for it.

AI is taking on more consequential decisions across the enterprise. Regulators, boards, customers and incident data are all pointing in the same direction, and a tool that is “probably fine” is no longer an acceptable answer. Scored, evidenced risk to prove AI works before it’s rolled out should be the new baseline for every organization.

#3070. Investors are doing just as well this year by shunning AI. How to invest if the tech trade keeps fizzling

A version of the S&P 500 without AI briefly pulled ahead of the traditional index this year and is now neck-and-neck as investors rotate into other areas of the market.

A proprietary Goldman Sachs index tracking the S&P 500 without stocks classified as "AI enablers" was up 12.4% through Oct. 22, edging ahead of the standard S&P 500's 12% gain. The Goldman index is now neck-and-neck with the S&P 500 as tech rallied in Monday trading.

Tech and AI-related companies make up about 45% of the S&P 500. That heavy weighting has helped power the index for years, but it's turned into a liability lately; the S&P 500 tech sector is down about 7% this month while other sectors have held up.

Investors have soured on debt and equity issued by companies like CoreWeave and Oracle. Shares of Meta Platforms sank almost 7% Thursday after it outlined more plans to spend heavily on capex and issue additional shares.

Companies supplying power and equipment for the buildout have been hit hard — names like GE Vernova, Bloom Energy, Vistra and Quanta Services all suffered steep declines during the recent selloff.

Goldman, which launched the measure earlier this year with S&P, uses the S&P 500 as its starting universe and excludes companies perceived to be enablers of AI before applying S&P 500 Index weighting methodology to the remaining universe of companies.

The ex-AI index lagged the S&P 500 for most of the year as investors continued to favor chipmakers, cloud-computing companies and other firms benefiting from heavy AI spending. However, that advantage has been narrowing and it disappeared last week.

Meanwhile, investors are rotating into defensive areas. ETFs like State Street Consumer Staples Select Sector SPDR ETF, State Street Health Select SPDR ETF and State Street Utilities Select Sector SPDR ETF are up 7% to 10% this month. Energy is ahead 10% too, though that's more related to the war in Iran.

Some analysts recommend sticking with non-AI companies for diversification and protection against more pain in tech. The "AI pendulum has swung back in favor of non-AI exposure over the last two weeks," Oppenheimer technical analyst Ari Wald said in a note on Oct. 24.

Two industries that Oppenheimer favors now are commercial services and insurance. The firm upgraded those industries to overweight last week, recommending Republic Services, Cintas, Verisk Analytics, Broadridge Financial Solutions, MetLife and Arthur J. Gallagher.

Berkshire Hathaway is also capitalizing on the rotation out of tech. Its Class B shares are up 8% this month, though it's still lagging behind the S&P 500 this year.

Berkshire owns a wide swath of operating companies, including insurance giant Geico and Burlington Northern Santa Fe railroad. It also has a $364 billion stock portfolio including companies like Apple, Coca-Cola, Alphabet and Bank of America. That diversification may help Berkshire continue to outperform if the tech sector drags down the S&P 500.

Trivector Research sees potential in "non-tech compounders." Healthcare giant Eli Lilly is one idea. The stock is up 22% on the strength of Lilly's weight-loss drugs. The company has more in the pipeline, including a next-generation obesity drug that Lilly plans to file for FDA approval early in 2027.

Viking Holdings, a cruise operator, is also proving durable. The company said on its August earnings call that 40% of its river capacity and 60% of its ocean capacity was already booked for 2027. "Based on recent events, we've seen our guests have proved to be resilient and are continuing to book 2027 and future seasons," the company told investors.

Viking stock is up 15% this year but it may still have upside. The average Wall Street target is $109, above recent prices around $82. Barclays recently upgraded the cruise operator to overweight with a $102 target, citing the company's "compelling risk/reward."

Brent Guerisoli: Thanks, Kirk, and welcome, everyone, to our third quarter 2026 earnings call. We are pleased to report another quarter of strong performance across Pennant. In Q3, we reported revenue of $302.3 million, an increase of 32%. Adjusted EBITDA of $24.7 million, an increase of 42.4%. Adjusted EBITDA prior to NCI of $26.1 million, an increase of 44%. And adjusted earnings per share of $0.35, an increase of 16.7%, each over the prior year quarter. Pennant continues to grow and perform at a remarkable pace. This quarter represents another important step forward in a multi-year track record of exceptional growth, consistent execution, and progress toward our long-term objectives. The strength of our performance is evident throughout our operations.

On a year-over-year basis, we are now serving nearly 40% more home health patients, 35% more hospice patients, and 10% more senior living residents than we were just 1 year ago. This is significant growth, and importantly, it reflects the effectiveness of our operating model and the continued execution of our local leaders and teams. We have always approached building Pennant with a long-term perspective. Our focus is not simply on delivering results in the short term, but on building an organization capable of generating exceptional growth and performance over many years. From that perspective, we see tremendous positive momentum across both of our core businesses.

Our home health and hospice segment continues to perform at a high level, delivering strong year-over-year growth. Our senior living segment likewise delivered solid results, even as our teams worked through the demands of integrating several new communities. While our underlying operating performance remained strong and in line with our expectations, we experienced higher-than-anticipated employee benefits costs during the quarter, including our newly acquired operations. These costs created additional margin pressure and modestly impacted our earnings for the quarter. We are taking steps to more predictably manage these costs going forward and have incorporated our current expectations for elevated benefits expenses into our fourth quarter projections.

While potential variability in these costs remains, we continue to believe we are positioned to achieve our full-year guidance. We remain confident in the fundamental strength of our business, our strategy, and the significant opportunities ahead of us. On the regulatory front, the home health final rule was released yesterday and includes a 2.1% net increase in the home health payment rate, or 1.5% as applied to our claims based on the proposed rule. After several years of negative rate updates, a small increase is a step in the right direction, but it is insufficient.

To preserve access to home health services, particularly in rural areas, home health reimbursements must account for the impacts of high inflation and must appropriately compensate high-quality providers. We will continue to work with our industry partners to advance positive home health policies, and we are encouraged to see the introduction of bills in the House and the Senate that call upon those bodies to redress the persistent underfunding of home health. The home health final rule also includes several program integrity measures, which CMS intends to use to target fraudulent and illegitimate providers. We support CMS' efforts to root out fraud, but we believe several of these measures are unnecessarily broad and will impose burdens on legitimate providers.

That said, we are prepared and equipped to adapt to the changes. We continue to drive progress on the five key initiatives that have been our focus for multiple years: leadership development, clinical excellence, margin, growth, and employee experience. Over the last several years, we have invested heavily in developing leaders, strengthening our clusters, expanding our geographic footprint, and building the infrastructure necessary to support a much larger organization. On the leadership front, we have added more than 100 CEOs-in-training this year and continue to deploy robust C-level training across key leader roles. These investments are increasingly visible in our results.

We have more talented leaders operating in more markets, a significantly broader portfolio of operations, and more opportunities to deploy The Pennant Model than at any point in our history. We believe the foundation we are building, combined with the momentum we are seeing throughout the organization, positions Pennant exceptionally well for continued growth and long-term success. With that, I'll turn the call over to John Gochnour to provide more detail on our third quarter operational results.

John Gochnour: Thank you, Brent, and good morning, everyone. As Brent highlighted, our Q3 results show robust year-over-year improvement across our operating segments. Our home health and hospice segment delivered excellent results. Segment revenue of $239.8 million increased $66.2 million or 38.2%. Segment adjusted EBITDA of $38.1 million increased $11.3 million or 42%. And segment adjusted EBITDA prior to NCI of $39.5 million increased $11.9 million or 43%, each over the prior year quarter. This improvement was driven by strong performance at mature operations and the effective transition of newly acquired operations. Of particular note is our strong same-store performance during a period of exceptional growth.

Over the last 2 years, we have added 75 locations to our home health and hospice segment. This growth has led to significant investments in leadership, infrastructure, and service center support, enabling us to transition larger and larger acquisitions more effectively. It has also demonstrated our ability to elevate leaders internally. As we have described before, our transition process is not led by a traditional corporate development team. Instead, our local operations teams and service center resources directly support these transitions. Our results, and especially our same-store performance, reflect the dynamic flywheel that this approach creates as local CEOs and CCOs elevate others within their teams so they can spend time supporting transitions.

In many cases, these newly elevated leaders have driven improved clinical, financial, and growth results in our same-store operations, even as our CEO and CCO group have helped effectively integrate these new agencies. As a result of these efforts across the segment, total home health admissions grew 39.4% and Medicare admissions grew 38%, offsetting a 2.2% decline in revenue per episode due to lower rates in our new Southeast locations. In same-store locations, our total admissions increased 8%, Medicare admissions increased 12%, and revenue per episode increased 1.6%, each over the prior year quarter, as our operators drove accelerated growth and effectively offset the Medicare rate cut.

We also saw compelling hospice growth with total admissions increasing 31.8%, total average daily census increasing 34.6%, and revenue per day improving 2.1%, each over the prior year quarter. Same-store growth was equally strong, with same-store admissions up 3.1%, ADC increasing 13%, and revenue per day improving 3.5%, each over the prior year quarter. Our local leaders continued to manage the business effectively. And despite the significant increase in benefits costs that Brent described earlier, we saw same-store margin increase 80 basis points compared to the prior year quarter. Clinically, we saw continued outperformance as our potentially preventable hospitalization rate improved 10 basis points to 9.9% across the portfolio compared to an industry average of 10.8%.

And our CMS-reported hospice quality composite score increased to 98.3% compared to an industry average of 96.2%. We know our clinical outcomes drive our growth and financial performance and have made us an attractive partner for prospective referral, joint venture, and payer partners. Turning to senior living, segment revenue of $62.4 million is up 12.6% and adjusted EBITDA of $5.7 million is up 3%, each over the prior year quarter. Since the beginning of last year, our senior living business has acquired 16 communities, including seven in this calendar year. This growth created some short-term operating challenges during the quarter, concentrated primarily in two markets with a high number of transitions.

In these markets, our growth temporarily outpaced leadership capacity, and several transitions and same-store operations did not perform at the level we expected. Combined with the elevated benefits costs that Brent described earlier, this impacted segment margins and caused segment-level adjusted EBITDA to be roughly flat compared to the prior year quarter. It is important to keep these challenges in perspective. They are concentrated rather than systemic, and they come against a backdrop of substantial growth in the senior living business as a whole.

We are excited about each of our newly added communities, many of which were acquired at low occupancy and at a substantial discount to market rates, and the opportunity they present for organic growth for years to come. As we have discussed many times, we expect lumpiness in our short-term results, especially in communities we have acquired with low occupancy. This lumpiness in senior living may continue in the short term as we integrate and fill these communities. Experienced leaders are actively engaged, concrete improvement plans are underway, and we expect steady operational progress in the near term and significant growth over the long term. Turning to growth.

On August 1, we acquired the real estate and operations of River Centre Assisted Living, a 63-unit assisted living community in Tucson, Arizona. This acquisition contributes to Pennant's strong and growing position in the Tucson market. During 2026, we doubled the number of communities we operate in Tucson, which has created a robust cluster of senior living operations in the market and complements our existing strength on the home health and hospice side. Despite recent capital expenditures and an attractive building, River Centre's low occupancy and poor financial performance allowed us to acquire it at a significant discount to market rates. This reflects our opportunistic acquisition approach, which can create short-term financial drag, but significant mid- and long-term upside.

In September, Pennant acquired the real estate associated with one of its existing operations, Mainplace Senior Living, located in Orange, California. The transaction reflects our disciplined real estate investment strategy and our conviction that selective real estate ownership is a natural complement to operational success, supports long-term operating stability, and creates enduring value. We have been operating Mainplace under a triple-net lease since 2019 and have created significant value through improved performance, which is reflected not only in the operating cash flows, but in the real estate. This purchase allowed us to capture much of the value we created through the operational turnaround.

Our integration of the 54 locations we purchased from UnitedHealth and Amedisys in the Southeast is nearly complete. In the third quarter, we transitioned the two largest and final waves of operations. As expected, the agencies experienced ordinary disruption associated with a transition of this size, which may modestly impact results through the end of the year. We continue to perform ahead of initial expectations and look forward to completing the transition in Q4 and shifting our focus toward optimization and long-term value creation. We continue to field numerous acquisition opportunities in each of our segments. On the home health and hospice side, we expect to be active as opportunities emerge and as we complete the integrations I just described.

On the senior living side, we are working to stabilize and optimize the numerous operations we have added in 2026 and intend to focus primarily on those efforts, though we may selectively pursue compelling and non-disruptive acquisitions in well-performing markets. With that, I'll hand it over to Lynette for a review of the financials. Lynette?

We reported total GAAP revenue of $302.3 million, adjusted EBITDA of $24.7 million, adjusted EBITDA prior to NCI of $26.1 million, GAAP diluted earnings per share of $0.26, and adjusted diluted earnings per share of $0.35. Key metrics for the 3 months ended September 30, 2026, include $103 million outstanding on our line of credit and $18.4 million cash on hand at quarter end, 1.95x net debt to adjusted EBITDA, and cash flows provided from operations of $25.1 million in Q3.

Our decentralized structure enables local leaders to create life-changing impacts for their patients, employees, and communities. Their stories demonstrate how our operating model enables local leaders to create life-changing impacts for their patients, employees and communities. CEO, Tella Silver; CCO, Ryan Withers; CMO, Denna McCloud; and future COO, Casey Woodworth lead Symbii Home Health and Hospice in the Provo, Utah market.

Symbii knows that delivering great care to patients is the foundation of all we do, and its clinical results are excellent, including a 5-star Home Health rating and a potentially preventable hospitalization rate of 6.9% compared to a national average of 10.8%. In addition, Symbii has cultivated a positive culture where employees celebrate wins and support one another. Propelled by their extraordinary clinical and cultural performance, Symbii has become a local powerhouse as demonstrated by its record-high census. This is the most recent chapter in a multi-year growth story that includes 33% compound annual revenue growth and 35% compound annual EBITDA growth over the last 3 years.

At Harvest Home and Inwood Crossing in Tomball, Texas, future CEO, Rod Phillips; and future CCO, Pearl Morrison are creating a community that blesses the lives of residents in the greater Houston area. Harvest Home joined the Pennant organization through acquisition in early 2025. Since then, Harvest Home's turnover has improved by over 20%, demonstrating the team's commitment to driving culture and creating an exceptional employee experience. Over the same period, Harvest Home has increased occupancy to 91%, leading to revenue growth of almost 20% and EBITDA growth of 276%.

Harvest Home's story is a recent example of Pennant's ability to acquire and transition underperforming senior living communities, apply our local leadership model, improve operating principles, and create meaningful benefits for residents, families, employees, and all Pennant owners. With that, I'll turn the call back over to Brent for concluding comments.

Brent Guerisoli: Thanks, Lynette. As we conclude, I want to thank our local leaders, clinicians, and team members. Rapid growth demands a great deal from our teams. Your willingness to take ownership, respond to challenges, and remain focused on providing life-changing service to patients and residents is what makes our model work. And so I think the things I would highlight is we remain ahead of sort of the progress that we initially projected in our guidance and in our updated guidance. And so we're not making any changes to our expectations, and we're very excited about the future.

The delta between where those businesses are performing and where our traditional same-store operations perform remains significant, and the opportunity to close that gap creates significant upside for our operations over the next couple of years. So really excited about the Southeast, about the quality of the teams, the quality of the people. It's just a really remarkable opportunity for Pennant, and we're happy to have the main key sort of milestones in the transition complete.

Raj Kumar: I appreciate all that color. And then maybe as a follow-up, kind of thinking about senior living, I think occupancy kind of on the same-store basis was down Y-o-Y. I know you kind of talked about in your prepared remarks in terms of some of the other impacts. I guess I'm kind of curious on the timeline in terms of recovery there. And so kind of curious on any of those impacts that you might have experienced during the quarter.

Andrew Rider: Hey, Raj. Thanks for the question. I really appreciate your thoughts there. We have described in the script, some of these pressures are really occurring related to the acquisition lift. And we're through kind of that initial phase of pressure that comes from just all the work that goes into transitioning, and now we kind of have our feet under us. We completed our last acquisition, and so there are varying stages of kind of finalizing that transition challenge. But this is really related to two primary markets where we have challenges related to this lift, and the occupancy challenge that's led to the same-store is also in those two markets.

We rely heavily on our local clusters and operators to complete acquisitions and these transitions. And so what can happen is we can get a little thin as we really tug on existing operators to make those transitions, and it can create distractions. And so we're focused on recovery. John Gochnour: Yes, we are sort of reaffirming that we expect to hit our annual guidance. There's a significant push being made across the organization, and we expect that those efforts will quickly bear fruit and that we've got the opportunity to turn that into a real positive for 2027. These deals that we've done are uniformly high-upside deals. They come with low occupancy and because of that, we're able to get them at favorable prices, favorable rents, which really create the long-term opportunity that we're focused on. And so when we look to the fourth quarter, I think we've projected an elevated benefits expense in that fourth quarter. #3063. Berkshire Hathaway's Top AI Holding Is Poised to Outperform

The conglomerate's fourth-largest position is in an internet business whose share price has fallen 28% from the peak.

Even in his final years running Berkshire Hathaway, Warren Buffett continued to show he could expand his circle of competence. For the famed investor, the learning process never stopped.

This is precisely what he did when he initiated the buying of Alphabet (GOOGL +3.34%) (GOOG +3.07%) in Berkshire Hathaway's portfolio in the third quarter of last year, a move that current CEO Greg Abel followed up with additional purchases. Between the Class A and Class C shares, the artificial intelligence (AI) hyperscaler represents the conglomerate's fourth-largest position.

Berkshire Hathaway's top AI holding, Alphabet, is poised to outperform the market. Here's why.

The market might be starting to worry about AI spending. Alphabet's capital expenditures (capex) will total roughly $200 billion in 2026. Next year, management projects it will rise substantially. No one could have predicted five years ago that the capital-light internet giant would embark on a major spending spree.

Free cash flow is negative, coming in at $9.1 billion in the red during the third quarter. Alphabet has started to fund its AI aspirations with external capital. Long-term debt rose 169% from the end of last year to $125.1 billion.

The AI stock, which has soared 124% in the past 36 months (as of Nov. 4), now trades at 28% below its peak. Shares dipped following the announcement of Q3 financial results, as investors digested a miss on both the top and bottom lines, with Google Search sales slowing to 12%.

This exact setup plays into the hands of long-term investors who look at the next five years. It's impossible not to get interested in the current valuation. Alphabet shares trade at a forward price-to-earnings ratio of 18.5. There's a lot of uncertainty surrounding AI. But this is a compelling entry point for one of the world's most outstanding businesses.

According to sell-side analysts' consensus estimates, Alphabet will grow its operating income at a compound annual rate of 28.1% from 2025 to 2028. For a company of this scale, that growth rate is impressive. Revenue surged 25% year over year in the most recent quarter.

Alphabet's leadership position in AI is demonstrated by its Google Cloud segment, which posted a robust 103% Q3 sales gain. That continues a streak of accelerating growth, indicating how much demand there is from customers for AI capabilities. The backlog sits at $561 billion.

Google Cloud benefits from the AI boom by being able to sell specific software and hardware to enterprise clients. Additionally, Alphabet's full suite of products and services also improves with the integration of AI.

While the next few years are impossible to forecast and introduce heightened uncertainty, this company is in a favorable position as it rides the AI wave. The stock can be a big winner.

Neil Patel has no position in any of the stocks mentioned. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Alphabet and Berkshire Hathaway. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

#3060. The Increasing Political Risk In IT Strategy

Kevin Dominik Korte: IT Innovation Strategist, Board Member. Expert in identity management, AI and open-source solutions.

​When most business leaders think of sanctions, trade restrictions or tariffs, they picture Coast Guard boats stopping merchant vessels filled with weapons. Seldom do we consider our tech exposure on the front lines of international politics. However, your technology supplier might meet every service-level agreement and still become unavailable to your business. All it takes is a government decision.

Consequently, executives should evaluate IT procurement through a geopolitical lens. When governments restrict semiconductor exports or regulate cross-border data flows, technology purchasing becomes inseparable from geopolitics. For business leaders, the response should be diversification, not a declaration of allegiance to one technology bloc. The objective is to preserve operational choices when political conditions change.

Consider a data center construction company buying optical transceivers for data centers from two vendors. Its procurement team may report supplier diversity. Yet both vendors could depend on the same optical chip manufacturer or critical material. Two contracts do not necessarily create two independent supply chains.

The same question belongs in software and cloud procurement: Can the business actually move, or does its alternative merely recreate the original dependency? Executives should therefore ask a different question. Instead of asking only whether a supplier is reliable, they should ask what would happen if that supplier were legally unable to deliver.

The United States frames advanced semiconductor restrictions around national security, including concerns that commercial computing capabilities can support Chinese military and intelligence applications. The Congressional Research Service documents successive efforts to restrict China’s access to advanced chips and manufacturing technology.

These concerns deserve serious consideration. A business cannot responsibly treat sensitive technologies as ordinary commodities simply because unrestricted trade would make purchasing easier.

The restriction on semiconductors also highlights the intersection between hardware and software. The export restrictions directly address U.S. fears that China will use its technological power for military or surveillance purposes. Thus, to restrict AI software development, the U.S. restricted access to the needed hardware.

In the pure software realm, the back-and-forth about access restrictions to the latest AI models should make the political risk a priority. Outside of AI, the restriction on U.S. cloud service providers from providing services to the International Criminal Court highlights how political decisions can affect cloud-service dependencies.

However, security policies create commercial consequences beyond their intended targets. The ICC sanctions have pushed much of the developed world to seek alternatives to U.S. cloud services. Likewise, the export restrictions on AI chips have led to new designs and more effective models.

Most critically, the lesson learned was not that American suppliers are unsuitable. It is that technical roadmaps can depend on licensing decisions and diplomatic negotiations.

The European Union emphasizes resilience and technological capacity. Its Chips Act established an ambition to double Europe’s global semiconductor market share to at least 20% by 2030, supported by investment mobilization and measures to strengthen the semiconductor ecosystem. These are policy objectives, not guarantees that European buyers can source every essential component locally.

Europe also addresses dependency through market rules. The Data Act, applicable since September 2025, creates requirements intended to facilitate switching between cloud and other data-processing providers. This offers businesses a useful foundation for portability, although legal rights cannot replace migration planning.

China combines technological self-reliance with controls over strategically important inputs and know-how. MERICS documents export licensing for gallium and germanium introduced in 2023, alongside restrictions affecting graphite and rare-earth magnet manufacturing technology. Its analysis connects these measures to security, industrial policy and geopolitical leverage.

Beijing has legitimate interests in protecting sensitive technologies, as do Washington and Brussels. Nevertheless, MERICS identifies opacity and discretionary implementation as particular challenges for foreign businesses.

Balance does not require pretending these systems are identical. Their institutions, transparency and objectives differ. The shared business consequence is narrower: Governments can alter access to technologies, materials and services that companies previously treated as stable commercial inputs.

The appropriate response is selective resilience rather than blanket duplication. Creating a redundancy for every business function would impose costs that many businesses cannot justify. Instead, executives should identify where interruption would create a significant business impact. Those dependencies deserve deeper scrutiny and funded alternatives.

For hardware, that scrutiny should extend beyond the immediate supplier. The semiconductor supply chain ranges from design tools via specialized materials to compliance testing. Independence at one stage does not establish independence across the chain.

For software, procurement should favor demonstrable portability. Require usable data exports, standardized open interfaces and practical transition support. The EU Data Act reinforces aspects of this approach, including open-interface and machine-readable export requirements for relevant services.

Open Source can provide a suitable alternative. Thus, instead of checking only for big names, evaluate options on the same operational basis. Ask whether another qualified team could maintain the system, whether documentation is sufficient and whether the organization possesses the skill or can procure it locally to assume greater responsibility.

Most importantly, test the exit. Move a representative workload, restore an independent backup and measure the time required. A second supplier becomes meaningful when the company can use it under pressure, not merely when procurement has reviewed a website or catalog entry.

Diversification is a comprehensive strategy. It should be treated as insurance with explicit costs, not as a procurement slogan. It must start in the board’s risk management strategy and flow down through management into operations. Document critical dependencies, affordable alternatives and recovery time alongside political risk.

Ultimately, the goal is not tech isolation with American, European or Chinese technological islands. It is a business that can work across markets without being blackmailable by one supplier, jurisdiction or political entity.
