He is a very good shooter and so the Celtics need to defend him well wherever he is on the court. He keyed a run by the Bucks to come back from 21 points down at the half to take the lead in the 4th quarter. I'm guessing that Jordan Walsh gets the start here, but with Joe playing mad scientist with the lineups, you never know.

Paul George vs Jaime Jaquez, JrAs with Herro, Jaquez is in his first season with the Bucks. He is averaging 16.4 points, 6.2 rebounds, and 2.8 assists per game. He is shooting 48.7% from the field and 44.7% from beyond the arc. In the first game against the Celtics, he finished with 18 points, 2 rebounds, 2 assists and 1 steal while shooting 43.8% from the field and 66.7% from beyond the arc. He is a good shooter and so, as with Herro, the Celtics need to stay with him and defend him well.

Honorable MentionJayson Tatum vs Kyle Kuzma Kuzma is averaging 9.9 points, 6.0 rebounds, and 3.0 assists per game. He is shooting 46.3% from the field and 28.9% from beyond the arc. In the first game against the Celtics, he finished with 6 points, 5 rebounds, 4 assists, and 1 steal while shooting 40% from the field and 33.3% from beyond the arc. Although he is struggling from the perimeter, he is very capable of hitting 3's if left open. Hopefully Jayson Tatum can pick up where he left off on Friday.

Keys to the GameDefense – Defense is always the biggest key to winning. Defense really does win championships and it wins games. The Celtics are 4th with a defensive rating of 106.4. The Bucks are 27th with a defensive rating of 118.6. The Celtics must work hard on defense and keep their focus on the defensive end so as not to allow any easy baskets for the Bucks. They especially need to defend the perimeter as the Bucks are 1st in the league attempting 44.1 three pointers per game.

Rebound – Next to defense, rebounding is always a big key to winning. The key to rebounding is effort and focus. The Bucks are 3rd with 49.0 rebounds per game while the Celtics are 14th with 43.9 rebounds per game. The Celtics have to fight as a team to try to grab every rebound to avoid the Bucks getting 2nd chance points because the Bucks are 3rd with 18.2 second chance points per game.

Don't Underestimate the Bucks – The Bucks have not been playing well so far this season, going just 1-8 in their first 9 games. However, the Bucks are still a rival in the Eastern Conference that can play hard, which makes up for a lot of problems. In the first game against the Bucks, the Celtics built a 21 point lead at the half but let the Bucks out-play them in the second half to take a 92-91 lead. They held on to win the game, but they need to give 100% effort for the entire game and not underestimate the Bucks. The Celtics have to give max effort on the boards and on defense and they have to give that effort for the entire game and not just 1 or 2 quarters. Effort and Focus – "Hard work beats talent when talent doesn't work hard." That quote pretty much says it all. Any team that works hard and hustles can beat a more talented team that doesn't play hard. The Celtics have to be aggressive on defense, on rebounds, on fighting for loose balls, on taking the ball to the basket and just overall playing harder than the Bucks. They have to play harder and stay focused on playing the right way for all 48 minutes. They also can't overlook the Bucks while anticipating their big game on Tuesday at Philadelphia. Stay focused on this game.

X-FactorsOn the Road – The Celtics are on the road for the second straight game and so will have the distractions of travel, staying in hotels, and playing in front of a hostile crowd. They need to stay focused and not allow any of those distractions to take their focus away from playing the right way. Historically, the Celtics are just 46-73 in Milwaukee. They need to stay focused and play hard and not let up.

Officiating – Officiating is always an x-factor in every game. Every crew officiates differently. Some call it tight, others let them play. The Celtics need to adjust to how the refs are calling the game and not allow bad calls or no calls to take away their focus from playing the game. The Celtics also have to be aware of the new points of emphasis for this season and try to avoid flopping, off‑arm push‑offs, reckless closeouts, delays before free throws, and illegal screens. They have been especially calling flops and push offs and so the Celtics need to make an effort to avoid doing both.

#3051. Kings send Nique Clifford to Thunder for draft assets: Trade grades

The Sacramento Kings have agreed to trade guard Nique Clifford to the Oklahoma City Thunder in exchange for an unprotected 2028 second-round draft pick via Utah and an unprotected 2030 second-round draft pick via Minnesota, the team announced Sunday, Nov. 8.

Clifford, 24, is a 6-foot-5, 210-pound guard out of Colorado State that was originally selected by Oklahoma City with the 24th overall pick in the first round of the 2025 NBA Draft. However, Clifford never logged a minute in a Thunder uniform following a trade to the Kings that sent Oklahoma City a protected 2027 first-round pick.

He appeared in 75 games for Sacramento during the 2025-26 season and started 28. Clifford averaged 8.6 points, 3.8 rebounds and 2.4 assists in about 25.1 minutes during his rookie campaign with the Kings, while shooting 41.8% from the field and 33% on 3-pointers.

Clifford was being molded into a perennial "three-and-D" type of player for the Kings. He saw a lot of playing time in his rookie campaign, in part due to the numerous injuries Sacramento sustained to its roster that year.

He scored a career-high 30 points in a 132-126 loss to the Cleveland Cavaliers on Feb. 8. Throughout the 2025-26 season, Clifford also spent some time down in the G-League, playing for the Stockton Kings, the Kings affiliate.

In his collegiate years, Clifford averaged 10.1 points and just under a steal. He shot 46.9% from the field and 36.4% on 3-pointers.

Clifford signed a four-year rookie contract with Kings worth up to $15.7 million with $6.3 million guaranteed, according to Spotrac. Clifford's average annual salary is about $3.9 million.

He'll earn another $3.2 million in base salary.

Clifford appeared to be a contributing piece to the Kings' rebuild. The consummate professional, Clifford came into work, did what he was asked and pushed himself to be the best version of himself.

There was an expectation that Clifford would take a leap into his second-year but instead it came with setbacks. Clifford saw his minutes diminish early in the season. In his last game against the San Antonio Spurs on Friday, Nov. 6, Clifford only logged 4 minutes, 30 seconds and scored five points on 2-of-2 from the field.

He only played more than 10 minutes once this season – against the Memphis Grizzlies on Oct. 31. Clifford appeared in five of their nine games, earning four DNPs by coach's decision.

It appeared that Clifford was on the opposite end of head coach Doug Christie's rotations and a change was warranted. The Kings get to open a roster spot while picking up assets.

The Thunder have had misfortune early in the season, facing season-ending injuries to key rotation players, and additional injuries that will keep guys out long-term. Jalen Williams suffered a fractured left fibula and a dislocated ankle that required surgery. He's out for the year.

Cason Wallace has a torn labrum in his left shoulder and he is also out indefinitely. Chet Holmgren was ruled out 8 to 10 weeks after a biological treatment for a small patellar tendon tear in his right knee.

Oklahoma City needs bodies. Clifford was being buried on the bench early this season, the Thunder believe there's a spark that he can bring to to the team.

The organization has built a reputation of maximizing reserves and role players getting the best out of them, the latest project will be Clifford.

This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: Kings send Nique Clifford to Thunder for draft assets: Trade grades

#3048. Doing a Roth Conversion Just Got Easier in 2027. Here's Why

You may have more leeway to convert funds in a tax-efficient manner.

If you've been saving for retirement consistently in a traditional IRA or 401(k) plan, you may have an unwanted surprise to contend with. Once required minimum distributions start, you may find that you have to take very large withdrawals from your retirement savings. And that could have a host of consequences, from large tax bills to surcharges on the premiums you pay for Medicare.

To avoid that, you may want to consider a Roth conversion. With a Roth conversion, you move funds from a traditional retirement plan into a Roth IRA. Once that conversion is complete, you get to enjoy all of the benefits that come with having a Roth IRA, such as tax-free investment gains, tax-free withdrawals, and no forced distributions.

Because a Roth conversion is a taxable event, it's one you have to plan for carefully. But you may find it a bit easier to convert in 2027 for one key reason.

When you do a Roth conversion, the sum you move into a Roth IRA is taxable. And so it's generally best to try to convert at relatively low tax brackets.

In 2027, the income thresholds for the seven different federal tax brackets are increasing. This means you should have more opportunity to convert at a lower tax rate.

This year, for example, if you're single, the 24% tax bracket caps out at $201,775. In 2027, it's rising to $208,325. That means you could conceivably convert an additional $6,550 to a Roth IRA in 2027 while staying within the 24% tax bracket.

Of course, it's your total income that's accounted for when determining what tax bracket you fall into. If you're still working, for example, and plan to do a Roth conversion, your salary plus the amount you convert will count toward your income (not to mention any other income you might have, such as interest or dividend payments from a taxable account).

The point, though, is that you may have a bit more leeway to move funds to a Roth IRA in 2027 while avoiding a higher tax bracket. So it's worth doing some calculations to see what conversion amount makes sense.

Often, the key to a successful Roth conversion is time. If you're attempting to move a large sum of money out of a traditional retirement plan and into a Roth IRA, spreading that conversion out across multiple tax years is often ideal.

So if your traditional IRA or 401(k) balance keeps growing, don't wait to at least start running through different Roth conversion scenarios. You may also want to consult a financial advisor or tax professional to maximize conversions when appropriate.

That means that we have that devaluation. So if we measure the properties in dollar terms remain very stable compared with the previous quarter. So nothing relevant there. And last year was completely the opposite. There was a devaluation.

So since we are long dollars, the devaluation in pesos terms generated that gain. So moving to the next page. The other component that also is affected by the difference of the FX and inflation is the net financial results. This year, we have a loss of ARS 9 billion that basically we have a gain related to net FX results since we have there to express in pesos term, our dollar-denominated debt. And since we have an appreciation of the peso that generated a profit. Against last year, that was the opposite. So it was a loss of ARS 38.8 billion.

About the income tax, as we always mentioned, every time that we have to post a loss in the investment properties, we have to post a loss also in the deferred tax and the opposite when we have an appreciation of the investment properties, then we have to express a loss in the income tax. Well here, we include the evolution of our rental EBITDA in dollar terms.

So going -- we can reduce that debt very fast if we don't continue with the same pace of CapEx and also the dividend payment that this year was high in terms of compared with the previous year. And as you can see on the right side, most of our debt is in the long term. So no major pressure in the short term. About the dividends, as I mentioned, so we just paid the $137 million, ARS 211 billion. In terms of dividend yield, that was almost 11%. So probably this is the fifth year in a row that IRSA is paying more than 10% dividend yield. So probably the highest dividend payer of Argentina during the last 5 years. So for that reason, we decided to increase the dividend this year and also it's a little more efficient in terms of the capital structure about the tax shield that we will generate with a little more debt. So remember that last year, you started to pay taxes again after using all the tax credit. So we believe that with this capital structure will be a little more efficient. So with this, we finish the formal presentation. Now we open the line for the Q&A session.

Santiago Donato: [Operator Instructions] First question here, we have from Sophia from Latin Securities. How much CapEx should we expect for the year -- for fiscal year '27? Given the ongoing projects and the CapEx expected next year, should we expect dividend distributions to remain at current levels?

Matias Gaivironsky: So we gave the guidance of CapEx during the year, probably we will have around $150 million altogether. So with all the projects that we have and some remaining payments on existing acquisitions, so acquisitions that we already did. So we have to pay some installments. So altogether will be $150 million. That is if we don't buy anything new. So if we buy something else, probably that number could increase. And about the dividend distribution, well, if we analyze the last year and specifically this year, probably is a little higher than the average.

So every time that we decide the dividend, we analyze what is our CapEx needs, what is our cash position, the debt position and the structure of our debt. So this year, we feel comfortable to increase a little. But going forward, probably that number would be -- if I have to give a guidance, probably it's more on the average of our history that is more around $70 million per year. But as you know, we don't have a fixed dividend policy. We like to pay dividends. If we have excess of cash, we like to return to our shareholders. But we don't have the fixed policy.

So we will see every October, that is the month of the -- our shareholders' meeting, the proposal of the next year.

Santiago Donato: Next question. With your strong balance sheet, are share buybacks under consideration in addition to dividends? If so, would it be proposed next October?

Matias Gaivironsky: No, we can do it if we want before October. So this is upon our Board of Directors' decision. So far, we decided to keep -- to pay the dividend. So any shareholder can buy back the shares by themselves, not directly from us. But it's something that we did it in the -- many times in the past. So makes sense. We believe that the price of the shares has enormous discount, so it could make sense to do it. Although, as I mentioned, we just paid a dividend yield of 11%. So we use part of the cash for the dividend.

Santiago Donato: We gave some minutes more for any additional questions. There are no more questions, then we return back to Matias for his closing remarks.

Matias Gaivironsky: Thank you, Santi. I think there is no much more to add from my side. We remain optimistic about the year ahead. So many projects, a lot going on. So we expect to continue with Ramblas del Plata, and we hope to start seeing cranes for the buildings starting next year. So very happy on what's going on there. So we really appreciate your interest and participation. Thank you very much for joining us today, and see you next quarter.

#3044. As AI becomes more fractured, one name stands out: AMD

As Anthropic rushes to takes its shares public, the AI trade is showing cracks, and they are not confined to fringe players.

We recently wrote about CoreWeave, which fell 15.5% on Oct. 14 as yields on its 2032 notes touched 15%, and its default-swap spreads nearly doubled in October. IREN is down more than 20% this year. Last Thursday, the contagion reached chipmakers, which makes sense since much of CRWV and IREN's spending is going there. AMD dropped 8.1% as Meta's financing plans and a supply warning from Lam Research exacerbated data-center fears about the pace of AI spending.

Because when you screen for factors that demonstrably generate outperformance over time, the list narrows quickly. My screen: price above the 200-day moving average; revenue growing at least as fast as the S&P 500 (5%+ per annum); EPS growing at least as fast (7%+); rating upgrades; a PEG below 3; and ROE and ROIC of at least 12%. Of the names reporting in the next two weeks, AMD is effectively the only one that makes the list. Yes, you can (and arguably should, as our staples article described) position your portfolio with slightly less tech exposure than the broad indices provide, but we can't ignore the market's biggest and most transformative sector entirely.

Especially because the growth in this case doesn't just meet my criteria; it blows past them. Consensus for Q3 calls for EPS of $1.94 on revenue of $13.06 billion, versus $1.20 and $9.25 billion a year ago. That's YoY growth of nearly 62% and 41%, respectively. The recent drawdown came from a sector selloff, not anything AMD reported, but it shows that if some names in the space get hit, even the larger players are likely to feel it. On Oct. 6, Lisa Su said AMD would substantially increase supply in 2027 because AI orders keep outrunning capacity.

So how do you balance factors we know work for a fast-growing company against a backdrop of cracks in the AI trade? Options.

Owning the stock outright means absorbing a roughly 9% to 11% implied earnings-related move (day of). Earnings are about a week out, and over the past four quarters the smallest move over a similar window was more than 9%, and the largest move, after the company reported its Q1 26 results, was 38%! Of course, that kind of volatility means options aren't cheap, and that rich premium is also a reason not to simply buy calls.

A call spread risk reversal does both jobs: it reduces risk if the cracks widen, and the short options offset the elevated volatility we would otherwise pay for. The bottom chart shows that, by sacrificing about $1,700 of upside for $5,000 in outperformance during a severe downside move, and given how jittery this trade has been lately, this is a way to stay in it with considerably less risk. $5,000 less, specifically. Of course, selling that out will tie up some cash, but less so than simply buying the stock. And selling both the out and the call reduces long call purchase by 66%

The Chicago Bulls drafted Terry with the 18th overall pick back in the 2022 NBA Draft out of Arizona. He appeared in 218 games over his first four seasons, but was unable to show enough potential to convince a team to dedicate a rotation spot for him heading into this season. The Bulls had declined Terry's fifth-year option, and dealt him to the 76ers at last year's deadline. After failing to get an NBA deal in free agency, he joined the Warriors a series of deals over the summer.

A 6'6 wing who just turned 24, Terry remains an intriguing 3-and-D prospect. #3039. Amazon Generated $202 Billion in Quarterly Sales. Most of Its Operating Profit Came From Just 1 Business.

Understanding where Amazon earns its money makes its enormous investment plans easier to evaluate.

Take a moment and think about the last time you used Amazon (AMZN +4.23%). Did you buy something? Pay for something to watch on Amazon Prime? Maybe you checked on the status of a package? All of these services make it easy to think of Amazon as an e-commerce business.

However, the company's latest results reveal something many people may not fully grasp: Most of its profit comes from a segment many people never knowingly use. It's Amazon Web Services (AWS), and it deserves a place in the sun.

Explaining AWS and what it does can get complicated, so think of it this way: AWS rents out the computing power and storage businesses need to run online services. By renting, businesses can save money by avoiding the cost of building and maintaining the expensive equipment and facilities needed to run websites, store customer data, or support applications.

In addition, as artificial intelligence (AI) grows, AWS is becoming increasingly important. Organizations are scaling up their use of AI, and AWS provides much of the technological muscle to meet the surging demand. This raises an interesting question: How important is AWS to Amazon?

The answer is very important. AWS comprises about 23% of Amazon's revenue, but it contributes 63% of Amazon's operating profit. Therefore, AWS is a central concern for Amazon investors. When one segment drives roughly two-thirds of a company's profitability, investors scrutinize that segment's health.

One reason AWS stands out is the nature of Amazon's overall business. Its e-commerce segment drives a staggering amount of revenue, roughly $650 billion. However, historically, it hasn't been very profitable. Even with a recent widening, it generates an operating margin of about 8%. AWS, in contrast, has always been lucrative. Its operating margin stands at about 38%.

The reason is simple: Cloud computing benefits from enormous economies of scale. Once a data center is operational, it can take on many new clients. Those customers often sign enterprise subscription agreements with Amazon, delivering steady, highly profitable revenue. E-commerce, in contrast, is less profitable because of logistics, physical labor, and fuel costs.

However, AWS has a downside: its cost. Adding new facilities and equipment to fuel AWS's growth is expensive -- extremely expensive. It requires construction of enormous buildings, electrical systems, state-of-the-art equipment, and research. In the end, it means hundreds of billions of dollars -- $220 billion for 2026 -- in capital expenditures for the company.

AMZN Capital Expenditures (TTM) data by YCharts.

The point is that Amazon hopes to recoup this money many times over as the demand for AWS's services continues to grow, but, in the short term, markets are increasingly concerned that Amazon could be overspending.

While Wall Street might fret over the size of Amazon's capital investments in AWS, its stock valuation could be a signal to investors. It currently trades at a price-to-earnings (P/E) multiple of 21.6. That's well below its three-year average of 39.3, and it's approaching its all-time-low P/E multiple of 18.2.

In other words, Amazon's giant investment spree could present long-term investors with a historic opportunity, or its low P/E multiple could be a warning sign. We simply don't know.

When someone buys Amazon stock, they're not just buying an e-commerce company. Indeed, as Amazon's latest capital investments prove, the company is betting big on AWS. Amazon is as much a technology services supplier as it is a retailer. Buying Amazon stock now means believing in the company's vision: that its colossal investments in AWS will not only pay for themselves, but also lay the groundwork for decades of profits to come.

Jake Lerch has positions in Amazon. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Amazon. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

#3036. Ripple strikes deal with Robinhood to expand its RLUSD digital dollar

Ripple has struck a deal with Robinhood to expand the reach of its digital dollar, RLUSD, strengthening trading and financing links between their institutional businesses and improving Robinhood's internal money management.

The partnership involves using RLUSD to settle institutional trades, automate Robinhood's treasury operations and expand access to digital asset trading and financing through Ripple Prime and Bitstamp, the global crypto exchange acquired by Robinhood last year.

It also helps meet Robinhood's ambition of becoming a global financial superapp, centralizing its customers' financial lives while expanding the underlying infrastructure that can serve both retail and institutional clients.

"Utility is what moves stablecoins forward. Working with Ripple, Bitstamp and Robinhood will have access to RLUSD for institutional settlement, Ripple Treasury for our operations and Ripple Prime for financing," Robinhood Crypto General Manager Johann Kerbrat said in a statement shared with CNBC. "That is what a connected, global financial system looks like."

Stablecoins have long been a workhorse of the crypto world, giving traders a way to move money among exchanges, buy and sell crypto assets, and park funds between trades without having to convert back into traditional currency. But as the crypto industry evolves beyond trading and markets move toward 24/7 liquidity, stablecoins are becoming essential financial infrastructure because of their ability to enable near-instant settlement and move dollar-denominated value at any time, regardless of traditional banking hours.

As firms look to do more with stablecoins beyond simply listing them on exchanges, stablecoin issuers are betting they'll favor a one-stop-shop approach that bundles the technology and services needed to move money, settle trades and manage cash.

"Stablecoins have evolved from a crypto trading tool into a critical piece of financial infrastructure," Ripple President Monica Long told CNBC. "The clearest evidence of this is where they're now being embedded — from corporate payments to capital markets. Our partnership with Robinhood reflects that evolution."

"This is about much more than trading," she added. "It's about fundamentally changing how money moves and is managed — giving institutions the ability to operate 24/7/365, unlocking liquidity and putting capital to work more efficiently."

Circle Internet Group, a Ripple competitor, is positioning itself for a similar future, where winning platforms, in addition to issuing stablecoins, also provide the infrastructure to put them to work. Earlier this year, for example, it launched the Circle Payments Network, connecting financial institutions and payment providers using its flagship USDC stablecoin and other digital assets for cross-border payments.

The network is Circle's answer to the 8-year-old Ripple Payments business, a service that helps businesses move money across borders, using any of several assets moving through that system, including USDC, Ripple-created XRP and, as of its debut in December 2024, RLUSD.

RLUSD's market cap has grown to more than $2.5 billion. Tether's USDT and Circle's USDC still dominate the total stablecoin market, which now exceeds $300 billion.

RLUSD will also be listed on Robinhood's trading platform, and is currently available to traders on Bitstamp as well as Robinhood Chain, the company's home-grown blockchain for tokenized stocks and other assets.

Robinhood, which reports third-quarter results for the three months ended in September after the market closes, rose about 2.5% in early trading Tuesday, snapping a three-day decline.

Correction: A previous headline misspelled RLUSD.

#3033. The loss to the Chiefs shows the Jets are falling apart

Over the last several weeks, we have seen the classic unraveling of a Jets season. The faces change, but the results always seem to stay the same.

Entering Week 7, the Jets faced a two game homestand against beatable opponents. Victories against both the Dolphins and the Raiders would get the team to .500 through eight games and give this team real momentum heading into a tough stretch facing the Chiefs and Bills back-to-back.

Of course, the Jets handed the previously winless Dolphins their first victory and then lost to the Raiders, dropping their record to 2-6. Not even at the halfway point, the season was over.

It is normal for the competitive portion of the season to end early for Jets fans. It feels like an annual tradition in November to be discussing NFL Draft position above all else.

The only thing the Jets still had going for them is it felt like the team was still united. Players were fighting for each other.

Things changed in the Week 9 loss to the Kansas City Chiefs.

The Jets looked like an imploding team. Fans could see it in obvious ways like Minkah Fitzpatrick making a couple of business decisions when he had opportunities to make plays. Armand Membou threw his helmet in frustration in an emotional outburst after allow a second half sack. Geno Smith was demonstrative in his frustration frequently as the game slipped away.

These are symptoms of a season that is slipping away and a team that is in a spiral.

Through each offseason NFL fans of all 32 teams convince themselves that their team has made all of the right moves, and their roster is improved. That's part of being a fan.

At this time of year, Jets fans frequently are forced to confront the reality that the team made bad moves in the previous offseason, and that has a lot to do with the team's struggles.

The Jets might not have gotten everything wrong in the 2026 offseason. David Bailey increasingly looks like a budding star. If the two pass catchers the Jets took in the first round of the NFL Draft after Bailey aren't dominating, they at least look promising.

Still, at this point I think the obvious is staring Jets fans in the face. This remains a bottom tier roster, and many of the offseason moves that provided hope in March were poor decisions in hindsight, particularly on the defensive side of the ball.

And on offense, the internal improvements fans hoped for just haven't been as big as fans wanted. Adonai Mitchell has grown into a starting receiver capable of throwing up a big game now and then, but he consistently leaves plays on the field and leaves fans wanting more. Armand Membou and Olu Fashanu remain competent starting tackles, but at this point they don't look like the elite bookends fans dream of when their team makes back-to-back first round picks at the position.

Of course, no discussion on a Jets loss would be complete without discussing Aaron Glenn, Frank Reich, and the Jets coaching staff.

The typical criticism this crew gets on a weekly basis mostly applies so I'd like to turn my attention elsewhere.

Despite getting blown out in the second half, a strong case can be made that the Jets played better than Kansas City in the first half. The Chiefs came out flat. They were making mistakes, and the Jets forced a couple of turnovers. Despite outgaining Kansas City, the Jets still trailed at halftime.

Why was this? There are no simple answers, but one thing stuck out to me about the way the Jets coaching staff approached the game.

They didn't seem to be interested in making big plays and scoring touchdowns. It felt like their objective was ball control, playing keep away, even if it came at the expense of offensive efficiency.

In theory, that sounds great. With the right mix of players, it could even work. But this undermanned Jets team was not going into Arrowhead Stadium and winning the game with field goals. The defense just isn't good enough to hold Patrick Mahomes and the Chiefs down, even if they were successful in keeping the ball from them for a quarter or two.

This was a game the Jets needed to play from ahead. Put some pressure on the Chiefs. Maybe they don't react to it well. Maybe David Bailey can fire upfield and make a big play that changes the game.

It felt like the conservative offensive gameplan the Jets chose was implemented to reduce the odds of being blown out, not the maximize the odds of winning the game. The Jets aren't going to beat a team like the Chiefs playing like that. Once this team went to the locker room behind despite arguably being the strong first half team, the game was probably over. And you somewhat counterintuitively actually maximize the odds of being blown out.

Add all this to the typical sloppy Jets football with no communication on defense and untimely penalty after untimely penalty, and you have a recipe for a 23 point blowout loss.

Unfortunately for the Jets, there is no end in sight. Next week this team has to figure out a way to deal with Josh Allen and the Buffalo Bills. If you've got any confidence that game will go differently, I'd love to hear why.

#3026. AI debt fears ease ahead of Oracle, Alphabet and Amazon updates. Here's what to watch.

Fears over artificial intelligence debt have eased after a bout of volatility. But more tests for AI debt are coming.

Oracle holds its Investor Day on Wednesday. And hyperscalers Alphabet and Amazon.com are scheduled to report quarterly results after the market close on Wednesday and Thursday, respectively.

Credit markets are on edge over a flood of AI debt, though fears have eased up a little lately. Meta Platforms' plans for a $95 billion stock offering, announced on Monday, helped bring down its credit-default swap spreads. Those spreads had risen last week when the company reported negative free cash flow in the third quarter. Other CDS spreads had moved higher too, though they have since backed off.

Investors had expected Meta to bring a large bond deal to market shortly after its earnings announcement, said Richard Cheng, head of Nuveen's investment-grade corporate sector team. The fact that it wasn't announced came as a relief.

"Just the absence of the bond deal itself is a direct catalyst for AI-related spread tightening," he said.

A credit spread is the difference in the yield between the corporate bonds and Treasurys of similar maturities. When spreads tighten, it means investors are becoming more confident about the bond issuer.

The market action over the last few days shows that investors are recognizing that "credit fears may have been overblown," said CNBC contributor Paul Meeks, head of technology research at Freedom Capital Markets.

"I expect that these better feelings, maybe not good but better, may continue as companies announce their quarters over the next few weeks."

Still, spreads on CDS remain wider over the past year due to a surge of debt issuance and free cash flows turning negative across the AI space. Meta's CDS spread, for instance, is still up 177% year to date, while Amazon's spread has gained 129%.

"It's not necessarily fundamentals," said CreditSights analyst Jordan Chalfin. "It's more, I'd say, 80% driven by technicals and sentiment."

Alphabet and Amazon pose the next big hurdle for tech bonds as they update their capex plans and free cash flow forecasts. Microsoft's earnings are also due Wednesday, but the company has yet to issue any bonds to pay for its AI spending.

Both Amazon and Alphabet reported negative free cash flow in the second quarter and analysts expect that trend to continue.

Analysts expect Alphabet to report free cash flow of -$2.3 billion while spending $55.2 billion on capital expenditures in the third quarter, according to FactSet consensus estimates. Amazon is expected to report -$9.9 billion in free cash flow against capex of $58.7 billion.

S&P Global Ratings estimated in an August report that the hyperscalers will have negative free operating cash flow in 2026 and 2027.

More critical will be their outlooks, Cheng says. "The singular focus on the investors' minds is really what the capex guidance trajectory looks like across the hyperscaler space."

Meeks believes elevated capex is a sign of strong AI demand. The hyperscalers have "decided that with all the evidence they have — and they have more than you and me — that this is worthwhile spending, and not just worthwhile; it's required," he said.

CreditSights' Chalfin doesn't expect the hyperscalers to announce major new bond issuance around their earnings reports. Oracle's updates may be more critical for credit markets. The company has issued $117 billion in long-term debt and is clinging to an investment-grade credit rating of BBB-, the lowest level of investment grade above junk, according to S&P.

"It's the most important IG tech credit, just given how it's a bit more stressed relative to the A-rated names," he said. "It's trading more like a high-yield credit, even though it's IG, and so there's just a lot of investor concern on that one."

One wrinkle to the AI debt story: balance sheets don't reveal the whole picture. The companies are using complicated off-balance sheet arrangements for data centers and chip financing, and they aren't fully transparent, S&P Global said in a September report.

"There are commitments they are entering into, for example, into data center leases or purchase commitments on chips that aren't necessarily treated as debt," Mark Habib, digital infrastructure sector lead at S&P Global Ratings, said on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" Monday.

S&P is trying to provide the market with more visibility on those commitments "to give a fuller picture of what kinds of obligations they're actually entering into," he added.

Oracle aside, hyperscaler credit ratings are all comfortably above A levels — reflecting the fact that they have broadly diversified revenue streams, ample coverage for interest payments, and capacity to add leverage if they choose.

Nuveen's Cheng isn't concerned, pointing out that while there has been some credit repricing, there is no credit crisis.

"They continue to have exceptional credit profiles, strong cash generation liquidity," he said of the largest hyperscalers.

"The market is really not concerned about credit quality at this point," Cheng added. "It's really just the trajectory of the capex needs and the supply of debt to fund that. Both of those are pointing in one direction — and that's up."

Correction: This story has been revised to reflect that Oracle's investment-grade credit rating is BBB-, according to S&P. A previous version mischaracterized the company's credit rating.

#3024. It was a little close for comfort, but Sixers close road trip with narrow win vs. Bulls

Sometimes in an afternoon road game you got to be happy just getting out of there with a win. The Sixers narrowly defeated the Chicago Bulls 127-121 Sunday afternoon.

Jaylen Brown went for a team-high 29 points and seven rebounds on 11-of-22 shooting. Tyrese Maxey zoomed his way to 27 points on 9-of-16 shooting with seven assists.

Joel Embiid labored his way to a better outing, finishing with 18 points shooting 7-of-19 from the floor along with 10 rebounds, eight of them coming on the offensive end. LeBron James bounced back in a big way, putting up 22 points, a Sixers high, going 8-of-16 from the floor along with five rebounds and five assists. Josh Giddey and Matas Buzelis led the Bulls with 19 apiece.

The Sixers were again without Adem Bona and Dominick Barlow. Norm Powell was out for Chicago, but Nic Claxton made his first appearance for the Bulls in this one.

The Sixers opened the game trying to get Embiid going from the field, but he missed a three and a post-up on their first two possessions. Chicago didn't meet any resistance, starting the game 10-of-15 from the field. Embiid did grab an offensive rebound falling down and dove out of bounds to save a loose ball — the Sixers scored second-chance points on both of those opportunities. His first field goal was a putback of his own blocked shot.

Edgecombe carried over his strong performance from the night before. He forced a steal and a tough shot on back-to-back possessions for their first quality stops on the night and helped kickstart a 7-0 Sixers run. His second corner three of the night added to that run on the other end of the floor.

Nick Nurse subbed out LeBron and Brown first rather than the usual Maxey and Brown, at least momentarily. Embiid got a much more comfortable post-up in a more familiar lineup and once again put back his own miss before being subbed out at the next dead ball. Brown checked into the game about 30 seconds later.

It took a couple of minutes to get some results, but Jabari Walker did a lot good things in the 2:57 he played to close the quarter. He found a cutting Maxey down the baseline with a nice bounce pass but Maxey smoked the layup. A few possessions later, Walker grabbed an offensive rebound but also smoked the layup. Brown was able to get that offensive rebound and after getting his putback attempt blocked, he kicked the ball out to the perimeter where it was swung to Kentavious Caldwell-Pope for a three. KCP found Walker with a cut and he finally got on the board as well, helping the Sixers take a one-point lead after a high scoring first.

Brown started the game 1-of-5 on jumpshots, but was 4-of-6 to start the game at the basket. Walker continued to have really good hustle minutes, pulling down two much needed more offensive rebounds. After a slow start LeBron backed down Isaac Okoro and drew a foul on his hook shot for the and-1.

That really seemed to do the trick as LeBron scored eight of the Sixers' next 10 points. Brown got a tough pull-up to go, and after a long rebound he tried to hit LeBron with a touchdown pass that got broken up by Okoro. They were still able to find LeBron on the long ball as KCP stole it right back. LeBron then hit a three and got into the paint for both a floater and a trip to the line.

Embiid checked back into the game and had a layup attempt blocked and missed an easy one on the next trip down the floor. Maxey did a good job to get each other involved, getting himself open off an Embiid post-up. His drive on the next possession got Embiid open under the free throw line and he finally buried a midrange jumper. Maxey nearly put Josh Giddey on a poster, but got fouled and threw his attempt off the back of the rim.

Offensively, it was a good example of playing through your struggles for Embiid as he continued to post-up Chicago's smaller bigs, putting him in great position to grab his misses and lay it back in. He also hit another jumper from the free throw line, helping the Sixers stay up seven at the half despite the Bulls scoring eight straight points right at the basket.

That didn't carry over halves though as Embiid missed three jumpers to start the third as the Bulls ripped off seven straight. Maxey drilled a three to get the Sixers going and they seemed to settle back in. Embiid got himself an open reverse layup and Brown took advantage of a steal to get himself to the basket again.

Right after LeBron picked up a tech, Brown hit an acrobatic layup through a lot of contact, and had a reasonable gripe that he didn't get a foul called as well. Even without the foul, the Sixers' offense started to run pretty smoothly. Brown still got to the line of the following possession, Edgecombe drilled another three for his first points since the first, and Embiid made a good read to find LeBron open on the block.

This was definitely the Sixers' best offensive rebounding performance of the season. Walker was a big reason for that, but it was a team-wide effort. Dean Wade became the fifth Sixer of the night to pull down an offensive rebound and when the Sixers came up empty again, Walker helped pop the fall up long enough for Anfernee Simons to grab his first offensive rebound of the night.

Walker hit a three from the top of the key to punctuate the night he was having, which was good because the Sixers needed every point they could get. Just about everyone on Chicago was still able to get to the basket with ease. They shot 13-of-17 from the field in the third, ending the quarter on a 6-0 run to cut the Sixers lead to six.

Edgecombe got to the line for the first points of the fourth, but not before Brown missed two at the line to give the people of Chicago free hot dogs. Edgecombe had a big transition dunk, but left the game a few moments later after colliding with Giddey contesting a shot. Thankfully it was not a long trip to the locker room and he would eventually return to the game.

It remained a struggle to keep the Bulls down long enough to put the game away, but the Sixers did continue to go on spurts to keep themselves at arms' length. Brown hit a couple of threes as he had found his jumper. LeBron went for a poster as well but also had to settle for a trip to the free throw line. James also hit a fadeaway midrange a few moments later.

Embiid missed a couple more jumpers and had another blocked by Jalen Smith shortly after checking back into the game. KCP drilled a three for some momentary breathing room, but Caleb Wilson drilled his second three of the night to make it a one-possession game with three and a half minutes to go.

After trying to buy a couple of minutes for Brown and LeBron while Edgecombe made sure he was good to go, Nurse put all the starters back in out of his timeout. Embiid did a great job to grab another offensive rebound off a missed James jumper and flip it back in for the layup. He got to the line on the following possession, but Maxey had given Okoro an easy and-1 in between to keep the Bulls right there.

A LeBron drive gave Maxey open space to make up for it, and he did with a three for his first points of the quarter. The Bulls were in the bonus though and Edgecombe put Wilson on the line on a non-shooting foul. Giddey was able to find Matas Buzelis for another wide open dunk to once again cut it to a three-point game.

Brown was able to get to the line on the following possession, but the Sixers not only came up empty off a LeBron steal, but Embiid was called for a foul trying to grab the rebound, putting Smith at the line. Smith was unable once again to keep it a one-score game, splitting the pair, and the Sixers were able to win the game from the line from there. A win too close for comfort, but afternoon games can always be funky especially on the road, so a win nonetheless.

#3022. 5 things we learned from the Chiefs’ get-right game against the Jets

For the first part of this game, it felt like the Kansas City Chiefs might be heading for another disappointing outing — only this time, it wasn't against one of the better teams in the NFL; it was against the cellar-dwelling, lame-duck New York Jets.

Early on, a sinking fear set in that if the Chiefs couldn't take care of business against the Jets, this team's flaws ran deeper than we thought.

Thankfully, Kansas City woke up in the second half and, in the words of the GOAT Mitch Holthus, laid the hammer down.

Here are five things we learned from the Chiefs' 35-12 victory over the Jets.

Good teams look great against bad teams, and bad teams look bad against great teams.

Will they catch the Denver Broncos and win the AFC West?

But that's okay. After going 6-11 last year, you want to see a return to competitiveness from this team, especially if the franchise keeps heading in the right direction. But if we look in the mirror honestly, this is probably a Wild Card team.

A Wild Card team that could go on a run and surprise some people, but their margin for error against good teams isn't slim; they are starting at a deficit in enough areas that the Chiefs need to play perfect football to win against the cream of the crop in this league. It didn't used to be this way, and maybe it won't be again someday. But for now, that's who this team is.

Just before the half, up by two points, the Chiefs had a chance to take the lead 17-12. They trotted out their much-maligned placekicker, Harrison Butker, for a 56-yard field goal attempt. He, of course, missed it, because Harrison Butker is in his missing 50+ yard field goals era.

Thankfully for the Chiefs, a flag was thrown on the play—a member of the Jets lined up in the neutral zone. The refs moved the ball five yards closer, and Butker got a second crack at it, only this time, it was just barely in his trouble zone of 50+ yards. But if Butker is one thing, it's that he's consistent. As before, he booted the ball just wide of the goalpost, and the Chiefs went into halftime clinging to a narrow lead.

As he left the field, reporters asked head coach Andy Reid what he needed to see from Butker in the second half, and his response was simple. "I need to see them go in."

Now, that's about as close as you will ever get to the old ball coach throwing one of his players under the bus.

The fans booed Butker as he left the field.

After the game, Butker said that he understood the fans' frustration and that he is booing himself for missing these kicks.

We are at the point where the leash is too long, especially when you are trying to keep pace in a division race with Denver.

The Chiefs narrowly dodged a possible season-derailing injury to quarterback Patrick Mahomes when rookie standout edge rusher David Bailey Jr. blew past right tackle Jaylon Moore nearly untouched and hit Mahomes' arm as he threw the ball.

All of Chiefs Kingdom's hearts sank when they saw Mahomes get up off the turf clutching his arm in pain. Thankfully, early reports say the injury is mild.

The issue is that this is not the first time Mahomes has been hung out to dry by his linemen.

It's not the second or third. It's been a continuous process for the last few years — the Chiefs haven't been able to find the right guys to protect the greatest player in franchise history. Kansas City also can't field a fully capable receiving unit.

General manager Brett Veach's biggest priority has to be to protect Patrick Mahomes. His second priority should be to give Mahomes the weapons he needs.

Players haven't panned out as we hoped. But guess what, that's the job. Brett Veach is paid to get it right, and when I see Mahomes lying on the ground in pain like we did today, I can't say that he did.

On the Chiefs' first drive of the game, they faced third and one from their own 34-yard line, and to everyone's amazement, the Chiefs did something fans have been clamoring for. They lined up with backup quarterback Justin Fields under center to take the snap and hopefully run for a first down. Unfortunately, Fields was stopped short of the one yard he needed for a first down, and to make matters worse, he fumbled the ball away to the other team.

I could easily see Andy Reid pointing to this turnover in the future as a reason why they don't run QB sneaks, but here is the thing: even though the Chiefs fumbled the ball, it was still the right call to make.

Failure to execute should not be the reason you remove a play from your call sheet.

The Chiefs needed help at wide receiver before Xavier Worthy went down with a hamstring injury. Soft-tissue injuries like this can linger for the rest of the season, especially at wide receiver.

Reports say Brett Veach is trying to add a guy before this week's trade deadline. But one might not be enough. The Chiefs probably need at least two new wide receivers

#3011. Falcons – Bengals recap: Adios to hope

Seasons start to slip away, and in any other division, they can come to a very swift end. The Falcons losing to the Ravens wasn't a huge deal, but the Falcons losing to the Bears right after that was a big deal, because it put them at 2-4 and raised the specter that quality football teams were simply going to be too much for them. Atlanta tried to put that to bed by beating the 49ers, but after a 16-0 drubbing in the rain at the hands of the Buccaneers, it was beat the high-flying Bengals in Spain or sit at three games under .500 and in a weak position even in the ultra-weak NFC South.

The Falcons did not beat the Bengals, and did not come particularly close to doing so. After a spirited first quarter things started to go sideways and then kept going sideways, with the Bengals outscoring the Falcons 27-7 the rest of the way. The defense had a disastrous day against a very good Cincinnati offense, as we feared, but the offense repeatedly turned promising drives into nothing much with penalties. Special teams struggled on returns heavily again and Nick Folk may have punched his ticket out of town with another miss, and now the Falcons have lost four of their last five games. You have to give a ton of credit to a Bengals team that is currently red hot, but it would be a mistake to overlook the major role Atlanta's own repeated errors played in making this a rout.

It's difficult to see the rest of this season amounting to much based on the way Atlanta's been playing, even though they're absurdly right in the thick of a divisional race where not a single team has more than three wins. The Falcons are spiritually in deep trouble even if the math says they're very much still alive, given that they're 1-2 in the division thus far, have lost to every quality team they've faced save the 49ers and sleepwalking early season Packers, and putting lousy things on tape.

The Falcons in their first year under Ian Cunningham and Kevin Stefanski have shown some good instincts with talent acquisition and have resisted the urge to give away resources chasing a dream they shouldn't chase, which makes me cautiously optimistic about the foundation here. But with a thrifty offseason in the cards, it's not exactly a surprise that the Falcons have weaknesses that have mounted as the season went on, and their one risky bet on an aging kicker in Nick Folk has utterly failed. A team that was supposed to be more competent and disciplined after last year's frequent letdowns just committed 12 penalties in a single game, many of them back-breaking ones in the red zone. And so on.

There is bountiful cap space and enough draft picks in 2027 to make the meaningful upgrades this team needs, and this regime will have to show this is about growing pains rather than a deeper dysfunction with team-building and how this team is coached. We're not having a conversation about jettisoning anyone from the staff or front office a year after the most significant overhaul to this team's power structure in years, but we are talking about the Falcons clearly not being good enough for the ninth straight season. The franchise can't be too impatient—it has bit them in the ass over and over again during that stretch—but those of us who have been spending Sunday after Sunday after Sunday watching this cannot help but be weary of it. The urgency will be there for 2027, regardless of how Atlanta finishes this year; they are very clearly not talented enough top to bottom yet, and that won't change even if they end up atop this ghastly division somehow.

Shrinking this back down to the smaller screen of the weeks ahead, however, the Falcons have so much to fix it's fair to go into the Chiefs game expecting the worst. If they can survive that effort and get a win, get right with the bye, and hit the ground running, perhaps they can still make something of this season and conquer the South.

Me? I won't be indulging in those hopes anytime soon, and will instead take the rest of the season one week at a time with a hope of seeing signs of a team building something worthwhile and surprising me along the way. A 3-6 team that keeps getting rocked the way this Falcons team has over the past month-plus can't ask for more than that from its fans, who have invested hope in this team over and over again in a weakened division and gotten very little from it.

The Falcons have enough weapons that defenses have to account for that you can sometimes sneak a depth option into the end zone with basically no one looking. The Falcons did that earlier this year with Nick Muse's first career touchdown grab, and they did in Sunday with Charlie Woerner's first career touchdown reception as Penix rolled out and found him streaking toward the end zone for Atlanta's first touchdown. The Falcons can't go to that well all the time, but there are opportunities for Muse, Woerner, and others to make their mark in the red zone when things tighten up.

Michael Penix Jr. with the…wheels? The book on the Falcons offense is that Penix can't and won't move, which makes him easy to tee off on, but in this one he took off running repeatedly and wasn't afraid to roll away from pressure, resulting in prolonged plays and some surprisingly great scrambles. Penix finished the first half with 51 yards on just three attempts and would've had more on a fourth if not for a Matthew Bergeron hold, and he looked decisive and fast. If this is something Penix can threaten defenses with a couple of times per week, it changes the complexion of this offense.

Bijan Robinson is still a god, even when his usage is inconsistent. He had one bad, boneheaded play when he fumbled a tough catch out of bounds, but other than that he was patient, found holes, functioned as a useful receiving option, and generally did Bijan things all day long. He turned 25 touches into 147 yards and a touchdown, and should be more involved in the passing game in particular going forward, though ideally on fewer third and long screens.

Drake London's physicality is so fun to watch. He made a number of tough catches, as he so often does, but he also provided some key blocks and went into every yards after the catch opportunity looking to lower his shoulder into a defender. It was a quieter day in terms of yardage, but he was still the favored target for Penix and did a nice job with the balls sent his way.

Brandon Dorlus was still a bully on Sunday, even if he didn't get a ton of help, and he set up a nice LaCale London sack where Joe Burrow tried too long and too hard to keep the play alive. On a day where the pass rush was inconsistent at best, Dorlus, London, Gervon Dexter, and Zach Harrison came up with the plays of consequence. Unfortunately, the team was largely stonewalled off the edge.

Jessie Bates was one of the few defenders who did anything consistent on Sunday. He flew all over the field making tackles, often serving as the last line of defense between a good Bengals play and a potential touchdown.

Khalil Herbert is a solid returner who has been a useful runner and receiver in the limited opportunities he's had. He should be RB3 when Brian Robinson Jr. is back, and right now I think you could get him a couple more touches a game and have that be a positive for the offense.

Again, if you're looking to not give up on the season and see some consequential football, the NFC South has obliged. The Falcons may not truly be out of this thing even if they lose to the Chiefs next week, and a win may put them in a strong position. This division is amazing, and I don't mean that as a compliment.

Penix not seeing things well over the middle of the field and delivering substandard passes because of it is one of his great Achilles heels at the moment. In this one, he missed a defender breaking in on the ball and nearly threw a pick, and then threw a weak ball to Bijan that was well behind him and intercepted by a diving Bengals defender. The fact that he's also still struggling mightily when pressured—the second heel, and a significant one—means he has plenty to work on if he's going to take the next step and become a better, more consistent quarterback the Falcons are eager to invest in over the long haul. Those twin faults and some simple hiccups in accuracy cost him dearly against the Bengals.

I've long been a fan of Olamide Zaccheaus, as everyone who has been here a while knows, but the Falcons need alternatives to relying on him. Penix routinely overthrows him even when he's open—which has not been all that often—and he's been a net negative as a punt returner thus far. That's not all his fault by a long shot, but it's probably time to work in more Chris Blair, rely on a third receiver less, or both.

Multiple holds and false starts, quick pressures and blown blitz pickups, and overmatched blockers on screens killed the Falcons again on Sunday, a mix of preventable mistakes and shaky line play. Everything for this team flows from how well they can block, given Penix's struggles against pressure, how heavily they'd like to utilize the ground game, and how fond they are of screens, and performances like Sunday undermine basically all of that.

A.J. Terrell has never had much luck against Ja'Marr Chase. Very few do, to be fair, but Terrell once again got cooked by one of the league's best receivers in the first quarter on a 47 yard touchdown bomb from Joe Burrow. Chase simply fought his way by Terrell and outran him, making it one of the easier, more straightforward deep bombs you'll see completed in the NFL. While he had a great pass breakup working against Tee Higgins to close out the second quarter, he allowed nine catches for over 90 yards and two touchdowns in the first half, one of the roughest efforts of his career, and the bad times continued into the second half.

We knew this would be a tough day for the defense, but I was hoping it wouldn't be as tough as it was early. The Falcons allowed two touchdowns on two drives to the Bengals in the first and early second quarter, failing to pick up Ja'Marr Chase repeatedly and not getting much in the way of pressure. Only C.J. Henderson's heroic work in coverage and Jessie Bates hustling even slowed the Bengals down, but things got worse on the subsequent drive as Chase just worked A.J. Terrell, a Terrell penalty erased a Gervon Dexter sack, and Burrow hit Tee Higgins for a touchdown. The opponent was a tough puzzle to solve, of course, but Atlanta's defense has now looked lost in back-to-back weeks against an elite ground game and elite passing game. That's not reassuring.

The pass rush was MIA. Amarius Mims is a wall at right tackle, but the entire line held up and gave Joe Burrow time all day, and that time was fatal for one of the most accurate passers in the game. The return of James Pearce Jr. was a pretty quiet one, and the interior pressure we've been seeing from this team largely evaporated. Combined with a tough day from the secondary, that was not survivable.

Oh, and just for good measure, the run defense was a mess again. The Bengals provided big holes and Chase Brown made a bunch of decisive cuts en route to one of his stronger days of the 2026 season. Jeff Ulbrich and company are going to have to do a lot of work in the weeks to come.

I never get more annoyed than I do when the Falcons offensive line commits penalties in the red zone to ruin a promising drive, and they decided to really work my first nerve in the first quarter. Matthew Bergeron lost a rep and held to back the Falcons up ten yards, and then Jawaan Taylor's false start backed them up another five yards and effectively ruined any chance of the Falcons scoring a touchdown. Bergeron and Taylor both chipped in penalties later, too. In a shootout, those kinds of mistakes are very costly, and they were Sunday. 2

Tommy Rees has stretches where he's doing clever things and playing to Atlanta's strengths, and stretches where I think he must be out of his mind. The Falcons were curiously light on Bijan carries when he was averaging close to eight yards a carry in the first half—he had just eight totes—but Rees snapped out of it a bit in the second half and called an effective run game that was periodically undone by penalties outside of his control. Then the Falcons got backed up by another penalty and had a 3rd and 12 just outside of the red zone, which called for something past the sticks. Instead, they called a screen that seemed doomed to fail from the start and was indeed doomed to fail, setting up a Folk field goal try down two touchdowns that Folk missed.

Non-stop penalties took anything good about this game plan on both sides of the ball and undermined it over and over again. The Falcons were penalized 12 times on Sunday, and they gave the Bengals free yards, took yards away from promising drives in the red zone, and impacted starting field position throughout. For the Falcons to have had a real chance of winning this, they needed to play disciplined football and avoid catching a ton of flags, and the fact that they couldn't do so does much to explain why this was a 17 point game instead of a closer one.

It's time to cut ties with Nick Folk. The magic he had the past couple of years is gone, and he missed his first field goal inside the 40 in many moons (and over 100 attempts) against the Bengals when the Falcons were trying to close the gap down 31-17. At his age, unfortunately, these things seem unlikely to get better, and Atlanta should bring in a young kicker and see if they can catch lightning in a bottle the rest of the way. The season is in major trouble, anyways, so you may as well look to the future.

Bijan for accounting for so much of Atlanta's production offensively and providing a few moments of joy along the way. These have been tough to hand out.

The Falcons are a 3-6 team, and their play has largely reflected that record over the past month. We're now seen more than half a season of play from them and it's fair to suggest this is who they are.

It's the Kansas City Chiefs, who aren't operating at the height of their powers but are yet another quality opponent in a long string of them.

#3010. The Ryan Dunn effect is real, and the numbers are ridiculous

The Phoenix Suns have won two consecutive games, and confidence is slowly beginning to build. Much of that confidence stems from the team's newfound ability to play defense, something noticeably absent through the first six games of the season. Playing a shorthanded Orlando Magic team certainly helped, but for the first time all season, Phoenix held an opponent under 110 points. Two nights later, they followed that performance by holding the Houston Rockets, one of the NBA's most productive offenses, under 100.

One of the more pleasant surprises early this season has been the play of Ryan Dunn, who currently leads the Suns in three-point shooting at 53.8%. And while every three-pointer he knocks down strengthens his case for additional opportunities and minutes, it's his defense and rebounding that have truly stood out. Why? Because those have been, quite honestly, the two biggest deficiencies for this team.

Phoenix is undersized, and securing rebounds has been a persistent challenge. Dunn helps alleviate that problem through his athleticism, physicality, and willingness to pursue the basketball. He possesses the explosiveness to go up and meet a rebound at its highest point rather than standing around waiting for it to come to him. Defensively, he's been everything the Suns hoped he would be when they drafted him out of Virginia. His confidence is clearly growing, and you can see that same confidence developing among his teammates when he's on the floor.

Want to know how impactful Ryan Dunn has been? When Dunn is on the court, the Suns have a net rating of +24.1. When he's off the floor, that number plummets to -18.6. That's a staggering +42.7 differential, the second largest in the entire NBA behind only Alex Caruso. Dunn also leads Phoenix with a cumulative plus/minus of +40.

Those numbers are absurd, especially for a player whose offensive limitations were considered one of his biggest obstacles entering the league. And while we're still dealing with a relatively small sample size, the difference in how this team performs with Dunn on the court is becoming increasingly difficult to ignore.

The Suns are a completely different team when Ryan Dunn is playing. They're not world beaters by any stretch of the imagination, but what Dunn brings to the floor is precisely what made Phoenix so enjoyable to watch a season ago. The hustle, the grit, the tenacity, and the willingness to do the dirty work that doesn't always show up in the box score.

Those qualities helped transform last year's Suns into a team that was both likable and productive. And as Phoenix begins to rediscover that identity, Ryan Dunn is emerging as one of the players most responsible for bringing it back. His impact goes well beyond the numbers, although those numbers are becoming pretty damn difficult to ignore. Jordan Ott has spent the early season searching for combinations that work. At this point, the evidence suggests one thing is becoming increasingly clear. Ryan Dunn needs to be part of the equation.

The Federal Reserve Board on Thursday requested public comment on two proposals related to establishing a regulatory framework for Board-supervised payment stablecoin issuers under the GENIUS Act.

The first proposal would require that Board-supervised payment stablecoin issuers fully back their stablecoins with certain permissible reserve assets, such as short-term Treasury bills and certain other high-quality, liquid assets. The proposal would also establish standardized capital requirements to address certain credit and operational risks of payment stablecoin activities, as well as risk management standards, in accordance with the law. Separately, the proposal would introduce rules for Board-supervised firms that safekeep the assets backing payment stablecoins. It would also clarify the permissibility of stablecoin and related activities for Board-supervised banks.

The second proposal would establish a tailored application process for Board-supervised banks applying to issue payment stablecoins. These applicants would be required to submit a business plan and financial information, among other documents. The proposal would also create a process governing appeals, hearings, and final determinations for applications.

The comment period will close 60 days after publication in the Federal Register.

#3005. Browns Week 9 loss: Shedeur’s progress, weapons galore, season in balance at trade deadline

The NFL can be fun if your team is winning. However, if your team is losing, it can be stressful and cause friction within the fanbase. After a short winning streak, the Cleveland Browns are now on a short losing streak, falling to the New Orleans Saints in Week 9. For many, patience is running thin, but there is a lot to discuss:

It feels as if we've seen this movie play out before. Bad 1st or 2nd half from the quarterback, good 1st or 2nd half from the quarterback. With quarterback Deshaun Watson inactive, 2nd-year quarterback Shedeur Sanders got the start against the Saints. There was plenty of bad. Plenty of good. Sanders had some nice throws, including this one to wide receiver Jerry Jeudy, was one that many were impressed with:

As far as the negatives, Sanders had moments in which he held the ball longer than he should've; the 4th-and-goal miscue at the goal line was his fault as he went the wrong way and ran into guard Austin Barber, who was pulling.

Overall, Sanders played okay. With that being said, Watson will likely start next week after clearing concussion protocol already. It doesn't make sense for a QB change when the season isn't over and the quarterback who you started the season with hasn't given you a reason to bench him.

Everyone knew how special tight end Harold Fannin was last year during his rookie season. This year? He might be even better. This clip shows why.

These are the types of plays that make you jump out of your seat and yell things that aren't safe for work (in a positive manner).

Rookie receivers Denzel Boston and KC Concepcion also showcased how good they can be.

It prompted ESPN analyst Mina Kimes to tweet this.

For what it's worth, the Browns defense played better than they did last week against the Pittsburgh Steelers. However, it wasn't enough. After watching Los Angeles Rams defensive end Myles Garrett get three sacks in his first game back and watching defensive end Jared Verse not make an impact once again, have to wonder if the Browns were better off not trading Garrett at all.

Yes, Cleveland had five sacks, but some of the sacks weren't being finished that could have added to that number. The run defense was up and down. The tackling has to be better, but the reason for the tackling being poor has something to do with their aggressive style. The defensive tackles the Browns have aren't bad, but they are small. The size doesn't necessarily matter because smaller, compact tackles fit the scheme, but they need someone big who can help clog the running lanes.

It was an average game from the unit, but it feels like the defense let the offense down.

Let me put on my pessimistic outfit for a minute. The Cleveland Browns are 5-4. The team has somewhat exceeded expectations. However, going back home against the Houston Texans at 6-3 would be better than coming back at 5-4. If the team were to lose against the Texans, the season wouldn't be technically over, but November is when the contenders start to emerge.

The Browns aren't contenders this year, and that's fine. However, when you look at the landscape of the AFC, you start to wonder if the Browns missed their opportunity. People questioned whether or not this team would win a game after how bad opening week went but Cleveland has somewhat fixed that, leading to fan expectations.

The team has talent that you can get excited for, but it's hard to think about whether the Browns missed their opportunity with the Week 9 loss and the one to the New York Jets.

Granted, it's too early to tell, and Cleveland is still, technically, tied for the last AFC playoff spot.

The New Orleans Saints are not a good team. At all. They have some good players, but they could be in the market for a new head coach next season.

Myles Garrett got three sacks in his first game back, but Jared Verse can't get one in nine games.

The running game is inconsistent; what else is new.

If the Browns have to go tempo to avoid slow starts on offense, so be it.

I wouldn't pick up Jared Verse's 5th-year option at this point. He has to earn it.

Expect the Browns to be active at some point before the trade deadline on Tuesday.

#3001. Robinhood shares fall as crypto slump weighs on profits, offsetting gains in new businesses

Robinhood shares were down around 8% in pre-market trading on Wednesday as investors digested weaker-than-expected third-quarter earnings despite growth in options trading and prediction markets.

Here's how the brokerage performed in its quarter ended Sept. 30, compared with Wall Street estimates, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:

Robinhood's net income fell to $468 million, or 51 cents per share, from $556 million, or 61 cents per share, a year ago. Revenue represented a 12% increase from $1.27 billion in the same quarter last year.

Despite that gain, transaction-based revenue of $867 million came in below Wall Street estimates from StreetAccount of $879 million, putting focus on whether Robinhood can sustain momentum across its trading businesses and reduce its reliance on volatile market activity.

Robinhood has been diversifying its business as it tries to expand its brokerage app into a broader financial services platform. Options trading and event contracts have become increasingly important sources of transaction revenue, while the company has continued to invest in wealth management, subscriptions and other offerings.

Transaction-based revenue grew 19% from the same period last year to $867 million, driven primarily by a more than 500% increase in event contracts revenue. Additionally, options revenue grew 31% to $399 million and equities revenue rose 41% to $121 million.

Those gains were partially offset by cryptocurrency revenue, which fell 55% to $120 million.

Chief Financial Officer Shiv Verma told CNBC event contracts on crypto movements did well in the quarter, offering investors another way to express a view on crypto despite the slump in prices and spot trading.

Net deposits on the Robinhood platform totaled $15.7 billion for the quarter, equal to a 17% annualized growth rate based on total platform assets at the end of Q2 2026. Over the past year, net deposits totaled $71 billion, representing 21% growth compared with total platform assets at the end of Q3 2025.

—With reporting from CNBC's Robert Hum and Kate Rooney
