#2995. Grades: Lions’ defensive dominance overshadows OL struggles

In the standings, style points do not count. The Detroit Lions' 19-9 win over the Miami Dolphins counts the same as if the Lions had blown the Dolphins out 38-3.

But in our weekly report cards, we only talk style points. We examine the good and the bad, because life isn't really just a binary of wins and losses. So let's hand out some mediocre grades in the Lions' Week 9 victory.

Jared Goff wasn't exceptionally bad in this game, but there was probably more bad than good. He was put into some tough positions early with pressure coming from seemingly every angle. It's hard to fault him for the interception when his arm was hit while throwing, but Goff also didn't handle the pressure particularly well in this game.

There are two plays in which I think illustrate Goff's self-made struggles in this game. The first was Detroit's run-back of the CFL-like play with Amon-Ra St. Brown 15 yards behind the line of scrimmage. The play successfully distracted the Dolphins defense from aptly covering Jahmyr Gibbs' wheel route of the backfield, but Goff, under mild pressure, didn't make that throw and checked it down instead. Then, late in the game, the Lions faced a third-and-7 from the Dolphins 25-yard line. With a defender in his face, Goff tried to hit St. Brown on an out route. When at his best, Goff steps into that throw knowing he's going to get hit and delivers a perfect ball. On Sunday, feeling the effects of the pressure, Goff faded away and delivered a ball several feet beyond St. Brown's reach.

Again, not a horrible day from Goff, but below average certainly.

I thought the running backs did a decent job in pass protection, but there weren't any standout plays in which it felt like they created any yardage on their own. The Lions managed just 1.55 yards after contract on Sunday, the second-lowest mark of any team in Week 9.

This unit certainly wasn't helped by the offensive line for much of this game, but I still left the game wanting more from Jahmyr Gibbs and Sione Vaki.

Last week's "sidecar" formation—with two tight ends in the backfield—was so successful vs. the Vikings. On Sunday, it didn't seem to have the same effectiveness. There were several times it felt like the tight ends weren't getting the push they got last week, and I think that impacted both the run and pass game.

That said, Sam LaPorta was an effective receiver that I wish Detroit had targeted more. He caught four of his five targets for 32 yards—though he also had a false start penalty.

Jameson Williams' drop would've been costly had the Lions not followed it up with a successful fake punt. And he made up for it with a 31-yard grab and a 9-yard run. But it was really Amon-Ra St. Brown's afternoon. He was the team's best offensive player on Sunday, constantly finding room in the Dolphins' zone coverage. He finished with eight catches on 10 targets for 86 yards.

Christian Mahogany's violation of team rules proved to be costly, as Miles Frazier struggled in his first NFL start. But he was far from alone in his troubles along the front five. The Lions gave up a 35.5% pressure rate (11th highest of Week 9), but they did at least improve as the game went on:

Q1 pressure rate: 55.6%Q2: 37.5%Q3: 14.3%Q4: 28.6%

This has been an odd trend all year, as pointed out by our own Al Karsten:

Frazier and rookie right tackle Blake Miller were the worst offenders on Sunday. Miller allowed three pressures, according to PFF, and Frazier finished with the worst overall grade on the offense (44.1).

But they finished strong, and the Lions were again able to run the clock out on offense on the backs of their offensive line.

The Lions absolutely stalled the Dolphins' rushing attack, holding the Dolphins to just 77 yards and 3.7 yards per carry. Dolphins running back Ollie Gordon had his worst game since September by both rushing yards (55) and yards per carry (3.4). And as a team, the Dolphins had just a 23.8% success rate, ranking 27 out of 28 teams this week, and their 28.6% stuffed rate was third-highest.

While pressure was a little inconsistent with the front four (35.5%, 11th best this week), they came up in big moments. All of Detroit's three sacks happened in the second half, helping secure their lead.

But the biggest impact of all from this unit cannot be seen easily on the box score. The Lions defensive line helped produce five holding penalties that absolutely killed several Dolphins drives. And if we're being honest, they probably should have been called for at least a handful more.

Aidan Hutchinson was quietly dominant. Derrick Moore looked extremely promising in his first major action. And Alim McNeill continues to be an absolute force in the middle of the defense.

Without Jack Campbell, it was tough to know how this unit would respond. Consider me very pleasantly surprised. I think Malcolm Rodriguez has been quietly having a very solid year, and he built on that performance in this game. He led the team with eight tackles, was a force in the run game, and had an impressive punchout on a third-down pass, preventing a conversion.

Trevor Nowaske may be the most trustworthy coverage linebacker on the team right now. On 15 coverage snaps, he wasn't even targeted.

Derrick Barnes continues to be more up and down than the rest of the room. There are still some coverage lapses that are concerning, but this was one of his best games as a run defender, and he tallied a QB hit, as well.

The Lions are still clearly trying to figure some things out in the cornerback room, especially without D.J. Reed in this game. I think Rock Ya-Sin is slowly coming back into form, and he put up a strong performance against the Dolphins. But against this young Dolphins receiving corps, I was hoping for more out of the likes of Roger McCreary and Ennis Rakestraw. McCreary probably got the worst of it, credited by PFF as allowing four catches on seven targets for 49 yards—and he also allowed a deep completion that was luckily negated by a holding penalty.

That said, this is the best game the Lions have gotten from their safety duo. Brian Branch was quiet, but steady working near the line of scrimmage. And Chuck Clark was essentially flawless as the deep defender. His interception was an impressively athletic play, and his return put Detroit immediately into field goal range.

A lot going on in special teams this week. The good: Jake Bates was a perfect 5-for-5 on his kicks, Jack Fox dropped his one punt inside the 15-yard line, Fox converted a fake punt with a great throw to Tay Martin, and the coverage teams were fine.

However, Bates kicked one kickoff short of the landing zone and placed another kickoff in the end zone for a 35-yard touchback. Christian Izien committed a holding penalty that erased some good field position on punt return. And worst of all, the Lions allowed a massive 46-yard pass on a fake punt from Miami.

In the end, I think it all evens out for an average grade.

I think the coaching staff deserves a ton of credit for navigating an extremely difficult week. The emotions from Jack Campbell's traumatic injury could not be easy to process and get the team ready to go, but clearly the Lions found a successful balance. They opened Wednesday's meeting by putting football completely aside and talking through their emotions about Campbell. They downgrade Wednesday's practice to a walkthrough. Life was more important than football, and they believed they could turn the page with the remaining shortened week. And they did.

There's not much about the game in terms of play-calling, game management, or anything else that I had any issues with. I don't put much of the offensive issues on Drew Petzing, as clearly the offensive line losing their one-on-ones had the biggest impact on the struggles.

I supposed we can complain about Dan Campbell's decision to punish Christian Mahogany and how it hurt this team's ability to perform. But without knowing Mahogany's actions that caused the punishment, I cannot fairly judge whether it was the right decision. That said, I'm okay with the coaching staff erring on the side of upholding the strict culture here.

The two final rules are largely similar to the proposed rules from 2025. The Board also requested comment on a proposal to better capture differences in banks' business models to generate fee income.

The Board conducts stress tests to ensure that large banks are sufficiently capitalized and able to lend to households and businesses even in a severe recession. In December 2024, the Board announced it would modify the test to improve its resilience.

"The stress test is an essential component of our regulatory capital framework," said Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle W. Bowman. "Today's changes preserve its resilience by ensuring that it is transparent, granular, and risk-sensitive. The public will now have greater assurance that the risks banks take will be reflected appropriately in their stress test losses and their capital requirements."

The first final rule requires the Board to invite public input annually on the stress test scenarios and any material model changes. It also updates the framework that guides the design of the hypothetical scenarios and adopts the models that will be used for the 2027 stress test. In addition, the final rule makes several adjustments to the stress test calendar. The final rule also updates the global market shock component, which is a set of shocks to specific market components applied to banks with large trading books. These banks will now be tested against two global market shock components each year, and the Board will use the shock that produces the largest losses for each firm to calculate the firm's stress test results.

The second final rule requires the Board, when calculating stress capital buffer requirements, to average the results from the two most recent annual supervisory stress tests for firms subject to the stress test in both years. The Board will begin averaging stress capital buffer requirements in 2028 to ensure that only models incorporating public input are used in the calculation.

The proposal would request public comment on a revision to the Board's noninterest income model that would improve the stress test's ability to capture business model diversity across firms. If adopted, these adjustments would replace the current noninterest income model that projects each bank's fee income under stress. Comments are due 60 days after publication in the Federal Register.

Together, the changes are likely to reduce year-over-year volatility in capital requirements by approximately 50 percent and are not expected to materially affect aggregate capital requirements.

#2991. LIVE DISCUSSION: Brooklyn Nets at Dallas Mavericks, 7:30 PM ET

There was a time not so long ago when the Brooklyn Nets were among the teams hoping to land Cooper Flagg. I even spotted one optimist on the Long Island Rail Road wearing DIY jerseys celebrating that very possibility after the 2024 NBA Draft.

That pipe dream turned into a miracle for the Dallas Mavericks, a team that contended for a play-in spot, fell into the lottery, then landed the No.1 overall pick after having a 1.8% chance at it. There's no denying Brooklyn's disappointment when the pick fell the No.8, but Egor Dëmin has seen his own success early in his career for fans to at least feel good.

Sunday will be a stark reminder of where the Nets are. They're 2-7, they've dropped 118 games in the prior two years, and Houston is holding their pick. Rebuilding is one thing, compounding it with avoidable self-inflicted wounds is another. This is a young team and it's a long season, but you play to win the game.

They played on Saturday night and lost a game that they should've won. Point blank. Nolan Traore has been playing like a star and it continued with 19 points against Atlanta, but Jordi Fernandez benched him the entire fourth quarter.

"Mikel had those five straight points, and I just let him roll," Fernandez said after the game. "Because you cannot just keep taking them in and out. I think that when I was about to sub Nolan in, Mikel made two or three threes and a mid-range pull-up. So I thought that was the right thing to do. Was it right? I don't know. Obviously, Nolan did very well. They scored 18 and 19. So that's a very good contribution from your two point guards."

Perhaps the strangest part in it all? They're only one game out from a play-in spot. Mikel Brown Jr. is sitting this one out (back-to-back) alongside Egor Dëmin (bone bruise).

On the other side, Cooper Flagg, Kyrie Irving and the 5-4 Mavericks are coming off a 112-100 win over the Utah Jazz in NBA Cup play Friday night.

Where: American Airlines Center, Dallas, TX

OUT: Tarik Biberovic (right heel bursitis)

OUT: Dereck Lively II (right foot surgery)

OUT: Sergio de Larrea (right knee sprain)

"If they want to win, they'll need to slow down an old friend. Kyrie Irving is back after missing last year with an ACL tear. He's averaging 21 points a night and the shooting splits are quality enough, but HOW he's getting his buckets are a bit different than what we're used to. His field goal attempts inside of three feet are at the lowest mark of his career and his three point rate is at the highest of his career. Chances are that'll change the further he gets away from the injury, but it's certainly something to keep an eye on. Either way, Irving remains a magnetic scorer and a blast to watch when his game is on." – Brian Fleurantin

#2988. Falcons trade Jessie Bates to Jaguars

Fresh off their fourth loss in five games, the Atlanta Falcons will be a seller at the trade deadline, moving safety Jessie Bates to the Jacksonville Jaguars for a 2027 second round pick and 2028 fifth round pick. The team's huge free agency splash in 2023 is gone after a fantastic run in Atlanta that spanned about three-and-a-half seasons, and the Falcons are loading up to try and remake their roster in 2027.

Per Jonathan Jones, who I cited above, the Falcons will eat some of the contract to facilitate a move. That's not surprising given that they're going to be sitting on plenty of cap space next year and clearly want more early draft selections for next year and beyond. With Bates moving to Jacksonville, I'd have to expect that DeMarcco Hellams, Sydney Brown, or both will be taking on his snaps next to Xavier Watts, but we'll get more clarity on that in the week ahead.

For the moment, let's appreciate what Bates gave the Falcons while he was here. Few safeties in franchise history were more impactful than Bates, who had 14 interceptions, three interceptions returned for touchdowns, 11 forced fumbles, and a fumble returned for a touchdown in his time in Atlanta. While he was typically solid-to-excellent in coverage and provided sure tackling throughout his tenure, the big plays were why the Falcons signed him and the big plays were worth every penny. He was a game changing player who lifted lousy defenses and headline great ones, and it goes without saying that this will be a greatly diminished Falcons defense in 2026 without him. I'll miss watching him play for my favorite team, and I'm grateful we got to do so for the past four years.

The Falcons looked at the writing on the wall for their 2026 and clearly felt their chances of making a real run were not worth as much as the long-term lift they could get from another second round pick next year; time will tell as always whether that calculus was the right one. It will be incumbent on a front office that has had some promising signings and trades to make sure that trading away a safety as good as Bates doesn't come back to haunt them, but given that Bates will be a free agent in 2027, getting a second rounder and a future fifth for him is strong value despite how amazing he is.

In the short term, as I said above, I'd expect run for Hellams and Brown. Getting Brown back at safety full-time would free up snaps at the nickel for Mike Hughes, Billy Bowman, and Avieon Terrell, who seem likely to split that role going forward on most Sundays. The fact that the team has a bit of a logjam at the position and that Bowman is an extremely physical player means we could see a lot more rotation back there the rest of the season.

We wish Bates well in Jacksonville, thank him for the phenomenal plays and fond memories, and hope the Falcons can turn their new draft picks into players who can help to create the next great team in Atlanta.

#2985. Coinbase net income surges 66% in third quarter, benefiting from bitcoin investment gains

Coinbase Global earned third-quarter adjusted net income of $719 million, up 66% from $433 million a year ago, largely due to a recovery in the cryptocurrency market.

Coinbase said it earned $2.51 a share in the latest quarter, although it wasn't immediately clear if that compared with the 6-cent-per-share profit that Wall Street analysts had estimated. Revenue of $1.20 billion trailed the $1.233 billion expected by analysts polled by LSEG.

Net income at the San Francisco-based platform surged thanks to the value of its volatile cryptocurrency investment portfolio, which can swing wildly even when the composition of the underlying holdings are little changed.

The third quarter value of Coinbase's crypto investment portfolio climbed due to a resurgence in the digital asset market. The price of bitcoin — often used as a gauge for all crypto assets — rose 39% in the three-month period ended Sept. 30 and the flagship cryptocurrency recently changed hands at roughly $80,809.

In the third quarter, Coinbase deepened its push into non-crypto products and services, including artificial intelligence integrations for traders, tokenized real-world assets and prediction markets.

In July, VP of product Max Branzburg told CNBC that Coinbase would debut an "everything exchange" spotlighting tokenized stocks and other real-world assets, derivatives trading, prediction markets and early-stage token sales. The trading platform also introduced Coinbase for Agents in early October, supporting users that want to use ChatGPT, Muse or other AI agents to manage their portfolios or research and trade various assets.

Coinbase also expanded its prediction market offerings, making a wider range of event contracts available to users.

In the third quarter, prediction markets revenue grew to more than $200 million on an annual basis, while the number of traders on those markets increased 60% compared with the second quarter.

#2983. $6.3 billion Binance hack is largest crypto theft on record

Binance said Friday that a security incident impacted about $6.3 billion in client assets, with around $3 billion frozen on-chain, marking the largest crypto hack on record.

The company later added it began recovering assets impacted by the breach after pledging to cover losses using its Secure Asset Fund for Users, which the company created in 2018 as a protection for clients in the event of a hack.

It wasn't clear how the attack took place. The world's largest crypto exchange initially said the hack may involve "a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, which allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions." However, Co-CEO Richard Teng later said the attack involved a more complex process rather than the misuse of a single engineer's permissions.

The FBI said Friday it was aware of the incident and was in touch with "relevant public and private partners to understand the scope of the activity, evaluate ​potential impacts, ​and ⁠coordinate appropriate investigative steps."

It wasn't clear either who was responsible for the breach. But TRM Labs, a blockchain intelligence and AI investigations company, pointed to North Korean hackers as the potential culprits. "Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists, including the Bybit hack and the KelpDAO hack in April 2026: small Tornado Cash withdrawals funding an operator wallet, staging that began well before the theft, and signatures obtained in advance then executed in one burst," the company said in a post.

Blockchain data platform Chainalysis also said this appears "be the work of North Korean cybercrime group TraderTraitor. This group has repeatedly targeted the cryptocurrency industry, exchanges, DeFi protocols, and investors, to raise funds for the regime. We base our intelligence assessment on on-chain activity observed in the hours following the hack."

Binance temporarily suspended withdrawals while it overhauls its withdrawal security systems and has revoked the affected address authorizations, Teng said. The exchange is also working with law enforcement and blockchain intelligence firms to trace and recover the stolen funds, while deposits remain unaffected.

Binance co-founder Yi He said deposits remained unaffected and continued to operate normally, while the exchange was working on enhancements to its withdrawal service and related address controls. It expects to begin resuming withdrawal services within the next 48 hours.

"We have found no evidence of any wallet private key leak. We will share a detailed technical post-mortem once the investigation is complete and the facts are fully verified," Binance said.

The announcement followed moves by several crypto firms, including Circle Internet Group, Tether and Ripple, to freeze funds tied to the hack.

Exploits are not uncommon in the crypto space. In 2025, Bybit suffered roughly $1.5 billion in losses due to a hack. More recently, Bitget lost more than $350 million worth of digital assets in a cyber theft incident. Over the past several years, bad actors have also drained billions of dollars in crypto from decentralized exchanges.

This week's breach "proves our exact point in proposing regulations for crypto markets earlier this month," Michael Selig, chairman of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, said Friday in a CNBC "Squawk on the Street" interview. The U.S. derivatives regulator on Oct. 5 proposed a framework that would effectively put crypto exchanges under federal government oversight — after Congress failed to approve legislation to regulate the asset.

"The real issue here is that these are unregulated offshore exchanges, and they don't have the same sorts of safeguards that we have in our financial markets here in the United States. We want to offer a federal option to these exchanges to come and register with the CFTC, and they would be subject to the same sorts of cyber security safeguards that we have in our markets today," he said.

Bitcoin fell more than 4% to $77,187.60 on Friday as the hack weighed on crypto markets.

Circle CEO Jeremy Allaire said Thursday evening in a social media post that the company had frozen more than 800 million in USD Coin associated with the incident. USDT stablecoin issuer Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino also said in on X that his firm had frozen more than 1.5 billion of its stablecoin that may have been related to a potential breach.

Jack McDonald, Ripple's senior vice president of stablecoins, said it was actively freezing affected funds held in RLUSD, its U.S. dollar-backed stablecoin.

#2980. Sixers Bell Ringer: Offense carries Sixers as they hang on vs. Bulls

Bell Ringer Standings:Tyrese Maxey – 3.5VJ Edgecombe – 2Jaylen Brown – 1.5Joel Embiid – 1LeBron James – 1Anfernee Simons – 1

The bad news is the Sixers' defense looked like that of a veteran team closing a road trip with a Sunday afternoon game.

The good news is the offense was balanced and had bright spots in a 127-121 win over the Bulls in Chicago Sunday. The Sixers still hold the best record in the NBA at 9-2 and are 5-1 on the road to start the season.

The Bulls shot 52.3% from the field and were down one possession at multiple times late, but Jaylen Brown and the Sixers seemed to come away with big buckets and big stops when they desperately needed them.

Next up, the Sixers welcome Jayson Tatum and the Boston Celtics to town Tuesday night. No word if there will be any lamb chops and gravy served at Xfinity Mobile Arena.

Tyrese Maxey: 27 points, 7 assists, 4 rebounds

Nick Nurse mixed up the way he staggered his starters Sunday, opting to give Maxey an extended look with the second unit. There were nice moments, but some struggles as well. Playing Maxey more with Joel Embiid seemed to help both players. Embiid didn't have his most efficient night, but he was much better than he was in Cleveland.

It felt like an easy 27 points for Maxey, who seemed to take nothing but threes and shots at the rim. He tried to send Josh Giddey into the shadow realm with a dunk, but was fouled. He hit a big triple down the stretch off a ridiculous LeBron pass.

And, of course, he was a blur in transition.

Jaylen Brown: 29 points, 7 rebounds, 4 assists, 1 steal

Brown was excellent throughout this game. The way he attacks downhill with physicality has to be such a welcome sight for Sixers fans. His ability to make tough fallaways in the paint is elite. The footwork on this play is an example of what the ability to make those short fadeaways opens up.

This was another game where Brown simply made winning plays down the stretch. He made a couple big threes as the Sixers were leaking oil midway through the fourth. He also made four free throws and turned Giddey over in the final minute.

And two more stats: Brown had just one turnover and was a +8. Take that, nerds.

LeBron James: 22 points, 5 rebounds, 5 assists, 1 steal

Coming off his worst game as a Sixer against the Cavs, James didn't get off to a great start with a couple early turnovers. His second stint started with him settling for a midrange jumper while being guarded by Giddey.

From there, James stopped messing around.

LeBron was much more aggressive getting downhill, either finding teammates or finishing at the rim. It's crazy that at 41 he can still take over games for extended stretches.

I know he's played for a million years, but passes like this are still stunning.

An honorable mention here for Walker who's done a commendable job filling in for Adem Bona at the five. While there were sleepy moments throughout the day for the Sixers, Walker did what he always does — hustled, crashed the glass and brought energy.

He's been popping up here as an honorable mention on what feels like a nightly basis. At this point, he should be in a competition for backup five minutes when Bona is healthy.

#2978. Falcons reportedly trade safety Jessie Bates to Jaguars for two draft picks

The Atlanta Falcons have apparently decided to play for the future. A day after falling to the Cincinnati Bengals 34-17 in Madrid, the Falcons reportedly traded safety Jessie Bates to the Jacksonville Jaguars for two draft picks, according to ESPN.

Jacksonville will give up a 2027 second-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round pick in exchange for Bates.

The safety has a pretty lengthy history of success in the NFL. Though Bates has made just one Pro Bowl in his career, he's been selected to three All-Pro second teams. His most recent selection came last season, when he made 98 tackles for the Falcons.

Bates, 29, is having another excellent start in 2026. Through nine games, he's registered 60 tackles and three forced fumbles. He'll take those skills to an already-dominant Jaguars defense, which is allowing the second-fewest points per game.

It cost Jacksonville a heavy price, especially considering Bates is in the final year of his contract. Barring an extension, he'll be a free agent at the end of the 2026 season.

But Jacksonville can sense the current roster has Super Bowl upside. Thanks to a tough defense and explosive offense, the Jaguars are 6-2 coming out of Week 9. While other AFC teams have been impressive, the Jaguars might have the best all-around team in the league. The addition of Bates should only help bolster that claim.

For the Falcons, the move signals the team will likely play for 2027. After Sunday's loss to the Bengals, the Falcons dropped to 3-6 on the season.

With the playoffs unlikely, the Falcons will start selling off any player who won't play a significant role with the team moving forward. Bates was the first — and could be the biggest — name traded as the team shifts its focus to the future.
